abstract: A network based on splines is described. It automatically adapts the number of units, unit parameters, and the architecture of the network for each application.

paragraphs: This paper addresses classification problems where examples from different classes lie very close together. In these narrow regions, a useful decision boundary must separate nearby points while following potentially complicated shapes. The proposed network builds that boundary from locally trained flat segments, allowing different regions to receive their own separating rules.

Its basic component combines a local linear discriminator with Gaussian functions describing how nearby training data are distributed relative to the separating plane. This combination makes the component sensitive to both separation and locality. A modified perceptron learning procedure finds the separators, and a constructive algorithm adds components to the hidden layer for two-class problems.

The output combines these local decisions into a smooth boundary assembled from linear pieces. Preliminary results show successful separation in cases where standard multilayer perceptrons and nearest-neighbor classification have high training error. The stated finding concerns fitting difficult boundaries in the training data; its significance is that local geometric structure can make closely spaced classes easier to separate.
summary.tldr: A network of local separators learns complex, narrow class boundaries by combining simple decisions fitted to nearby data.

title: A Network of Localized Linear Discriminants

abstract: Hybrid connectionistfHMM systems model time both using a Markov chain and through properties of a connectionist network. In this paper, we discuss the nature of the time dependence currently employed in our systems using recurrent networks (RNs) and feed-forward multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs). In particular, we introduce local recurrences into a MLP to produce an enhanced input representation. This is in the form of an adaptive gamma filter and incorporates an automatic approach for learning temporal dependencies. We have experimented on a speaker(cid:173) independent phone recognition task using the TIMIT database. Results using the gamma filtered input representation have shown improvement over the baseline MLP system. Improvements have also been obtained through merging the baseline and gamma filter models.

paragraphs: Hybrid neural-network and hidden Markov speech recognizers represent time in two places: the Markov chain and the neural network. This paper examines the temporal behavior of recurrent networks and feed-forward multilayer perceptrons within such systems. Its practical focus is improving the input representation supplied to a multilayer perceptron.

The authors introduce local recurrent connections through an adaptive gamma filter. This adds a mechanism for learning temporal dependencies automatically, allowing the representation to incorporate information across time. The modification targets the neural-network side of the hybrid recognizer, where the form of the input influences the speech distinctions the network can learn.

Experiments use speaker-independent phone recognition on the TIMIT database. The gamma-filtered representation improves performance over the baseline multilayer perceptron, and combining the baseline and gamma-filter models also produces improvements. These findings support learning temporal structure within the input representation and show that the combined models can be useful together, even when the recognizer already includes a Markov model of time.
summary.tldr: An adaptive gamma filter learns temporal input dependencies and improves speaker-independent phone recognition in a hybrid neural-network/HMM system.

title: Learning Temporal Dependencies in Connectionist Speech Recognition

abstract: Whereas optical character recognition (OCR) systems learn to clas(cid:173) sify single characters; people learn to classify long character strings in parallel, within a single fixation . This difference is surprising because high dimensionality is associated with poor classification learning. This paper suggests that the human reading system avoids these problems because the number of to-be-classified im(cid:173) ages is reduced by consistent and optimal eye fixation positions, and by character sequence regularities. An interesting difference exists between human reading and optical character recog(cid:173) nition (OCR) systems. The input/output dimensionality of character classification in human reading is much greater than that for OCR systems (see Figure 1) . paragraphs: The paper examines an apparent puzzle in reading. The optical character recognition systems it discusses classify individual characters, while people can process long character strings during a single eye fixation. Recognizing several characters together appears to create a much larger classification problem, yet human reading handles this input in parallel.

The proposed explanation is that readers do not face every possible image of every possible string. Consistent, suitably placed eye fixations reduce the variety of visual inputs that need to be classified. Regularities in character sequences further reduce the effective range of patterns. These two sources of structure make the task more constrained than its raw dimensionality suggests.

The argument links eye placement and sequence structure to the difficulty of learning visual classifications. It suggests that the reading system's success depends partly on how its inputs are organized before and during recognition. The contribution is an explanation of how a seemingly high-dimensional task may become manageable through regularities in viewing and in the material being read.
summary.tldr: Consistent eye fixations and character-sequence regularities may make parallel recognition of long strings manageable for human readers.

title: Human Reading and the Curse of Dimensionality

paragraphs: The paper addresses the Bayesian problem of comparing alternative models. Estimating parameters within one model and assessing the relative probabilities of different models are distinct tasks. The authors emphasize that methods already useful for regression, prediction uncertainty, and hyperparameters face greater difficulties when applied to the second task.

Their proposed approach extends Markov chain Monte Carlo with a method called chaining. Its purpose is to estimate how probable different models are relative to one another. In the Bayesian setting described in the supplied text, parameter uncertainty is represented by distributions, with prior information combined with the likelihood of observed data to obtain a posterior.

The authors report effective relative-probability estimates and present results on a robot arm problem, comparing chaining with a standard Gaussian approximation framework. The contribution is a sampling-based route to model comparison within this probabilistic treatment of uncertainty. The stated comparison places the method alongside an established approximation, while the abstract’s main finding is that chaining makes these otherwise challenging probability estimates effective.
summary.tldr: Monte Carlo chaining extends sampling methods to estimate the relative Bayesian probabilities of competing models.

title: Bayesian Model Comparison by Monte Carlo Chaining

abstract: We investigate the behavior of a Hebbian cell assembly of spiking neurons formed via a temporal synaptic learning curve. This learn(cid:173) ing function is based on recent experimental findings . It includes potentiation for short time delays between pre- and post-synaptic neuronal spiking, and depression for spiking events occuring in the reverse order. The coupling between the dynamics of the synaptic learning and of the neuronal activation leads to interesting results. We find that the cell assembly can fire asynchronously, but may also function in complete synchrony, or in distributed synchrony. The latter implies spontaneous division of the Hebbian cell assem(cid:173) bly into groups of cells that fire in a cyclic manner. We invetigate the behavior of distributed synchrony both by simulations and by analytic calculations of the resulting synaptic distributions.

paragraphs: This paper studies a Hebbian cell assembly: a group of spiking neurons whose connections change through a timing-dependent learning rule. The rule is motivated by experimental findings. A short delay from a presynaptic spike to a postsynaptic spike strengthens the connection, while spikes occurring in the reverse order weaken it.

The analysis considers the interaction between changing synaptic connections and changing neuronal activity. Connections influence when neurons fire, and spike timing in turn influences the connections. The authors find several possible collective behaviors: neurons can fire asynchronously, synchronize completely, or exhibit what they call distributed synchrony.

In distributed synchrony, the assembly spontaneously separates into groups that fire in a repeating cycle. This provides a form of coordinated activity without requiring every neuron to fire together. The paper investigates that behavior through simulations and analytical calculations of the resulting synaptic distributions. Its contribution is to show how the coupled dynamics of timing-based learning and neural activation can support distinct patterns of coordination within an assembly.
summary.tldr: Timing-dependent synaptic learning can produce assemblies that split spontaneously into groups firing in a repeating cycle.

title: Distributed Synchrony of Spiking Neurons in a Hebbian Cell Assembly

abstract: We describe a unified framework for the understanding of structure representation in primate vision. A model derived from this framework is shown to be effectively systematic in that it has the ability to interpret and associate together objects that are related through a rearrangement of common "middle-scale" parts, represented as image fragments. The model addresses the same concerns as previous work on compositional representation through the use of what+where receptive fields and attentional gain modulation. It does not require prior exposure to the individual parts, and avoids the need for abstract symbolic binding.

A model derived from this framework is shown to be effectively systematic in that it has the ability to interpret and associate together objects that are related through a rearrangement of common "middle-scale" parts, represented as image fragments. The model addresses the same concerns as previous work on compositional representation through the use of what+where receptive fields and attentional gain modulation. It does not require prior exposure to the individual parts, and avoids the need for abstract symbolic binding.

paragraphs: The paper examines how a visual system can recognize relationships between objects built from shared parts arranged differently. It proposes a unified framework for representing visual structure in primate vision, then derives a model that can interpret and associate objects connected by these rearrangements.

The model represents parts as image fragments at an intermediate scale. Its receptive fields combine information about what appears with information about where it appears, while attention changes the strength of responses. Together, these mechanisms address the compositional problem: representing both the pieces of an object and their arrangement.

The stated result is effective systematicity: the model can connect related arrangements of common parts without requiring earlier exposure to each part individually. It also avoids requiring an abstract symbolic mechanism to bind parts together. This matters because it offers a way to explain structured visual representation using receptive fields and attentional modulation, with the demonstrated capability centered on relationships among rearranged image fragments.
summary.tldr: A visual model combines part identity, location, and attention to associate objects formed by rearranging shared image fragments.

title: A Productive, Systematic Framework for the Representation of Visual Structure

abstract: Recently, interest is growing to develop an effective communication in- terface connecting the human brain to a computer, the ’Brain-Computer Interface’ (BCI). One motivation of BCI research is to provide a new communication channel substituting normal motor output in patients with severe neuromuscular disabilities. In the last decade, various neuro- physiological cortical processes, such as slow potential shifts, movement related potentials (MRPs) or event-related desynchronization (ERD) of spontaneous EEG rhythms, were shown to be suitable for BCI, and, con- sequently, different independent approaches of extracting BCI-relevant EEG-features for single-trial analysis are under investigation. Here, we present and systematically compare several concepts for combining such EEG-features to improve the single-trial classiﬁcation. Feature combi- nations are evaluated on movement imagination experiments with 3 sub- jects where EEG-features are based on either MRPs or ERD, or both. Those combination methods that incorporate the assumption that the sin- gle EEG-features are physiologically mutually independent outperform the plain method of ’adding’ evidence where the single-feature vectors are simply concatenated. These results strengthen the hypothesis that MRP and ERD reﬂect at least partially independent aspects of cortical processes and open a new perspective to boost BCI effectiveness.

paragraphs: Brain-computer interfaces seek to turn brain activity into a communication channel, including for people with severe neuromuscular disabilities. This paper asks how to combine different measurements from EEG to improve classification of individual trials. It focuses on movement-related potentials and changes in spontaneous EEG rhythms associated with event-related desynchronization.

The authors systematically compare combination strategies using movement-imagination experiments involving three subjects. Features describe movement-related potentials, rhythm changes, or both. A straightforward strategy joins the feature vectors into one larger vector. Other strategies incorporate an assumption that the individual features reflect physiologically independent sources of information.

In these experiments, methods incorporating independence outperform simple concatenation. This supports the hypothesis that the two feature types capture at least partly independent aspects of cortical activity. The finding matters because the usefulness of combining measurements depends on how their relationship is represented, not merely on including more measurements. The reported evidence points toward a way to improve BCI classification within the evaluated setting.
summary.tldr: In movement-imagination experiments with three subjects, EEG feature combinations that assume physiological independence outperform simple feature concatenation.

title: Combining Features for BCI

abstract: In supervised learning scenarios, feature selection has been studied widely in the literature. Selecting features in unsupervised learning scenarios is a much harder problem, due to the absence of class labels that would guide the search for relevant information. And, almost all of previous unsupervised feature selection methods are "wrapper" techniques that require a learning algorithm to evaluate the candidate feature subsets. In this paper, we propose a "filter" method for feature selection which is independent of any learning algorithm. Our method can be performed in either supervised or unsupervised fashion. The proposed method is based on the observation that, in many real world classification problems, data from the same class are often close to each other. The importance of a feature is evaluated by its power of locality preserving, or, Laplacian Score. We compare our method with data variance (unsupervised) and Fisher score (supervised) on two data sets. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of our algorithm.

paragraphs: Selecting useful features becomes harder when class labels are unavailable to guide the choice. The paper proposes Laplacian Score as a filter method, meaning it evaluates features independently of a particular learning algorithm. This differs from wrapper methods that rely on a learner to assess candidate feature subsets.

The method judges a feature by its ability to preserve locality. Its motivation is that, in many classification problems, examples belonging to the same class tend to be near one another. A feature that preserves these local relationships may therefore retain useful information even when class labels are absent. The method can also be used in a supervised setting.

The authors compare Laplacian Score with data variance for unsupervised selection and Fisher score for supervised selection on two datasets. The experiments support the method's effectiveness and efficiency. The contribution is a feature-selection criterion grounded in local relationships among examples, with applicability across labeled and unlabeled settings. Its motivation relies on a common pattern in classification data, rather than a claim that nearby examples always share a class.
summary.tldr: Laplacian Score selects features by how well they preserve local relationships, independently of a learning algorithm.

title: Laplacian Score for Feature Selection

abstract: We extend radial basis function (RBF) networks to the scenario in which multiple correlated tasks are learned simultaneously, and present the cor- responding learning algorithms. We develop the algorithms for learn- ing the network structure, in either a supervised or unsupervised manner. Training data may also be actively selected to improve the network’s gen- eralization to test data. Experimental results based on real data demon- strate the advantage of the proposed algorithms and support our conclu- sions.

We develop the algorithms for learn- ing the network structure, in either a supervised or unsupervised manner. Training data may also be actively selected to improve the network’s gen- eralization to test data. Experimental results based on real data demon- strate the advantage of the proposed algorithms and support our conclu- sions.

paragraphs: The paper extends radial basis function networks to learn several correlated tasks simultaneously. The focus is on a setting where relationships among tasks can be incorporated into the learning approach. The authors present learning algorithms for this multi-task version of the network, making simultaneous training the organizing feature of the method.

Their algorithms also address learning the network structure. They develop both supervised and unsupervised ways to do this, providing alternative routes depending on the form of learning guidance available. Structure learning is therefore part of the proposed approach, alongside learning multiple tasks through the network.

The paper additionally allows training data to be actively selected with the aim of improving generalization to test data. Experiments on real data demonstrate advantages of the proposed algorithms and support the authors' conclusions. Taken together, the work connects three choices: learning correlated tasks jointly, learning the network's structure, and selecting training data actively. The stated empirical findings support this combination as an approach to multi-task RBF learning.
summary.tldr: The paper extends RBF networks to correlated tasks with structure-learning algorithms and optional active selection of training data.

title: Radial Basis Function Network for Multi-task Learning

abstract: We introduce a novel adaptive non-parametric anomaly detection approach, called GEM, that is based on the minimal covering properties of K-point entropic graphs when constructed on N training samples from a nominal probability distribution. Such graphs have the property that as N their span recovers the entropy minimizing set that supports at least = K/N (100)% of the mass of the Lebesgue part of the distribution. When a test sample falls outside of the entropy minimizing set an anomaly can be declared at a statistical level of significance = 1 - . A method for implementing this non-parametric anomaly detector is proposed that approximates this minimum entropy set by the influence region of a K-point entropic graph built on the training data. By implementing an incremental leave-one-out k-nearest neighbor graph on resampled subsets of the training data GEM can efficiently detect outliers at a given level of significance and compute their empirical p-values. We illustrate GEM for several simulated and real data sets in high dimensional feature spaces.

paragraphs: GEM detects anomalies by learning a region associated with nominal, or normal, observations. It is non-parametric, so the proposed detector is built from training-sample geometry. The central idea is to estimate an entropy-minimizing set covering a chosen proportion of the nominal distribution and treat observations outside that set as potential anomalies.

The construction uses entropic graphs containing K points from N training samples. Their stated limiting covering property connects the graph's span to a set containing at least the K/N fraction of the distribution's continuous part. The uncovered fraction determines the statistical significance level associated with declaring an observation anomalous.

For implementation, the authors approximate the target set through a graph's influence region. An incremental leave-one-out nearest-neighbor construction on resampled training subsets enables efficient outlier detection and empirical p-value computation. Examples on simulated and real datasets in high-dimensional feature spaces illustrate the method. The contribution connects a geometric representation of normal data with statistically interpretable anomaly decisions.
summary.tldr: GEM uses entropic graphs to estimate normal-data regions and detect outliers with significance levels and empirical p-values.

title: Geometric entropy minimization (GEM) for anomaly detection and localization

abstract: Extensive games are a powerful model of multiagent decision-making scenarios with incomplete information. Finding a Nash equilibrium for very large instances of these games has received a great deal of recent attention. In this paper, we describe a new technique for solving large games based on regret minimization. In particular, we introduce the notion of counterfactual regret, which exploits the degree of incomplete information in an extensive game. We show how minimizing counterfactual regret minimizes overall regret, and therefore in self-play can be used to compute a Nash equilibrium. We demonstrate this technique in the domain of poker, showing we can solve abstractions of limit Texas Hold’em with as many as 1012 states, two orders of magnitude larger than previous methods.

paragraphs: The paper develops a regret-minimization technique for solving large extensive games with incomplete information. Such games describe decisions made over time when players do not know everything relevant to the situation. Finding a Nash equilibrium becomes computationally demanding as the number of possible game states grows.

The central contribution is counterfactual regret, a quantity designed to exploit the game’s incomplete-information structure. The authors show that minimizing this quantity also minimizes overall regret. This connection makes counterfactual regret useful for equilibrium computation: through self-play, the technique can be used to compute a Nash equilibrium.

The practical demonstration concerns poker. The method solves abstractions of limit Texas Hold’em containing as many as one trillion states, a scale two orders of magnitude larger than previous methods. The fact that these are abstractions matters: the reported achievement concerns those game representations. Together, the regret connection and the poker demonstration show how a theoretically motivated objective can support equilibrium computation at substantially larger scales.
summary.tldr: Counterfactual regret links incomplete-information game structure to regret minimization, enabling self-play equilibrium computation for much larger poker abstractions.

title: Regret Minimization in Games with Incomplete Information

abstract: Speech dereverberation remains an open problem after more than three decades of research. The most challenging step in speech dereverberation is blind chan- nel identiﬁcation (BCI). Although many BCI approaches have been developed, their performance is still far from satisfactory for practical applications. The main difﬁculty in BCI lies in ﬁnding an appropriate acoustic model, which not only can effectively resolve solution degeneracies due to the lack of knowledge of the source, but also robustly models real acoustic environments. This paper proposes a sparse acoustic room impulse response (RIR) model for BCI, that is, an acous- tic RIR can be modeled by a sparse FIR ﬁlter. Under this model, we show how to formulate the BCI of a single-input multiple-output (SIMO) system into a l1- norm regularized least squares (LS) problem, which is convex and can be solved efﬁciently with guaranteed global convergence. The sparseness of solutions is controlled by l1-norm regularization parameters. We propose a sparse learning scheme that infers the optimal l1-norm regularization parameters directly from microphone observations under a Bayesian framework. Our results show that the proposed approach is effective and robust, and it yields source estimates in real acoustic environments with high ﬁdelity to anechoic chamber measurements.

We propose a sparse learning scheme that infers the optimal l1-norm regularization parameters directly from microphone observations under a Bayesian framework. Our results show that the proposed approach is effective and robust, and it yields source estimates in real acoustic environments with high ﬁdelity to anechoic chamber measurements.

paragraphs: Removing reverberation from speech requires identifying how a room changes the original sound. Blind channel identification attempts this without knowing the source signal, which creates ambiguities among possible explanations of the microphone recordings. The paper proposes an acoustic model intended to address these ambiguities while still representing real recording environments.

The model represents a room impulse response as a sparse finite impulse response filter, with relatively few active filter coefficients. Under this assumption, identifying a system with one source and multiple outputs becomes a least-squares problem with an l1 penalty. The resulting optimization is convex and can be solved efficiently with guaranteed global convergence.

The penalty parameters determine how strongly the solution favors sparsity. A Bayesian learning scheme infers those parameters directly from microphone observations, making their selection part of the method. Reported results show effective, robust source estimation in real acoustic environments, with high fidelity to measurements made in an anechoic chamber. The optimization guarantee applies to the formulated problem under the sparse response model.
summary.tldr: A sparse room-response model turns blind acoustic channel identification into convex optimization, with Bayesian learning selecting the sparsity penalties.

title: Blind channel identification for speech dereverberation using l1-norm sparse learning

abstract: We present a sparse approximation approach for dependent output Gaussian processes (GP). Employing a latent function framework, we apply the convolution process formalism to establish dependencies between output variables, where each latent function is represented as a GP. Based on these latent functions, we establish an approximation scheme using a conditional independence assumption between the output processes, leading to an approximation of the full covariance which is determined by the locations at which the latent functions are evaluated. We show results of the proposed methodology for synthetic data and real world applications on pollution prediction and a sensor network.

paragraphs: When several quantities are predicted together, their relationships can be part of the model. This paper studies Gaussian processes with dependent outputs and proposes a sparse approximation for them. The aim is to represent connections among output functions while approximating the full covariance structure that describes their joint variation.

The model builds those connections through latent functions, each represented by a Gaussian process. A convolution construction uses the latent functions to establish dependencies between outputs. The approximation then assumes conditional independence between output processes based on the latent functions, with the resulting covariance approximation determined by the locations where those functions are evaluated.

This construction makes the latent representation central to both dependency modeling and approximation. The evaluation locations help determine how the full relationship among outputs is summarized. The authors present results on synthetic data and on pollution prediction and a sensor network. These examples demonstrate the proposed methodology in both controlled data and applications involving multiple related quantities, illustrating the scope of the approximation framework.
summary.tldr: A latent-function construction yields sparse approximations for dependent-output Gaussian processes using a conditional-independence assumption.

title: Sparse Convolved Gaussian Processes for Multi-output Regression

abstract: The discovery of causal relationships between a set of observed variables is a fundamental problem in science. For continuous-valued data linear acyclic causal models are often used because these models are well understood and there are well-known methods to fit them to data. In reality, of course, many causal relationships are more or less nonlinear, raising some doubts as to the applicability and usefulness of purely linear methods. In this contribution we show that in fact the basic linear framework can be generalized to nonlinear models with additive noise. In this extended framework, nonlinearities in the data-generating process are in fact a blessing rather than a curse, as they typically provide information on the underlying causal system and allow more aspects of the true data-generating mechanisms to be identified. In addition to theoretical results we show simulations and some simple real data experiments illustrating the identification power provided by nonlinearities.

paragraphs: Discovering causal relationships from observed variables requires a model of how those variables are generated. Linear acyclic models are widely used for continuous data because their properties and fitting methods are well understood. However, actual relationships can be nonlinear, motivating a framework that can accommodate a broader range of mechanisms.

This paper extends the linear framework to nonlinear models with additive noise. Its key finding is that nonlinearity can provide information about the underlying causal system. Within the proposed framework, nonlinear relationships typically allow more aspects of the generating mechanisms to be identified, making their structure potentially useful for causal discovery.

The authors present theoretical results together with simulations and simple real-data experiments illustrating this identification power. The claim is qualified: nonlinearities typically help under the additive-noise modeling framework, rather than guaranteeing complete causal recovery from any dataset. The contribution is both a broader causal model and an explanation of how departures from linearity can improve what observations reveal about their generating process.
summary.tldr: Nonlinear additive-noise models can make more aspects of causal mechanisms identifiable from observed data.

title: Nonlinear causal discovery with additive noise models

abstract: We study pool-based active learning in the presence of noise, i.e. the agnostic setting. Previous works have shown that the effectiveness of agnostic active learning depends on the learning problem and the hypothesis space. Although there are many cases on which active learning is very useful, it is also easy to construct examples that no active learning algorithm can have advantage. In this paper, we propose intuitively reasonable sufficient conditions under which agnostic active learning algorithm is strictly superior to passive supervised learning. We show that under some noise condition, if the classification boundary and the underlying distribution are smooth to a finite order, active learning achieves polynomial improvement in the label complexity; if the boundary and the distribution are infinitely smooth, the improvement is exponential.

paragraphs: Active learning chooses which examples to have labeled from a pool of unlabeled data. This paper studies whether that choice reduces the number of labels needed when noise is present, the agnostic setting. The authors emphasize that the benefit depends on the problem and hypothesis space: some problems offer no advantage to any active-learning algorithm.

The paper gives sufficient conditions under which active learning is strictly better than passive supervised learning. The conditions concern noise, the classification boundary, and the underlying input distribution. Under the stated noise condition, finite-order smoothness of both the boundary and distribution yields a polynomial improvement in label complexity.

When the boundary and distribution are infinitely smooth, the reported improvement becomes exponential. This distinguishes two levels of regularity and their consequences for the value of selective labeling. The results identify settings where active learning has a provable advantage; they do not claim that smoothness is necessary or that every noisy classification problem benefits. Their significance is a conditional explanation of when label selection can substantially reduce supervision.
summary.tldr: Under stated noise and smoothness conditions, agnostic active learning achieves polynomial or exponential label-complexity improvements over passive learning.

title: Sufficient Conditions for Agnostic Active Learnable

abstract: The method of common spatio-spectral patterns (CSSPs) is an extension of common spatial patterns (CSPs) by utilizing the technique of delay embedding to alleviate the adverse effects of noises and artifacts on the electroencephalogram (EEG) classification. Although the CSSPs method has shown to be more powerful than the CSPs method in the EEG classification, this method is only suitable for two-class EEG classification problems. In this paper, we generalize the two-class CSSPs method to multi-class cases. To this end, we first develop a novel theory of multi-class Bayes error estimation and then present the multi-class CSSPs (MCSSPs) method based on this Bayes error theoretical framework. By minimizing the estimated closed-form Bayes error, we obtain the optimal spatio-spectral filters of MCSSPs. To demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method, we conduct extensive experiments on the data set of BCI competition 2005. The experimental results show that our method significantly outperforms the previous multi-class CSPs (MCSPs) methods in the EEG classification.

paragraphs: EEG classification must cope with noise and artifacts in recorded brain signals. Common spatio-spectral patterns extend common spatial patterns by using delay embedding, incorporating delayed signal information into the filtering approach. Although the spatio-spectral method had shown advantages, the version discussed in this paper was restricted to problems with two classes.

The authors extend it to multiple classes through a theory of multiclass Bayes error estimation. Their method, called MCSSPs, chooses spatio-spectral filters by minimizing an estimated Bayes error that has a closed-form expression. This ties filter selection to an estimate of classification error and supplies a shared objective for the multiclass problem.

The distinction between estimated and actual Bayes error matters: the filters are optimized according to the proposed estimate. Experiments on the BCI competition 2005 dataset report significantly better EEG classification than previous multiclass common spatial pattern methods. The contribution combines a multiclass error-estimation framework with a practical filtering method, and the reported evaluation supports the usefulness of that combination.
summary.tldr: A multiclass Bayes-error estimate guides spatio-spectral EEG filter optimization, improving classification over earlier multiclass spatial-pattern methods in reported experiments.

title: Optimizing Multi-Class Spatio-Spectral Filters via Bayes Error Estimation for EEG Classification

abstract: A non-parametric Bayesian model is proposed for processing multiple images. The analysis employs image features and, when present, the words associated with accompanying annotations. The model clusters the images into classes, and each image is segmented into a set of objects, also allowing the opportunity to assign a word to each object (localized labeling). Each object is assumed to be represented as a heterogeneous mix of components, with this realized via mixture models linking image features to object types. The number of image classes, number of object types, and the characteristics of the object-feature mixture models are inferred non-parametrically. To constitute spatially contiguous objects, a new logistic stick-breaking process is developed. Inference is performed efficiently via variational Bayesian analysis, with example results presented on two image databases.

paragraphs: This paper brings three image-analysis tasks into one probabilistic model: grouping similar images, dividing each image into objects, and associating words with those objects. It uses visual features and can also incorporate accompanying annotations when they are available. Connecting these tasks lets the model describe both the collection as a whole and the contents of individual images.

An important modeling assumption is that an object can contain a mixture of different visual components. Mixture models connect these components to object types, rather than requiring every object to have a uniform appearance. The model infers the number of image classes and object types, along with the feature mixtures, through a nonparametric Bayesian approach.

The authors also introduce a logistic stick-breaking process to form spatially contiguous objects, addressing the need for segments to occupy connected image regions. They use variational Bayesian inference for efficient computation and present examples from two image databases. The contribution is a unified way to connect collection-level organization, object segmentation, and localized words within the same analysis.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian model jointly groups images, segments objects, and links objects to words while inferring how many image classes and object types are needed.

title: A Bayesian Model for Simultaneous Image Clustering, Annotation and Object Segmentation

abstract: A sizable literature has focused on the problem of estimating a low-dimensional feature space capturing a neuron's stimulus sensitivity. However, comparatively little work has addressed the problem of estimating the nonlinear function from feature space to a neuron's output spike rate. Here, we use a Gaussian process (GP) prior over the infinite-dimensional space of nonlinear functions to obtain Bayesian estimates of the "nonlinearity" in the linear-nonlinear-Poisson (LNP) encoding model. This offers flexibility, robustness, and computational tractability compared to traditional methods (e.g., parametric forms, histograms, cubic splines). Most importantly, we develop a framework for optimal experimental design based on uncertainty sampling. This involves adaptively selecting stimuli to characterize the nonlinearity with as little experimental data as possible, and relies on a method for rapidly updating hyperparameters using the Laplace approximation. We apply these methods to data from color-tuned neurons in macaque V1. We estimate nonlinearities in the 3D space of cone contrasts, which reveal that V1 combines cone inputs in a highly nonlinear manner. With simulated experiments, we show that optimal design substantially reduces the amount of data required to estimate this nonlinear combination rule.

paragraphs: Understanding a neuron's stimulus sensitivity requires more than identifying relevant stimulus features. Researchers must also estimate how those features combine to determine its firing rate. This paper addresses that nonlinear mapping within the linear-nonlinear-Poisson encoding model, using a Gaussian process prior to represent a flexible family of possible response functions.

The Bayesian model provides uncertainty estimates as well as estimated responses. The authors use this uncertainty to choose stimuli adaptively, directing experiments toward observations that help characterize the nonlinear function. A method for rapidly updating hyperparameters through the Laplace approximation supports this experimental design procedure.

Applied to recordings from color-sensitive neurons in macaque V1, the method estimates responses across a three-dimensional space of cone contrasts. The estimates indicate strongly nonlinear combinations of cone inputs. In simulated experiments, adaptive design substantially reduces the data needed to estimate that combination rule. The response analysis and the simulated data-efficiency finding are distinct contributions.
summary.tldr: Gaussian process response models guide adaptive stimulus selection and reduce data requirements in simulated neural experiments.

title: Active learning of neural response functions with Gaussian processes

abstract: We provide rigorous guarantees on learning with the weighted trace-norm under arbitrary sampling distributions. We show that the standard weighted-trace norm might fail when the sampling distribution is not a product distribution (i.e. when row and column indexes are not selected independently), present a corrected variant for which we establish strong learning guarantees, and demonstrate that it works better in practice. We provide guarantees when weighting by either the true or empirical sampling distribution, and suggest that even if the true distribution is known (or is uniform), weighting by the empirical distribution may be beneficial.

We show that the standard weighted-trace norm might fail when the sampling distribution is not a product distribution (i.e. when row and column indexes are not selected independently), present a corrected variant for which we establish strong learning guarantees, and demonstrate that it works better in practice. We provide guarantees when weighting by either the true or empirical sampling distribution, and suggest that even if the true distribution is known (or is uniform), weighting by the empirical distribution may be beneficial.

paragraphs: When learning from sampled matrix entries, the pattern of observation matters. This paper studies weighted trace-norm learning under arbitrary sampling distributions. In particular, it examines what happens when the row and column of an observed entry are not selected independently, so the sampling distribution is not a product distribution.

The authors show that the standard weighted trace-norm can fail in that setting. They introduce a corrected variant and establish strong learning guarantees for it. This addresses a specific weakness in the original weighting approach: dependence between sampled row and column indexes can matter enough to require changing the method.

The guarantees cover weights based on either the true sampling distribution or its empirical estimate. The authors also report better practical performance for the corrected variant. A further suggestion is that empirical weighting may help even when the true distribution is known or uniform. That possibility makes the observed sampling pattern relevant beyond situations where it merely substitutes for unknown distributional information; the abstract presents this benefit as a suggestion, not a universal guarantee.
summary.tldr: A corrected weighted trace-norm provides learning guarantees when sampled row and column indexes may be dependent.

title: Learning with the weighted trace-norm under arbitrary sampling distributions

abstract: Many visual and auditory neurons have response properties that are well explained by pooling the rectified responses of a set of self-similar linear filters. These filters cannot be found using spike-triggered averaging (STA), which estimates only a single filter. Other methods, like spike-triggered covariance (STC), define a multi-dimensional response subspace, but require substantial amounts of data and do not produce unique estimates of the linear filters. Rather, they provide a linear basis for the subspace in which the filters reside. Here, we define a 'subunit' model as an LN-LN cascade, in which the first linear stage is restricted to a set of shifted ("convolutional") copies of a common filter, and the first nonlinear stage consists of rectifying nonlinearities that are identical for all filter outputs; we refer to these initial LN elements as the 'subunits' of the receptive field. The second linear stage then computes a weighted sum of the responses of the rectified subunits. We present a method for directly fitting this model to spike data. The method performs well for both simulated and real data (from primate V1), and the resulting model outperforms STA and STC in terms of both cross-validated accuracy and efficiency.

paragraphs: Some visual and auditory neurons respond in ways that are well described by pooling rectified outputs from several similar filters. Estimating only one filter with spike-triggered averaging misses this structure. Spike-triggered covariance identifies a multidimensional response subspace, but requires substantial data and supplies a basis for that space rather than unique estimates of the underlying filters.

The paper defines a subunit model with two successive linear–nonlinear stages. Its first filters are shifted copies of a shared filter, and all their outputs pass through identical rectifying nonlinearities. A second linear stage combines the resulting subunit responses using weights. These restrictions give the model a specific, shared structure that can be fitted directly to spike observations.

The fitting method performs well on simulated data and recordings from primate V1. The resulting model exceeds spike-triggered averaging and covariance in cross-validated accuracy and efficiency. The findings support directly estimating a structured collection of subunits when that architecture captures the response properties of the neurons being studied.
summary.tldr: Directly fitting shared, shifted neural subunits improves predictive accuracy and efficiency over spike-triggered averaging and covariance in the reported evaluations.

title: Efficient and direct estimation of a neural subunit model for sensory coding

abstract: We propose a scalable approach for making inference about latent spaces of large networks. With a succinct representation of networks as a bag of triangular motifs, a parsimonious statistical model, and an efficient stochastic variational inference algorithm, we are able to analyze real networks with over a million vertices and hundreds of latent roles on a single machine in a matter of hours, a setting that is out of reach for many existing methods. When compared to the state-of-the-art probabilistic approaches, our method is several orders of magnitude faster, with competitive or improved accuracy for latent space recovery and link prediction.

With a succinct representation of networks as a bag of triangular motifs, a parsimonious statistical model, and an efficient stochastic variational inference algorithm, we are able to analyze real networks with over a million vertices and hundreds of latent roles on a single machine in a matter of hours, a setting that is out of reach for many existing methods. When compared to the state-of-the-art probabilistic approaches, our method is several orders of magnitude faster, with competitive or improved accuracy for latent space recovery and link prediction.

paragraphs: This paper addresses how to infer hidden roles and latent structure in very large networks using a probabilistic model. The computational challenge is to retain useful information about network organization while making inference feasible at a scale that many existing methods cannot handle. The proposed approach combines a compact representation with efficient statistical learning.

Networks are represented as collections of triangular motifs. This succinct description is paired with a parsimonious statistical model and a stochastic variational inference algorithm. The three components work together: the representation summarizes network structure, the model expresses latent roles, and the inference procedure estimates that structure efficiently.

The authors report analyzing real networks with more than a million vertices and hundreds of latent roles on one machine within hours. Compared with state-of-the-art probabilistic methods, their approach is several orders of magnitude faster while achieving competitive or improved accuracy for latent-space recovery and link prediction. These findings show substantial computational gains without sacrificing accuracy in the reported comparisons.
summary.tldr: A triangular-motif representation and stochastic variational inference make probabilistic latent-role analysis feasible for million-vertex networks.

title: A Scalable Approach to Probabilistic Latent Space Inference of Large-Scale Networks

abstract: Typical blur from camera shake often deviates from the standard uniform convolutional assumption, in part because of problematic rotations which create greater blurring away from some unknown center point. Consequently, successful blind deconvolution for removing shake artifacts requires the estimation of a spatially-varying or non-uniform blur operator. Using ideas from Bayesian inference and convex analysis, this paper derives a non-uniform blind deblurring algorithm with several desirable, yet previously-unexplored attributes. The underlying objective function includes a spatially-adaptive penalty that couples the latent sharp image, non-uniform blur operator, and noise level together. This coupling allows the penalty to automatically adjust its shape based on the estimated degree of local blur and image structure such that regions with large blur or few prominent edges are discounted. Remaining regions with modest blur and revealing edges therefore dominate the overall estimation process without explicitly incorporating structure-selection heuristics. The algorithm can be implemented using an optimization strategy that is virtually parameter free and simpler than existing methods. Detailed theoretical analysis and empirical validation on real images serve to validate the proposed method.

paragraphs: Camera shake can blur different image regions by different amounts, especially when rotation produces greater blur farther from an unknown center. Recovering a sharp image therefore requires estimating a spatially varying blur operator. This paper develops a blind deblurring algorithm using ideas from Bayesian inference and convex analysis to handle that non-uniformity.

Its objective includes a spatially adaptive penalty coupling the unknown sharp image, blur operator, and noise level. As these estimates change, the penalty adjusts to local blur and image structure. Regions with severe blur or few prominent edges receive less influence, allowing regions with moderate blur and informative edges to guide estimation.

This automatic adjustment performs the selection of useful image evidence without explicit structure-selection heuristics. The authors describe an optimization strategy that is simpler than existing methods and virtually free of parameters requiring adjustment. Theoretical analysis and experiments on real images support the method, connecting its adaptive weighting mechanism to the practical challenge of recovering images affected by uneven camera shake.
summary.tldr: A spatially adaptive penalty guides non-uniform camera deblurring toward image regions with more informative edges and less severe blur.

title: Non-Uniform Camera Shake Removal Using a Spatially-Adaptive Sparse Penalty

abstract: Continuous-valued word embeddings learned by neural language models have recently been shown to capture semantic and syntactic information about words very well, setting performance records on several word similarity tasks. The best results are obtained by learning high-dimensional embeddings from very large quantities of data, which makes scalability of the training method a critical factor. We propose a simple and scalable new approach to learning word embeddings based on training log-bilinear models with noise-contrastive estimation. Our approach is simpler, faster, and produces better results than the current state-of-the art method of Mikolov et al. (2013a). We achieve results comparable to the best ones reported, which were obtained on a cluster, using four times less data and more than an order of magnitude less computing time. We also investigate several model types and find that the embeddings learned by the simpler models perform at least as well as those learned by the more complex ones.

paragraphs: Word embeddings represent words with continuous-valued vectors that can capture semantic and syntactic relationships. Learning strong embeddings from large datasets can require substantial computation, especially when the vectors have many dimensions. This paper targets that training cost while preserving the quality of the resulting word representations.

The authors propose training log-bilinear models with noise-contrastive estimation as a simple, scalable route to learning embeddings. They report that the approach is simpler, faster, and produces better results than the cited method of Mikolov and colleagues. The contribution ties the choice of training procedure to the practical feasibility of obtaining useful representations from large text collections.

The reported results are comparable to the best previously reported results, which used a cluster, while requiring four times less data and more than an order of magnitude less computing time. Comparisons among several model types also find that simpler models learn embeddings performing at least as well as those from more complex models. In these experiments, additional model complexity was therefore unnecessary for obtaining competitive embedding quality.
summary.tldr: Training log-bilinear models with noise-contrastive estimation produces competitive word embeddings with substantially less data and computation.

title: Learning word embeddings efficiently with noise-contrastive estimation

abstract: We model the joint clustering and outlier detection problem using an extension of the facility location formulation. The advantages of combining clustering and outlier selection include: (i) the resulting clusters tend to be compact and semantically coherent (ii) the clusters are more robust against data perturbations and (iii) the outliers are contextualised by the clusters and more interpretable. We provide a practical subgradient-based algorithm for the problem and also study the theoretical properties of algorithm in terms of approximation and convergence. Extensive evaluation on synthetic and real data sets attest to both the quality and scalability of our proposed method.

We provide a practical subgradient-based algorithm for the problem and also study the theoretical properties of algorithm in terms of approximation and convergence. Extensive evaluation on synthetic and real data sets attest to both the quality and scalability of our proposed method.

paragraphs: This paper treats clustering and outlier detection as one joint decision problem. It extends a facility-location formulation to determine both the groups in the data and which observations should be designated as outliers. Making these decisions together allows the selected clusters and exceptions to provide context for each other.

The authors identify three benefits of integration. The resulting clusters tend to be compact and semantically coherent, and they are more robust to perturbations of the data. Meanwhile, outliers become easier to interpret because their unusualness is considered in relation to the clusters. The groups therefore help explain the exceptions, while the selection of exceptions contributes to the groups’ quality.

The paper supplies a practical algorithm based on subgradients and examines its approximation and convergence properties. Evaluations on synthetic and real datasets support both the quality and scalability of the method. The overall finding is that a unified formulation can serve both tasks effectively, with theory addressing algorithmic behavior and experiments assessing the usefulness of the resulting clusters and outliers.
summary.tldr: Jointly selecting clusters and outliers produces coherent groups and contextualized exceptions through a scalable facility-location formulation.

title: On Integrated Clustering and Outlier Detection

abstract: Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) is a successful approach for sampling from continuous densities. However, it has difficulty simulating Hamiltonian dynamics with non-smooth functions, leading to poor performance. This paper is motivated by the behavior of Hamiltonian dynamics in physical systems like optics. We introduce a modification of the Leapfrog discretization of Hamiltonian dynamics on piecewise continuous energies, where intersections of the trajectory with discontinuities are detected, and the momentum is reflected or refracted to compensate for the change in energy. We prove that this method preserves the correct stationary distribution when boundaries are affine. Experiments show that by reducing the number of rejected samples, this method improves on traditional HMC.
originalAbstract: Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) is a successful approach for sampling from continuous densities. However, it has difficulty simulating Hamiltonian dynamics with non-smooth functions, leading to poor performance. This paper is motivated by the behavior of Hamiltonian dynamics in physical systems like optics. We introduce a modification of the Leapfrog discretization of Hamiltonian dynamics on piecewise continuous energies, where intersections of the trajectory with discontinuities are detected, and the momentum is reflected or refracted to compensate for the change in energy. We prove that this method preserves the correct stationary distribution when boundaries are affine. Experiments show that by reducing the number of rejected samples, this method improves on traditional HMC.

paragraphs: Hamiltonian Monte Carlo samples continuous distributions by simulating motion governed by an energy function. Non-smooth functions can make that simulated motion difficult to compute and harm sampling performance. This paper addresses the problem by drawing inspiration from physical reflection and refraction, where motion changes when a trajectory crosses an interface.

The authors modify the leapfrog discretization for piecewise continuous energies. The method detects where a simulated trajectory encounters a discontinuity and adjusts momentum through reflection or refraction to account for the energy change. Handling those encounters explicitly gives the simulation a way to respond to boundaries that its usual smooth-motion calculations do not accommodate well.

The authors prove preservation of the correct stationary distribution when the boundaries are affine. That boundary condition is part of the theoretical guarantee. Experiments show improved performance over traditional Hamiltonian Monte Carlo through fewer rejected samples. The paper thus combines a boundary-aware integration method with a correctness result for the stated setting and empirical evidence of improved sampling behavior.
summary.tldr: Reflecting or refracting momentum at energy discontinuities improves HMC empirically and preserves the target stationary distribution for affine boundaries.

title: Reflection, Refraction, and Hamiltonian Monte Carlo

abstract: Matrix factorization (MF) collaborative filtering is an effective and widely used method in recommendation systems. However, the problem of finding an optimal trade-off between exploration and exploitation (otherwise known as the bandit problem), a crucial problem in collaborative filtering from cold-start, has not been previously addressed.In this paper, we present a novel algorithm for online MF recommendation that automatically combines finding the most relevantitems with exploring new or less-recommended items.Our approach, called Particle Thompson Sampling for Matrix-Factorization, is based on the general Thompson sampling framework, but augmented with a novel efficient online Bayesian probabilistic matrix factorization method based on the Rao-Blackwellized particle filter.Extensive experiments in collaborative filtering using several real-world datasets demonstrate that our proposed algorithm significantly outperforms the current state-of-the-arts.

paragraphs: Matrix factorization is widely used for collaborative filtering, but an online recommender also has to decide what to learn about next. This becomes especially important during cold start, when recommendations must balance current estimates of relevance with opportunities to gather information about new or rarely recommended items.

The paper introduces Particle Thompson Sampling for Matrix-Factorization to combine those two aims automatically. It uses the Thompson sampling framework together with an efficient online Bayesian matrix-factorization method. A Rao-Blackwellized particle filter provides the probabilistic machinery for updating the model as recommendation feedback arrives, bringing uncertainty-aware decision making into the matrix-factorization setting.

This matters because choosing an item can both serve the user now and inform future recommendations. The algorithm treats that exploration–exploitation tradeoff as part of recommendation itself. Experiments on several real-world collaborative-filtering datasets report significant improvements over the compared state-of-the-art approaches. The stated findings support the combination of online Bayesian updates and Thompson sampling as an effective approach in those evaluations.
summary.tldr: Particle Thompson Sampling combines online Bayesian matrix factorization with exploration to improve recommendations on several real-world datasets.

title: Efficient Thompson Sampling for Online ￼Matrix-Factorization Recommendation

abstract: We propose a novel and efficient algorithm for the collaborative preference completion problem, which involves jointly estimating individualized rankings for a set of entities over a shared set of items, based on a limited number of observed affinity values. Our approach exploits the observation that while preferences are often recorded as numerical scores, the predictive quantity of interest is the underlying rankings. Thus, attempts to closely match the recorded scores may lead to overfitting and impair generalization performance. Instead, we propose an estimator that directly fits the underlying preference order, combined with nuclear norm constraints to encourage low--rank parameters. Besides (approximate) correctness of the ranking order, the proposed estimator makes no generative assumption on the numerical scores of the observations. One consequence is that the proposed estimator can fit any consistent partial ranking over a subset of the items represented as a directed acyclic graph (DAG), generalizing standard techniques that can only fit preference scores. Despite this generality, for supervision representing total or blockwise total orders, the computational complexity of our algorithm is within a $\log$ factor of the standard algorithms for nuclear norm regularization based estimates for matrix completion. We further show promising empirical results for a novel and challenging application of collaboratively ranking of the associations between brain--regions and cognitive neuroscience terms.

paragraphs: Preference completion estimates individualized rankings over a shared set of items from limited observations. This paper argues that numerical scores can distract from the quantity that matters for prediction: item order. Closely reproducing recorded scores may overfit, even when the desired outcome is simply to rank items correctly.

The proposed estimator fits preference order directly and uses nuclear norm constraints to encourage low-rank parameters. Apart from approximate correctness of the observed order, it makes no generative assumption about numerical scores. summary.tldr: A low-rank preference estimator fits partial ranking orders directly without assuming a generative model for numerical scores.

title: Preference Completion from Partial Rankings

abstract: We study a class of non-parametric density estimators under Bayesian settings. The estimators are obtained by adaptively partitioning the sample space. Under a suitable prior, we analyze the concentration rate of the posterior distribution, and demonstrate that the rate does not directly depend on the dimension of the problem in several special cases. Another advantage of this class of Bayesian density estimators is that it can adapt to the unknown smoothness of the true density function, thus achieving the optimal convergence rate without artificial conditions on the density. We also validate the theoretical results on a variety of simulated data sets.

Another advantage of this class of Bayesian density estimators is that it can adapt to the unknown smoothness of the true density function, thus achieving the optimal convergence rate without artificial conditions on the density. We also validate the theoretical results on a variety of simulated data sets.

paragraphs: Density estimation learns how probability is distributed across possible observations. This paper studies Bayesian estimators that build their representation by adaptively dividing the sample space into regions. Because the partition can adapt, the method belongs to a nonparametric class rather than requiring one fixed density shape.

The theoretical analysis asks how quickly the posterior distribution concentrates as evidence accumulates. Under a suitable prior, the authors establish concentration rates and show that, in several special cases, those rates do not depend directly on the dimension of the problem. The restriction to special cases matters: the result is not a general claim that dimension never affects density estimation.

A second finding concerns adaptation to the unknown smoothness of the true density. The estimators can achieve an optimal convergence rate without imposing the artificial density conditions discussed in the abstract. Simulated datasets provide validation of the theory. Together, the results explain when adaptive partitioning can offer both statistical efficiency and flexibility without requiring smoothness to be specified in advance.
summary.tldr: Adaptive Bayesian partition estimators achieve optimal convergence while adapting to unknown smoothness, with dimension-independent rates in several special cases.

title: Convergence rates of a partition based Bayesian multivariate density estimation method

abstract: In this work, we introduce interactive structure learning, a framework that unifies many different interactive learning tasks. We present a generalization of the query-by-committee active learning algorithm for this setting, and we study its consistency and rate of convergence, both theoretically and empirically, with and without noise.
originalAbstract: In this work, we introduce interactive structure learning, a framework that unifies many different interactive learning tasks. We present a generalization of the query-by-committee active learning algorithm for this setting, and we study its consistency and rate of convergence, both theoretically and empirically, with and without noise.

paragraphs: The paper introduces interactive structure learning as a common framework for multiple interactive learning tasks. The emphasis is on learning through interaction within a shared formulation. Bringing these tasks together allows the authors to study an algorithmic approach and its behavior across the framework, rather than treating every task as a separate problem.

Within this setting, the authors generalize query-by-committee, an active learning algorithm. The resulting structural version connects the choice of learning queries to the broader structure-learning framework. This is the paper's algorithmic contribution: adapting an existing active learning approach so that it can be studied in the newly unified setting.

The analysis examines consistency and rate of convergence, asking whether learning approaches the intended result and how quickly it progresses. The authors investigate these questions both theoretically and empirically, considering settings with noise as well as without it. The stated contribution combines a unifying formulation, a generalized algorithm, and an assessment of its learning behavior across those feedback conditions.
summary.tldr: Interactive structure learning unifies several interactive tasks and extends query-by-committee with theoretical and empirical analysis under noisy and noiseless feedback.

title: Interactive Structure Learning with Structural Query-by-Committee

abstract: Spatio-temporal action detection in videos is typically addressed in a fully-supervised setup with manual annotation of training videos required at every frame. Since such annotation is extremely tedious and prohibits scalability, there is a clear need to minimize the amount of manual supervision. In this work we propose a unifying framework that can handle and combine varying types of less demanding weak supervision. Our model is based on discriminative clustering and integrates different types of supervision as constraints on the optimization. We investigate applications of such a model to training setups with alternative supervisory signals ranging from video-level class labels over temporal points or sparse action bounding boxes to the full per-frame annotation of action bounding boxes. Experiments on the challenging UCF101-24 and DALY datasets demonstrate competitive performance of our method at a fraction of supervision used by previous methods. The flexibility of our model enables joint learning from data with different levels of annotation. Experimental results demonstrate a significant gain by adding a few fully supervised examples to otherwise weakly labeled videos.

paragraphs: Locating actions in video requires identifying both where an action occurs and when it happens. Training systems for this task usually requires manually drawing action boxes in every frame, which makes collecting training data expensive. This paper develops a framework that can learn from several kinds of annotation, including combinations of detailed and incomplete labels.

The model uses discriminative clustering and translates available supervision into constraints on its optimization. Those constraints can express a class label for an entire video, a marked time point, a small number of action boxes, or complete frame-by-frame boxes. This gives the different annotation types a shared role in training while preserving the information each provides.

Experiments on UCF101-24 and DALY report competitive detection performance using a fraction of the supervision required by previous methods. Adding a few fully annotated examples to weakly labeled videos also produces a significant improvement. The findings support collecting a mixture of annotation types as a useful way to train action localization systems.
summary.tldr: A unified action-localization model combines sparse and detailed video annotations to achieve competitive results with substantially less supervision.

title: A flexible model for training action localization with varying levels of supervision

abstract: Sensory processing is often characterized as implementing probabilistic inference: networks of neurons compute posterior beliefs over unobserved causes given the sensory inputs. How these beliefs are computed and represented by neural responses is much-debated (Fiser et al. 2010, Pouget et al. 2013). A central debate concerns the question of whether neural responses represent samples of latent variables (Hoyer & Hyvarinnen 2003) or parameters of their distributions (Ma et al. 2006) with efforts being made to distinguish between them (Grabska-Barwinska et al. 2013). A separate debate addresses the question of whether neural responses are proportionally related to the encoded probabilities (Barlow 1969), or proportional to the logarithm of those probabilities (Jazayeri & Movshon 2006, Ma et al. 2006, Beck et al. 2012). Here, we show that these alternatives -- contrary to common assumptions -- are not mutually exclusive and that the very same system can be compatible with all of them. As a central analytical result, we show that modeling neural responses in area V1 as samples from a posterior distribution over latents in a linear Gaussian model of the image implies that those neural responses form a linear Probabilistic Population Code (PPC, Ma et al. 2006). In particular, the posterior distribution over some experimenter-defined variable like "orientation" is part of the exponential family with sufficient statistics that are linear in the neural sampling-based firing rates.
