paragraphs: The paper examines how neural activity might represent uncertainty about the causes of sensory input. One debate asks whether responses encode individual samples or parameters of a probability distribution. Another asks whether activity relates directly to probabilities or to their logarithms. The authors show that these descriptions can be compatible within the same system.

Their central analytical result starts from a specific model: neural responses in visual area V1 are samples from a posterior over latent variables in a linear Gaussian model of images. Under that assumption, those responses also constitute a linear probabilistic population code. A sampling interpretation can therefore coexist with a population-level description of the represented distribution.

More specifically, the posterior over an experimenter-defined variable such as orientation belongs to the exponential family, with sufficient statistics that depend linearly on sampling-based firing rates. This explains how activity described as samples can also provide the quantities needed to describe a distribution. The result establishes compatibility under the stated model, rather than selecting a single universally correct account of neural coding.
summary.tldr: Under a linear Gaussian image model, sampling-based neural responses also form a linear probabilistic population code.

title: A probabilistic population code based on neural samples

abstract: Stein variational gradient descent (SVGD) was recently proposed as a general purpose nonparametric variational inference algorithm: it minimizes the Kullback–Leibler divergence between the target distribution and its approximation by implementing a form of functional gradient descent on a reproducing kernel Hilbert space [Liu & Wang, NIPS 2016]. In this paper, we accelerate and generalize the SVGD algorithm by including second-order information, thereby approximating a Newton-like iteration in function space. We also show how second-order information can lead to more effective choices of kernel. We observe significant computational gains over the original SVGD algorithm in multiple test cases.
originalAbstract: Stein variational gradient descent (SVGD) was recently proposed as a general purpose nonparametric variational inference algorithm: it minimizes the Kullback–Leibler divergence between the target distribution and its approximation by implementing a form of functional gradient descent on a reproducing kernel Hilbert space [Liu & Wang, NIPS 2016]. In this paper, we accelerate and generalize the SVGD algorithm by including second-order information, thereby approximating a Newton-like iteration in function space. We also show how second-order information can lead to more effective choices of kernel. We observe significant computational gains over the original SVGD algorithm in multiple test cases.

paragraphs: The paper develops a faster version of Stein variational gradient descent, or SVGD, a method for approximating probability distributions. SVGD improves an approximation by reducing its Kullback–Leibler divergence from a target distribution. Its updates take the form of gradient descent over functions in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space.

The proposed method adds second-order information to those updates. In ordinary optimization, such information describes curvature and can help determine how an update should respond to the shape of an objective. Here, the authors use it to approximate a Newton-style iteration in function space, extending the machinery used by the original SVGD algorithm.

Second-order information also informs the choice of kernel, another component of the approximation procedure. The authors show how it can lead to more effective kernel choices and report substantial computational gains over SVGD across multiple test cases. The contribution therefore has two connected parts: a curvature-informed update and a way to use the same information when choosing the kernel that supports it.
summary.tldr: A Newton-style extension of SVGD uses second-order information for updates and kernel selection, with computational gains in multiple tests.

title: A Stein variational Newton method

abstract: Many machine learning methods depend on human supervision to achieve optimal performance. However, in tasks such as DensePose, where the goal is to establish dense visual correspondences between images, the quality of manual annotations is intrinsically limited. We address this issue by augmenting neural network predictors with the ability to output a distribution over labels, thus explicitly and introspectively capturing the aleatoric uncertainty in the annotations. Compared to previous works, we show that correlated error fields arise naturally in applications such as DensePose and these fields can be modeled by deep networks, leading to a better understanding of the annotation errors. We show that these models, by understanding uncertainty better, can solve the original DensePose task more accurately, thus setting the new state-of-the-art accuracy in this benchmark. Finally, we demonstrate the utility of the uncertainty estimates in fusing the predictions of produced by multiple models, resulting in a better and more principled approach to model ensembling which can further improve accuracy.

paragraphs: Dense correspondence tasks require detailed visual matches, but human annotations for them have intrinsic inaccuracies. In DensePose, this makes the quality of supervision a central issue. The paper equips neural predictors to output distributions over labels, allowing them to represent uncertainty arising from annotation noise rather than producing only a single label prediction.

A key contribution is accounting for errors that vary together across the predicted field. The authors show that such correlated errors arise naturally in these applications and can be modeled by deep networks. This treats annotation uncertainty as structured information, giving the model a richer account of how labels can be unreliable.

The resulting models improve accuracy on the original DensePose task and establish a new state of the art on that benchmark. The uncertainty estimates also help combine predictions from multiple models, producing further accuracy gains. Thus, modeling supervision noise serves both the individual predictor and the process of deciding how to fuse several predictors.
summary.tldr: Modeling correlated annotation uncertainty improves DensePose predictions and provides a principled way to combine multiple models.

title: Correlated Uncertainty for Learning Dense Correspondences from Noisy Labels

abstract: We investigate the problem of learning category-specific 3D shape reconstruction from a variable number of RGB views of previously unobserved object instances. Most approaches for multiview shape reconstruction operate on sparse shape representations, or assume a fixed number of views. We present a method that can estimate dense 3D shape, and aggregate shape across multiple and varying number of input views. Given a single input view of an object instance, we propose a representation that encodes the dense shape of the visible object surface as well as the surface behind line of sight occluded by the visible surface. When multiple input views are available, the shape representation is designed to be aggregated into a single 3D shape using an inexpensive union operation. We train a 2D CNN to learn to predict this representation from a variable number of views (1 or more). We further aggregate multiview information by using permutation equivariant layers that promote order-agnostic view information exchange at the feature level. Experiments show that our approach is able to produce dense 3D reconstructions of objects that improve in quality as more views are added.

paragraphs: Reconstructing a new object’s dense 3D shape becomes easier when more views are available, but many methods use sparse representations or require a fixed number of images. This paper develops category-specific reconstruction from one or more RGB views of previously unseen object instances, with a representation designed to combine information across varying view counts.

For each view, the representation describes both the visible object surface and the surface hidden behind it along the line of sight. Predictions from different views can then be combined into one 3D shape through an inexpensive union operation. A two-dimensional convolutional network learns to predict these representations from the input images.

The model also exchanges information among views at the feature level using permutation-equivariant layers, so that this exchange does not depend on an arbitrary ordering of the inputs. Experiments show dense reconstructions whose quality improves as additional views are provided. The result supports both parts of the design: a representation that can be merged cheaply and learned features that can share evidence across views.
summary.tldr: A dense shape representation and order-agnostic feature exchange combine variable numbers of RGB views, with reconstruction quality improving as views are added.

title: Multiview Aggregation for Learning Category-Specific Shape Reconstruction

abstract: The predict-then-optimize framework is fundamental in many practical settings: predict the unknown parameters of an optimization problem, and then solve the problem using the predicted values of the parameters. A natural loss function in this environment is to consider the cost of the decisions induced by the predicted parameters, in contrast to the prediction error of the parameters. This loss function was recently introduced in [Elmachtoub and Grigas, 2017], which called it the Smart Predict-then-Optimize (SPO) loss. Since the SPO loss is nonconvex and noncontinuous, standard results for deriving generalization bounds do not apply. In this work, we provide an assortment of generalization bounds for the SPO loss function. In particular, we derive bounds based on the Natarajan dimension that, in the case of a polyhedral feasible region, scale at most logarithmically in the number of extreme points, but, in the case of a general convex set, have poor dependence on the dimension. By exploiting the structure of the SPO loss function and an additional strong convexity assumption on the feasible region, we can dramatically improve the dependence on the dimension via an analysis and corresponding bounds that are akin to the margin guarantees in classification problems.

paragraphs: In predict-then-optimize systems, a model estimates unknown parameters and an optimizer uses those estimates to choose a decision. Prediction errors matter through the decisions they induce. The Smart Predict-then-Optimize loss captures this decision cost, but its nonconvexity and discontinuity prevent standard generalization results from applying directly.

This paper develops several generalization bounds for that loss. One route uses the Natarajan dimension, a measure of learning complexity. When the feasible region is polyhedral, these bounds grow at most logarithmically with its number of extreme points. For general convex feasible sets, however, the same approach has an unfavorable dependence on dimension.

The authors then exploit the loss's structure together with an additional strong convexity assumption on the feasible region. Under that assumption, they substantially improve the dimensional dependence through an analysis resembling margin guarantees in classification. The findings show how properties of the downstream optimization problem affect statistical guarantees for decision-focused prediction, and why the geometry of feasible decisions matters alongside the prediction model.
summary.tldr: New generalization bounds for decision-based prediction loss reveal how feasible-region geometry controls statistical complexity.

title: Generalization Bounds in the Predict-then-Optimize Framework

abstract: Metric-based meta-learning techniques have successfully been applied to few-shot classification problems. In this paper, we propose to leverage cross-modal information to enhance metric-based few-shot learning methods. Visual and semantic feature spaces have different structures by definition. For certain concepts, visual features might be richer and more discriminative than text ones. While for others, the inverse might be true. Moreover, when the support from visual information is limited in image classification, semantic representations (learned from unsupervised text corpora) can provide strong prior knowledge and context to help learning. Based on these two intuitions, we propose a mechanism that can adaptively combine information from both modalities according to new image categories to be learned. Through a series of experiments, we show that by this adaptive combination of the two modalities, our model outperforms current uni-modality few-shot learning methods and modality-alignment methods by a large margin on all benchmarks and few-shot scenarios tested. Experiments also show that our model can effectively adjust its focus on the two modalities. The improvement in performance is particularly large when the number of shots is very small.

Based on these two intuitions, we propose a mechanism that can adaptively combine information from both modalities according to new image categories to be learned. Experiments also show that our model can effectively adjust its focus on the two modalities. The improvement in performance is particularly large when the number of shots is very small.

paragraphs: Few-shot image classification asks a model to learn new categories from very few labeled examples. This paper extends metric-based approaches by bringing together visual features and semantic representations learned from unlabeled text. The motivation is that images and language offer different kinds of evidence, and their usefulness can vary across categories.

The proposed mechanism adjusts how it combines the two modalities according to the new image categories being learned. Some concepts may be easier to distinguish visually, while others benefit more from semantic information. Text representations can also supply prior knowledge and context when the available images provide weak support. Adaptive combination lets the model vary its emphasis instead of assigning both sources a fixed role.

Across all benchmarks and few-shot settings tested, the authors report large improvements over single-modality methods and methods based on aligning modalities. Their experiments also show that the model changes its focus between visual and semantic information. The largest gains occur with especially few examples, supporting the usefulness of semantic context when visual evidence is scarce.
summary.tldr: Adaptively combining image features with text-derived semantics improves few-shot classification, especially when labeled examples are very scarce.

title: Adaptive Cross-Modal Few-shot Learning

abstract: Videos are a rich source of multi-modal supervision. In this work, we learn representations using self-supervision by leveraging three modalities naturally present in videos: visual, audio and language streams. To this end, we introduce the notion of a multimodal versatile network -- a network that can ingest multiple modalities and whose representations enable downstream tasks in multiple modalities. In particular, we explore how best to combine the modalities, such that fine-grained representations of the visual and audio modalities can be maintained, whilst also integrating text into a common embedding. Driven by versatility, we also introduce a novel process of deflation, so that the networks can be effortlessly applied to the visual data in the form of video or a static image. We demonstrate how such networks trained on large collections of unlabelled video data can be applied on video, video-text, image and audio tasks. Equipped with these representations, we obtain state-of-the-art performance on multiple challenging benchmarks including UCF101, HMDB51, Kinetics600, AudioSet and ESC-50 when compared to previous self-supervised work. Our models are publicly available.
originalAbstract: Videos are a rich source of multi-modal supervision. In this work, we learn representations using self-supervision by leveraging three modalities naturally present in videos: visual, audio and language streams. To this end, we introduce the notion of a multimodal versatile network -- a network that can ingest multiple modalities and whose representations enable downstream tasks in multiple modalities. In particular, we explore how best to combine the modalities, such that fine-grained representations of the visual and audio modalities can be maintained, whilst also integrating text into a common embedding. Driven by versatility, we also introduce a novel process of deflation, so that the networks can be effortlessly applied to the visual data in the form of video or a static image. We demonstrate how such networks trained on large collections of unlabelled video data can be applied on video, video-text, image and audio tasks. Equipped with these representations, we obtain state-of-the-art performance on multiple challenging benchmarks including UCF101, HMDB51, Kinetics600, AudioSet and ESC-50 when compared to previous self-supervised work. Our models are publicly available.

paragraphs: Videos contain visual, audio, and language streams that can provide supervision for one another. This paper uses those naturally available modalities to learn representations without labeled training videos. Its goal is a versatile network that can accept multiple modalities and provide useful representations for downstream tasks across them.

The authors investigate how to combine the streams while retaining detailed visual and audio representations and incorporating text into a shared embedding. They also introduce a process called deflation, which allows the networks to be applied to either videos or static images. These choices address versatility both across types of information and across forms of visual input.

Networks trained on large collections of unlabeled video are applied to video, video-text, image, and audio tasks. Compared with previous self-supervised work, the learned representations achieve state-of-the-art results on multiple benchmarks, including UCF101, HMDB51, Kinetics600, AudioSet, and ESC-50. The findings support learning from video’s multiple streams as a route to representations useful beyond a single modality or task.
summary.tldr: Self-supervised learning from video, audio, and language produces versatile representations for video, image, audio, and cross-modal tasks.

title: Self-Supervised MultiModal Versatile Networks

abstract: A convolutional neural network strongly robust to adversarial perturbations at reasonable computational and performance cost has not yet been demonstrated. The primate visual ventral stream seems to be robust to small perturbations in visual stimuli but the underlying mechanisms that give rise to this robust perception are not understood. In this work, we investigate the role of two biologically plausible mechanisms in adversarial robustness. We demonstrate that the non-uniform sampling performed by the primate retina and the presence of multiple receptive fields with a range of receptive field sizes at each eccentricity improve the robustness of neural networks to small adversarial perturbations. We verify that these two mechanisms do not suffer from gradient obfuscation and study their contribution to adversarial robustness through ablation studies.

paragraphs: Small adversarial changes to an image can challenge neural network perception. The paper investigates whether two mechanisms inspired by primate vision can improve resistance to these changes. Its motivation is the apparent stability of primate visual perception under small stimulus perturbations, while recognizing that the biological mechanisms responsible for that stability remain incompletely understood.

The first mechanism is nonuniform sampling, inspired by how the retina samples visual information unevenly. The second supplies multiple receptive fields of different sizes at each eccentricity, or position relative to the center of vision. Together, these mechanisms change how visual information is sampled and how much surrounding context is available at a location.

The authors demonstrate improved robustness to small adversarial perturbations and use ablation studies to examine the contribution of each mechanism. They also verify that the improvements do not arise from gradient obfuscation, which could make gradient-based attacks misleadingly ineffective. The findings support these particular biological design ideas as useful contributors to robustness, without establishing a complete explanation of robust primate vision.
summary.tldr: Retina-inspired sampling and multiple receptive-field sizes improve neural-network robustness to small adversarial perturbations in the reported studies.

title: Biologically Inspired Mechanisms for Adversarial Robustness

abstract: Humans flexibly solve new problems that differ from those previously practiced. This ability to flexibly generalize is supported by learned concepts that represent useful structure common across different problems. Here we develop a naturalistic drawing task to study how humans rapidly acquire structured prior knowledge. The task requires drawing visual figures that share underlying structure, based on a set of composable geometric rules and simple objects. We show that people spontaneously learn abstract drawing procedures that support generalization, and propose a model of how learners can discover these reusable drawing procedures. Trained in the same setting as humans, and constrained to produce efficient motor actions, this model discovers new drawing program subroutines that generalize to test figures and resemble learned features of human behavior. These results suggest that two principles guiding motor program induction in the model - abstraction (programs can reflect high-level structure that ignores figure-specific details) and compositionality (new programs are discovered by recombining previously learned programs) - are key for explaining how humans learn structured internal representations that guide flexible reasoning and learning.

paragraphs: The paper studies how people acquire reusable knowledge that helps them solve unfamiliar problems. Its experimental setting is a drawing task in which figures share underlying structure built from simple objects and composable geometric rules. This lets the authors examine whether learners discover procedures that transfer beyond the particular figures they have practiced.

People spontaneously learn abstract drawing procedures that support generalization. To explain this behavior, the authors develop a model that discovers reusable drawing programs. It is trained in the same setting as the human participants and constrained to produce efficient motor actions. Under these conditions, it discovers subroutines that transfer to test figures and resemble learned aspects of human behavior.

The results point to two organizing principles. Abstraction allows a drawing procedure to capture shared structure while ignoring figure-specific details. Compositionality allows new procedures to be built by recombining previously learned ones. Together, these principles offer an account of how structured internal representations could support flexible learning, with the drawing experiments providing evidence for that account.
summary.tldr: Human drawing behavior and a motor-program model support abstraction and recombination as mechanisms for learning reusable procedures.

title: Learning abstract structure for drawing by efficient motor program induction

abstract: Deep classifiers have achieved great success in visual recognition. However, real-world data is long-tailed by nature, leading to the mismatch between training and testing distributions. In this paper, we show that the Softmax function, though used in most classification tasks, gives a biased gradient estimation under the long-tailed setup. This paper presents Balanced Softmax, an elegant unbiased extension of Softmax, to accommodate the label distribution shift between training and testing. Theoretically, we derive the generalization bound for multiclass Softmax regression and show our loss minimizes the bound. In addition, we introduce Balanced Meta-Softmax, applying a complementary Meta Sampler to estimate the optimal class sample rate and further improve long-tailed learning. In our experiments, we demonstrate that Balanced Meta-Softmax outperforms state-of-the-art long-tailed classification solutions on both visual recognition and instance segmentation tasks.

paragraphs: Visual recognition datasets often contain many examples of some classes and few of others. This long-tailed distribution can create a mismatch between training and testing label frequencies. The paper identifies a specific consequence: ordinary Softmax produces biased gradient estimates under the long-tailed setup, affecting the learning signal used to train a classifier.

The authors introduce Balanced Softmax as an unbiased extension designed to accommodate this label distribution shift. They also derive a generalization bound for multiclass Softmax regression and show that their loss minimizes that bound. This connects the proposed change to an analysis of prediction performance beyond the training data, rather than relying only on experimental comparisons.

Balanced Meta-Softmax adds a complementary Meta Sampler that estimates an optimal sampling rate for each class. The combined approach adjusts both the learning objective and class sampling. In the reported experiments, it outperforms state-of-the-art long-tailed methods on visual recognition and instance segmentation. These results support addressing the distribution mismatch through both components within the evaluated tasks.
summary.tldr: Balanced Meta-Softmax combines a distribution-adjusted classification loss with learned class sampling to improve long-tailed visual recognition.

title: Balanced Meta-Softmax for Long-Tailed Visual Recognition

abstract: Multivariate Hawkes processes are commonly used to model streaming networked event data in a wide variety of applications. However, it remains a challenge to extract reliable inference from complex datasets with uncertainty quantification. Aiming towards this, we develop a statistical inference framework to learn causal relationships between nodes from networked data, where the underlying directed graph implies Granger causality. We provide uncertainty quantification for the maximum likelihood estimate of the network multivariate Hawkes process by providing a non-asymptotic confidence set. The main technique is based on the concentration inequalities of continuous-time martingales. We compare our method to the previously-derived asymptotic Hawkes process confidence interval, and demonstrate the strengths of our method in an application to neuronal connectivity reconstruction.

paragraphs: Multivariate Hawkes processes model streams of events across a network. Inferring connections from those streams requires more than a single estimated graph: researchers also need to quantify uncertainty in the inferred relationships. This paper develops a statistical framework for that purpose using a directed network whose relationships express Granger causality.

The authors construct a non-asymptotic confidence set for the maximum likelihood estimate of the network Hawkes process. Such a guarantee addresses uncertainty at finite sample sizes instead of relying only on behavior as the amount of data grows without bound. The main mathematical tools are concentration inequalities for continuous-time martingales, used to control fluctuations in the event-driven estimation problem.

The method is compared with a previously derived asymptotic confidence interval for Hawkes processes. An application to reconstructing neuronal connectivity demonstrates the strengths of the proposed approach. The contribution combines estimation with an explicit uncertainty statement, making the inferred network more informative than a point estimate alone. The causal interpretation is specifically the Granger-causal one supplied by the model.
summary.tldr: A finite-sample confidence-set method quantifies uncertainty in Hawkes-network estimates of Granger-causal relationships.

title: Uncertainty Quantification for Inferring Hawkes Networks

abstract: We extensively study how to combine Generative Adversarial Networks and learned compression to obtain a state-of-the-art generative lossy compression system. In particular, we investigate normalization layers, generator and discriminator architectures, training strategies, as well as perceptual losses. In contrast to previous work, i) we obtain visually pleasing reconstructions that are perceptually similar to the input, ii) we operate in a broad range of bitrates, and iii) our approach can be applied to high-resolution images. We bridge the gap between rate-distortion-perception theory and practice by evaluating our approach both quantitatively with various perceptual metrics, and with a user study. The study shows that our method is preferred to previous approaches even if they use more than 2x the bitrate.

paragraphs: Lossy image compression must balance the amount of stored information with the quality of the reconstructed image. This paper studies how to combine learned compression with generative adversarial networks to produce reconstructions that look pleasing and remain perceptually similar to their inputs. Its focus includes the relationship among bitrate, distortion, and perceived quality.

The authors examine several ingredients of the system together: normalization layers, generator and discriminator architectures, training strategies, and perceptual losses. They report an approach that works across a broad range of bitrates and can process high-resolution images. These properties make the contribution broader than a compression method demonstrated at only one operating point.

Evaluation includes both quantitative perceptual metrics and a user study, connecting theoretical concerns about compression and perception with observed preferences. Participants prefer the proposed method to earlier approaches even when those alternatives use more than twice the bitrate. The result indicates a substantial perceptual advantage in the reported comparisons: spending more bits did not make the compared reconstructions more appealing to users.
summary.tldr: A generative compression system produces perceptually strong reconstructions that users prefer even over alternatives using more than twice the bitrate.

title: High-Fidelity Generative Image Compression

abstract: The theory of discrete-time online learning has been successfully applied in many problems that involve sequential decision-making under uncertainty. However, in many applications including contractual hiring in online freelancing platforms and server allocation in cloud computing systems, the outcome of each action is observed only after a random and action-dependent time. Furthermore, as a consequence of certain ethical and economic concerns, the controller may impose deadlines on the completion of each task, and require fairness across different groups in the allocation of total time budget $B$. In order to address these applications, we consider continuous-time online learning problem with fairness considerations, and present a novel framework based on continuous-time utility maximization. We show that this formulation recovers reward-maximizing, max-min fair and proportionally fair allocation rules across different groups as special cases. We characterize the optimal offline policy, which allocates the total time between different actions in an optimally fair way (as defined by the utility function), and impose deadlines to maximize time-efficiency. In the absence of any statistical knowledge, we propose a novel online learning algorithm based on dual ascent optimization for time averages, and prove that it achieves $\tilde{O}(B^{-1/2})$ regret bound.

paragraphs: In some allocation problems, an action's result arrives only after a random delay that depends on the chosen action. Hiring for a task and allocating a server are examples in the abstract. Decisions must therefore account for elapsed time, completion deadlines, and how a total time budget is divided among groups.

The paper formulates this setting as continuous-time utility maximization. Different utility choices recover reward maximization, max-min fairness, and proportional fairness as special cases. It characterizes an optimal offline policy that divides time according to the selected fairness objective and uses deadlines to improve time efficiency. Fairness is thus defined through the utility function rather than imposed as one universal allocation rule.

When the relevant statistics are unknown, the authors propose an online algorithm based on dual ascent for time averages. They prove a regret bound of order B to the power of minus one-half, up to logarithmic factors, where B is the total time budget. This connects learning under action-dependent delays with explicit allocation preferences and provides a guarantee that improves as the time budget grows.
summary.tldr: A continuous-time allocation framework combines action-dependent delays, deadlines, and group fairness with an online algorithm that has a diminishing regret bound.

title: Group-Fair Online Allocation in Continuous Time

abstract: In an increasing number of AI scenarios, collaborations among different organizations or agents (e.g., human and robots, mobile units) are often essential to accomplish an organization-specific mission. However, to avoid leaking useful and possibly proprietary information, organizations typically enforce stringent security constraints on sharing modeling algorithms and data, which significantly limits collaborations. In this work, we introduce the Assisted Learning framework for organizations to assist each other in supervised learning tasks without revealing any organization's algorithm, data, or even task. An organization seeks assistance by broadcasting task-specific but nonsensitive statistics and incorporating others' feedback in one or more iterations to eventually improve its predictive performance. Theoretical and experimental studies, including real-world medical benchmarks, show that Assisted Learning can often achieve near-oracle learning performance as if data and training processes were centralized.

paragraphs: Organizations can benefit from one another's information while pursuing different prediction tasks, yet restrictions on sharing data and modeling methods often prevent direct collaboration. Assisted Learning proposes a framework for supervised learning in which organizations help one another without revealing their algorithms, underlying data, or even the tasks they are trying to solve.

An organization requests assistance by broadcasting statistics that relate to its task but are described as nonsensitive. Other organizations provide feedback, which the requesting organization incorporates into its own learning process. This exchange can happen once or over several iterations. Collaboration therefore proceeds through useful statistical feedback while each participant retains its own learning setup.

Theoretical and experimental studies, including medical benchmarks, indicate that the framework can often approach the performance of an oracle with centralized data and training. The qualification matters: near-centralized performance is reported as something frequently achievable, not guaranteed for every collaboration. The findings suggest that carefully structured assistance can recover substantial predictive benefits even when pooling the original learning resources is restricted.
summary.tldr: Assisted Learning lets organizations improve predictions through statistical feedback while keeping their data, algorithms, and tasks private.

title: Assisted Learning: A Framework for Multi-Organization Learning

abstract: Algorithm configuration procedures optimize parameters of a given algorithm to perform well over a distribution of inputs. Recent theoretical work focused on the case of selecting between a small number of alternatives. In practice, parameter spaces are often very large or infinite, and so successful heuristic procedures discard parameters ``impatiently'', based on very few observations. Inspired by this idea, we introduce ImpatientCapsAndRuns, which quickly discards less promising configurations, significantly speeding up the search procedure compared to previous algorithms with theoretical guarantees, while still achieving optimal runtime up to logarithmic factors under mild assumptions. Experimental results demonstrate a practical improvement.

paragraphs: Algorithm configuration searches for parameter settings that perform well across a distribution of problem instances. When the parameter space is very large or infinite, evaluating every candidate thoroughly is impractical. This paper studies how to discard weak candidates early while retaining a theoretical guarantee about the efficiency of the overall search.

ImpatientCapsAndRuns takes inspiration from practical heuristics that reject less promising configurations after only a few observations. Its central idea is to make this impatience part of a principled configuration procedure. By reducing the effort spent on candidates that appear uncompetitive, the method can devote the search more effectively to promising alternatives within a large pool.

Under mild assumptions, the procedure achieves optimal runtime up to logarithmic factors. It also significantly accelerates search compared with previous algorithms that provide theoretical guarantees, and experiments demonstrate a practical improvement. The result connects an aggressive early-discard strategy with a formal efficiency guarantee, extending attention beyond the small collections of alternatives emphasized in earlier theoretical work.
summary.tldr: ImpatientCapsAndRuns quickly rejects unpromising configurations while achieving optimal search runtime up to logarithmic factors under mild assumptions.

title: ImpatientCapsAndRuns: Approximately Optimal Algorithm Configuration from an Infinite Pool

abstract: Optimal transport (OT) is a powerful geometric and probabilistic tool for finding correspondences and measuring similarity between two distributions. Yet, its original formulation relies on the existence of a cost function between the samples of the two distributions, which makes it impractical when they are supported on different spaces. To circumvent this limitation, we propose a novel OT problem, named COOT for CO-Optimal Transport, that simultaneously optimizes two transport maps between both samples and features, contrary to other approaches that either discard the individual features by focusing on pairwise distances between samples or need to model explicitly the relations between them. We provide a thorough theoretical analysis of our problem, establish its rich connections with other OT-based distances and demonstrate its versatility with two machine learning applications in heterogeneous domain adaptation and co-clustering/data summarization, where COOT leads to performance improvements over the state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: Optimal transport compares distributions by assigning costs to moving between their samples. This requires a meaningful cost across the two datasets, which becomes difficult when they occupy different spaces. CO-Optimal Transport, or COOT, addresses this problem by considering correspondences between features alongside correspondences between samples.

The method jointly optimizes two transport maps: one linking samples and another linking their features. This retains individual feature information while learning how the two feature spaces correspond. It provides an alternative to methods that compare only within-dataset distances between samples or explicitly model feature relations beforehand. The two matching problems are treated as parts of one formulation.

The paper analyzes the resulting problem theoretically and establishes connections to other distances based on optimal transport. It also evaluates COOT in heterogeneous domain adaptation and in co-clustering or data summarization, reporting improvements over state-of-the-art methods in those applications. The findings illustrate how jointly matching the rows and features of datasets can make distribution comparison useful when a direct sample-to-sample cost is difficult to specify.
summary.tldr: COOT jointly matches samples and features, enabling transport-based comparisons across different spaces and improving two evaluated applications.

title: CO-Optimal Transport

abstract: In correlation clustering we are given a set of points along with recommendations whether each pair of points should be placed in the same cluster or into separate clusters. The goal cluster the points to minimize disagreements from the recommendations. We study the correlation clustering problem in the online setting., where points arrive one at a time, and upon arrival the algorithm must make an irrevocable cluster assignment decision. While the online version is natural, there is a simple lower bound that rules out any algorithm with a non-trivial competitive ratio. In this work we go beyond worst case analysis, and show that the celebrated Pivot algorithm performs well when given access to a small number of random samples from the input. Moreover, we prove that Pivot is robust to additional adversarial perturbations of the sample set in this setting. We conclude with an empirical analysis validating our theoretical findings.

paragraphs: Correlation clustering groups points using pairwise recommendations about whether they belong together or apart. The objective is to minimize disagreements with those recommendations. In the online version, points arrive individually and each cluster assignment is irreversible, making early decisions consequential before the full input is available.

A worst-case lower bound rules out any non-trivial competitive ratio for this online problem. The paper changes the information available to the algorithm by allowing a small number of random samples from the input. In that setting, the authors show that the Pivot algorithm performs well, moving the analysis beyond unrestricted worst-case inputs without extra information.

The guarantee also accounts for adversarial changes to the sample set: Pivot remains robust to additional perturbations in the studied setting. An empirical analysis supports the theoretical findings. The contribution is therefore conditional on access to sampled input information, showing how that modest additional resource can enable useful guarantees despite the original online problem's impossibility result.
summary.tldr: With a small random input sample, Pivot admits useful online correlation-clustering guarantees that remain robust to adversarial sample perturbations.

title: Robust Online Correlation Clustering

abstract: This paper introduces a concept of layer aggregation to describe how information from previous layers can be reused to better extract features at the current layer. While DenseNet is a typical example of the layer aggregation mechanism, its redundancy has been commonly criticized in the literature. This motivates us to propose a very light-weighted module, called recurrent layer aggregation (RLA), by making use of the sequential structure of layers in a deep CNN. Our RLA module is compatible with many mainstream deep CNNs, including ResNets, Xception and MobileNetV2, and its effectiveness is verified by our extensive experiments on image classification, object detection and instance segmentation tasks. Specifically, improvements can be uniformly observed on CIFAR, ImageNet and MS COCO datasets, and the corresponding RLA-Nets can surprisingly boost the performances by 2-3% on the object detection task. This evidences the power of our RLA module in helping main CNNs better learn structural information in images.

paragraphs: A convolutional network can reuse information from earlier layers to improve the features extracted by later ones. This paper describes that reuse as layer aggregation. DenseNet provides a familiar example, but concerns about redundancy motivate a lighter way to carry information through the depth of a network.

The proposed recurrent layer aggregation module, or RLA, uses the sequential arrangement of network layers. Recurrence operates along depth, allowing information from preceding layers to contribute to current feature extraction. The module is designed to be lightweight and compatible with established convolutional architectures, including ResNets, Xception, and MobileNetV2.

Experiments evaluate classification, object detection, and instance segmentation, with improvements reported across CIFAR, ImageNet, and MS COCO. For object detection, the abstract reports performance gains of two to three percent. The authors interpret these results as evidence that recurrent aggregation helps networks learn structural image information. The practical contribution is a reusable architectural component whose effectiveness is demonstrated across several vision tasks and network families.
summary.tldr: Recurrent layer aggregation efficiently reuses earlier-layer information and improves several convolutional architectures across image understanding tasks.

title: Recurrence along Depth: Deep Convolutional Neural Networks with Recurrent Layer Aggregation

abstract: Attention maps are popular tools for explaining the decisions of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for image classification. Typically, for each image of interest, a single attention map is produced, which assigns weights to pixels based on their importance to the classification. We argue that a single attention map provides an incomplete understanding since there are often many other maps that explain a classification equally well. In this paper, we propose to utilize a beam search algorithm to systematically search for multiple explanations for each image. Results show that there are indeed multiple relatively localized explanations for many images. However, naively showing multiple explanations to users can be overwhelming and does not reveal their common and distinct structures. We introduce structured attention graphs (SAGs), which compactly represent sets of attention maps for an image by visualizing how different combinations of image regions impact the confidence of a classifier. An approach to computing a compact and representative SAG for visualization is proposed via diverse sampling. We conduct a user study comparing the use of SAGs to traditional attention maps for answering comparative counterfactual questions about image classifications. Our results show that the users are significantly more accurate when presented with SAGs compared to standard attention map baselines.

paragraphs: An attention map highlights image pixels that matter to a classifier’s decision, but one map may hide alternative explanations. This paper investigates that multiplicity by using beam search to find several explanations for each image. The results show that many images admit multiple relatively localized explanations of their classification.

Simply displaying all those maps can overwhelm a viewer and obscure what they share. The authors introduce structured attention graphs to represent sets of maps compactly. These graphs show how different combinations of image regions affect classifier confidence, making common and distinct structures visible. A diverse sampling approach selects a compact, representative graph for presentation.

A user study compares these graphs with standard attention maps on comparative counterfactual questions about image classifications. Users shown the graphs answer significantly more accurately than users shown the attention-map baselines. The finding supports presenting relationships among multiple explanations when the goal is to help people reason about how changes in image evidence relate to a classifier’s decision.
summary.tldr: Structured attention graphs organize multiple image explanations and improve users’ accuracy on comparative counterfactual questions.

title: One Explanation is Not Enough: Structured Attention Graphs for Image Classification

abstract: Several problems in neuroimaging and beyond require inference on the parameters of multi-task sparse hierarchical regression models. Examples include M/EEG inverse problems, neural encoding models for task-based fMRI analyses, and climate science. In these domains, both the model parameters to be inferred and the measurement noise may exhibit a complex spatio-temporal structure. Existing work either neglects the temporal structure or leads to computationally demanding inference schemes. Overcoming these limitations, we devise a novel flexible hierarchical Bayesian framework within which the spatio-temporal dynamics of model parameters and noise are modeled to have Kronecker product covariance structure. Inference in our framework is based on majorization-minimization optimization and has guaranteed convergence properties. Our highly efficient algorithms exploit the intrinsic Riemannian geometry of temporal autocovariance matrices. For stationary dynamics described by Toeplitz matrices, the theory of circulant embeddings is employed. We prove convex bounding properties and derive update rules of the resulting algorithms. On both synthetic and real neural data from M/EEG, we demonstrate that our methods lead to improved performance.

This paper develops a hierarchical Bayesian framework intended to retain those relationships while making inference more efficient.

The result is a structured approach to inference that addresses temporal dependence in both the signal parameters and the noise.
summary.tldr: A structured Bayesian framework models spatial and temporal dependencies in signals and noise while enabling efficient inference with convergence guarantees.

title: Efficient hierarchical Bayesian inference for spatio-temporal regression models in neuroimaging

abstract: We initiate an investigation of private sampling from distributions. Given a dataset with $n$ independent observations from an unknown distribution $P$, a sampling algorithm must output a single observation from a distribution that is close in total variation distance to $P$ while satisfying differential privacy. Sampling abstracts the goal of generating small amounts of realistic-looking data. We provide tight upper and lower bounds for the dataset size needed for this task for three natural families of distributions: arbitrary distributions on $\{1,\ldots ,k\}$, arbitrary product distributions on $\{0,1\}^d$, and product distributions on on $\{0,1\}^d$ with bias in each coordinate bounded away from 0 and 1. We demonstrate that, in some parameter regimes, private sampling requires asymptotically fewer observations than learning a description of $P$ nonprivately; in other regimes, however, private sampling proves to be as difficult as private learning. Notably, for some classes of distributions, the overhead in the number of observations needed for private learning compared to non-private learning is completely captured by the number of observations needed for private sampling.

paragraphs: This paper asks how much data is needed to generate one realistic observation while protecting the individuals in the dataset. The input consists of independent samples from an unknown distribution. The algorithm must satisfy differential privacy and produce an output whose distribution is close to the original distribution in total variation distance.

The authors establish tight upper and lower bounds on the required dataset size for three distribution families. These are arbitrary distributions over a finite set, product distributions over binary vectors, and binary product distributions whose coordinate probabilities stay away from zero and one. Matching bounds identify how much data the sampling task requires within these settings.

The comparison with distribution learning reveals two different regimes. Sometimes private sampling needs asymptotically fewer observations than even nonprivate learning of a distribution description. Elsewhere, sampling is as difficult as private learning. For some distribution classes, the sample requirement for private sampling fully captures the extra observations that privacy adds to learning. Thus generating a small amount of data has its own statistical demands, distinct from learning a complete distribution.
summary.tldr: Tight sample bounds show when generating one differentially private observation is easier than learning its underlying distribution.

title: Differentially Private Sampling from Distributions

abstract: The existence of adversarial examples poses concerns for the robustness of convolutional neural networks (CNN), for which a popular hypothesis is about the frequency bias phenomenon: CNNs rely more on high-frequency components (HFC) for classification than humans, which causes the brittleness of CNNs. However, most previous works manually select and roughly divide the image frequency spectrum and conduct qualitative analysis. In this work, we introduce Shapley value, a metric of cooperative game theory, into the frequency domain and propose to quantify the positive (negative) impact of every frequency component of data on CNNs. Based on the Shapley value, we quantify the impact in a fine-grained way and show intriguing instance disparity. Statistically, we investigate adversarial training(AT) and the adversarial attack in the frequency domain. The observations motivate us to perform an in-depth analysis and lead to multiple novel hypotheses about i) the cause of adversarial robustness of the AT model; ii) the fairness problem of AT between different classes in the same dataset; iii) the attack bias on different frequency components. Finally, we propose a Shapley-value guided data augmentation technique for improving the robustness. Experimental results on image classification benchmarks show its effectiveness.

paragraphs: One explanation for convolutional networks' vulnerability to adversarial examples is their reliance on high-frequency image information. Earlier frequency analyses often divide the spectrum manually and draw qualitative conclusions. This paper develops a finer quantitative approach using Shapley values, a contribution measure from cooperative game theory.

The method measures whether individual frequency components help or hurt the network's behavior. Its analysis reveals differences across individual examples, making the picture more detailed than a single broad claim about high-frequency reliance. The authors also examine adversarial training and attacks statistically in the frequency domain.

These observations motivate hypotheses about why adversarial training improves robustness, how its effects differ across classes, and which frequency components attacks favor. The abstract presents these as hypotheses arising from analysis, rather than established universal explanations. The authors then use Shapley values to guide a data augmentation method. Image-classification benchmark experiments support its effectiveness at improving robustness, connecting a more detailed account of frequency contributions to a practical training intervention.
summary.tldr: Shapley values quantify frequency contributions to CNN behavior and guide an augmentation method that improves robustness in benchmark experiments.

title: Rethinking and Improving Robustness of Convolutional Neural Networks: a Shapley Value-based Approach in Frequency Domain

abstract: Knowledge Distillation (KD) is a well-known training paradigm in deep neural networks where knowledge acquired by a large teacher model is transferred to a small student.KD has proven to be an effective technique to significantly improve the student's performance for various tasks including object detection. As such, KD techniques mostly rely on guidance at the intermediate feature level, which is typically implemented by minimizing an $\ell_{p}$-norm distance between teacher and student activations during training. In this paper, we propose a replacement for the pixel-wise independent $\ell_{p}$-norm based on the structural similarity (SSIM).By taking into account additional contrast and structural cues, more information within intermediate feature maps can be preserved. Extensive experiments on MSCOCO demonstrate the effectiveness of our method across different training schemes and architectures. Our method adds only little computational overhead, is straightforward to implement and at the same time it significantly outperforms the standard $\ell_p$-norms.Moreover, more complex state-of-the-art KD methods using attention-based sampling mechanisms are outperformed, including a +3.5 AP gain using a Faster R-CNN R-50 compared to a vanilla model.

paragraphs: Knowledge distillation improves a small object detector by transferring information from a larger teacher. Many methods align intermediate feature maps by minimizing a distance between corresponding activations. This paper changes that comparison, arguing that treating feature locations independently misses contrast and structural information within the maps.

The proposed method replaces the usual pixel-wise norm with structural similarity, or SSIM. This makes the training guidance sensitive to additional relationships in the feature maps, preserving more of the teacher's intermediate information. The change is straightforward to implement and adds only a small amount of computational overhead.

Experiments on MSCOCO show effectiveness across multiple architectures and training schemes. The method significantly outperforms standard norm-based comparisons and also exceeds more complex distillation methods that use attention-based sampling. A reported Faster R-CNN R-50 result improves by 3.5 AP over a vanilla model. These findings indicate that changing how teacher and student features are compared can materially improve distillation without requiring a complex additional mechanism.
summary.tldr: Using structural similarity to match teacher and student features improves object-detection distillation with little computational overhead.

title: Structural Knowledge Distillation for Object Detection

abstract: Deploying AI-powered systems requires trustworthy models supporting effective human interactions, going beyond raw prediction accuracy. Concept bottleneck models promote trustworthiness by conditioning classification tasks on an intermediate level of human-like concepts. This enables human interventions which can correct mispredicted concepts to improve the model's performance. However, existing concept bottleneck models are unable to find optimal compromises between high task accuracy, robust concept-based explanations, and effective interventions on concepts---particularly in real-world conditions where complete and accurate concept supervisions are scarce. To address this, we propose Concept Embedding Models, a novel family of concept bottleneck models which goes beyond the current accuracy-vs-interpretability trade-off by learning interpretable high-dimensional concept representations. Our experiments demonstrate that Concept Embedding Models (1) attain better or competitive task accuracy w.r.t. standard neural models without concepts, (2) provide concept representations capturing meaningful semantics including and beyond their ground truth labels, (3) support test-time concept interventions whose effect in test accuracy surpasses that in standard concept bottleneck models, and (4) scale to real-world conditions where complete concept supervisions are scarce.

paragraphs: Concept bottleneck models make predictions through intermediate concepts that people can understand and correct. This creates a useful interaction: fixing a mistaken concept can improve the final prediction. Existing approaches, however, struggle to combine accurate predictions, meaningful explanations, and effective corrections, especially when concept annotations are incomplete.

Concept Embedding Models replace a restrictive concept representation with interpretable, high-dimensional representations. The aim is to retain the human-facing concept layer while allowing it to carry richer information. In the reported experiments, these representations capture meaningful semantics both within and beyond the supplied concept labels, helping explain why the concept layer need not force a large accuracy sacrifice.

The authors report task accuracy that matches or exceeds standard neural models without concepts. Human-style concept interventions at test time improve accuracy more than in standard concept bottleneck models. The models also scale to settings where complete concept supervision is scarce. Together, these findings support richer concept representations as a way to improve prediction and intervention within the same model.
summary.tldr: Concept Embedding Models use richer interpretable concept representations to support accurate predictions and more effective concept corrections.

title: Concept Embedding Models: Beyond the Accuracy-Explainability Trade-Off

abstract: Optical Chemical Structure Recognition (OCSR) deals with the translation from chemical images to molecular structures, this being the main way chemical compounds are depicted in scientific documents. Traditionally, rule-based methods have followed a framework based on the detection of chemical entities, such as atoms and bonds, followed by a compound structure reconstruction step. Recently, neural architectures analog to image captioning have been explored to solve this task, yet they still show to be data inefficient, using millions of examples just to show performances comparable with traditional methods. Looking to motivate and benchmark new approaches based on atomic-level entities detection and graph reconstruction, we present CEDe, a unique collection of chemical entity bounding boxes manually curated by experts for scientific literature datasets. These annotations combine to more than 700,000 chemical entity bounding boxes with the necessary information for structure reconstruction. Also, a large synthetic dataset containing one million molecular images and annotations is released in order to explore transfer-learning techniques that could help these architectures perform better under low-data regimes. Benchmarks show that detection-reconstruction based models can achieve performances on par with or better than image captioning-like models, even with 100x fewer training examples.

paragraphs: Optical Chemical Structure Recognition converts pictures of chemical compounds into molecular structures that software can process. Traditional systems detect entities such as atoms and bonds before assembling the structure. More recent neural systems approach the task like image captioning, but the paper identifies their heavy demand for training examples as a motivation for revisiting explicit detection and reconstruction.

CEDe provides expert-curated annotations for chemical images drawn from scientific literature datasets. Its annotations include more than 700,000 bounding boxes around chemical entities, together with information needed to reconstruct molecular structures. This gives researchers supervision for the intermediate recognition steps, rather than only the final molecular description.

The authors also release a synthetic dataset containing one million molecular images and annotations to support investigation of transfer learning under limited real-data availability. Their benchmarks show that detection-and-reconstruction models can match or exceed captioning-style models while using 100 times fewer training examples. The result supports this structured approach as a potentially more data-efficient route to recognizing chemical diagrams.
summary.tldr: CEDe supplies expert chemical-image annotations and benchmarks showing that explicit detection and reconstruction can greatly reduce training-data requirements.

title: CEDe: A collection of expert-curated datasets with atom-level entity annotations for Optical Chemical Structure Recognition

abstract: Masked Autoencoders (MAE) based on a reconstruction task have risen to be a promising paradigm for self-supervised learning (SSL) and achieve state-of-the-art performance across different benchmark datasets. However, despite its impressive empirical success, there is still limited theoretical understanding of it. In this paper, we propose a theoretical understanding of how masking matters for MAE to learn meaningful features. We establish a close connection between MAE and contrastive learning, which shows that MAE implicit aligns the mask-induced positive pairs. Built upon this connection, we develop the first downstream guarantees for MAE methods, and analyze the effect of mask ratio. Besides, as a result of the implicit alignment, we also point out the dimensional collapse issue of MAE, and propose a Uniformity-enhanced MAE (U-MAE) loss that can effectively address this issue and bring significant improvements on real-world datasets, including CIFAR-10, ImageNet-100, and ImageNet-1K. Code is available at https://github.com/zhangq327/U-MAE.

paragraphs: Masked autoencoders learn representations by reconstructing information hidden from their inputs. Their empirical success raises a theoretical question: why should solving this reconstruction task produce features useful for later prediction tasks? This paper investigates the role of masking itself, connecting the reconstruction objective to another major form of self-supervised learning.

The authors establish a relationship with contrastive learning in which masked autoencoders implicitly align positive pairs induced by masking. In plain terms, the training process encourages related masked views to have compatible representations. Using this connection, they develop downstream guarantees and analyze how the masking ratio affects learning, giving a theoretical account of how the pretraining task relates to later usefulness.

The same analysis identifies dimensional collapse, where the learned representation uses fewer effective dimensions. To address it, the authors introduce a Uniformity-enhanced MAE loss. They report that this objective effectively addresses the collapse issue and significantly improves results on CIFAR-10, ImageNet-100, and ImageNet-1K. The theoretical connection therefore motivates a concrete modification to training.
summary.tldr: A connection between masked autoencoding and contrastive learning motivates a uniformity-enhanced loss that addresses dimensional collapse and improves reported performance.

title: How Mask Matters: Towards Theoretical Understandings of Masked Autoencoders

abstract: When learning from sensitive data, care must be taken to ensure that training algorithms address privacy concerns. The canonical Private Aggregation of Teacher Ensembles, or PATE, computes output labels by aggregating the predictions of a (possibly distributed) collection of teacher models via a voting mechanism. The mechanism adds noise to attain a differential privacy guarantee with respect to the teachers' training data. In this work, we observe that this use of noise, which makes PATE predictions stochastic, enables new forms of leakage of sensitive information. For a given input, our adversary exploits this stochasticity to extract high-fidelity histograms of the votes submitted by the underlying teachers. From these histograms, the adversary can learn sensitive attributes of the input such as race, gender, or age. Although this attack does not directly violate the differential privacy guarantee, it clearly violates privacy norms and expectations, and would not be possible $\textit{at all}$ without the noise inserted to obtain differential privacy. In fact, counter-intuitively, the attack $\textbf{becomes easier as we add more noise}$ to provide stronger differential privacy. We hope this encourages future work to consider privacy holistically rather than treat differential privacy as a panacea.

paragraphs: Private Aggregation of Teacher Ensembles, or PATE, combines predictions from multiple teacher models through noisy voting. The added noise provides a differential privacy guarantee concerning the teachers' training data. This paper identifies a different privacy concern: the randomness of the resulting predictions can reveal information about how the teachers voted on a particular input.

The authors describe an adversary that exploits this stochastic behavior to reconstruct high-fidelity vote histograms. Those histograms reveal the distribution of teacher votes and can expose sensitive attributes of the input, including race, gender, or age. The reported attack relies on the noise added for differential privacy and would not be possible without that noise.

Counterintuitively, the attack becomes easier as more noise is added to strengthen differential privacy. This does not directly break the stated differential privacy guarantee, because the leakage concerns a different privacy expectation. The result shows why a formal guarantee about training data does not by itself resolve every sensitive-information risk associated with a learning system's outputs.
summary.tldr: Noise in PATE can enable recovery of teacher vote histograms and sensitive input attributes without directly violating its differential privacy guarantee.

title: In Differential Privacy, There is Truth: on Vote-Histogram Leakage in Ensemble Private Learning

abstract: We present a series of new differentially private (DP) algorithms with dimension-independent margin guarantees. For the family of linear hypotheses, we give a pure DP learning algorithm that benefits from relative deviation margin guarantees, as well as an efficient DP learning algorithm with margin guarantees. We also present a new efficient DP learning algorithm with margin guarantees for kernel-based hypotheses with shift-invariant kernels, such as Gaussian kernels, and point out how our results can be extended to other kernels using oblivious sketching techniques. We further give a pure DP learning algorithm for a family of feed-forward neural networks for which we prove margin guarantees that are independent of the input dimension. Additionally, we describe a general label DP learning algorithm, which benefits from relative deviation margin bounds and is applicable to a broad family of hypothesis sets, including that of neural networks. Finally, we show how our DP learning algorithms can be augmented in a general way to include model selection, to select the best confidence margin parameter.

paragraphs: This paper develops private learning algorithms whose guarantees depend on prediction margins without depending on input dimension. A margin captures how confidently a model separates its predictions. Connecting privacy guarantees with margin-based learning provides a way to characterize performance that does not automatically worsen merely because the input has more coordinates.

For linear models, the authors provide a pure differentially private algorithm with relative-deviation margin guarantees, alongside an efficient private algorithm with margin guarantees. They also develop an efficient method for kernel models using shift-invariant kernels, including Gaussian kernels, and describe extensions to other kernels through oblivious sketching. A further pure-private algorithm covers a family of feed-forward neural networks.

The paper additionally treats label privacy through a general algorithm applicable to broad hypothesis families, including neural networks. Finally, it explains how to add model selection to the private learning procedures to choose a confidence-margin parameter. The contribution spans several model classes and privacy formulations; the abstract distinguishes pure privacy, computational efficiency, and label privacy rather than assigning every property to every algorithm.
summary.tldr: The paper develops private learning algorithms with dimension-independent margin guarantees for linear models, kernel models, and a family of neural networks.

title: Differentially Private Learning with Margin Guarantees

abstract: State-of-the-art 3D-aware generative models rely on coordinate-based MLPs to parameterize 3D radiance fields. While demonstrating impressive results, querying an MLP for every sample along each ray leads to slow rendering.Therefore, existing approaches often render low-resolution feature maps and process them with an upsampling network to obtain the final image. Albeit efficient, neural rendering often entangles viewpoint and content such that changing the camera pose results in unwanted changes of geometry or appearance.Motivated by recent results in voxel-based novel view synthesis, we investigate the utility of sparse voxel grid representations for fast and 3D-consistent generative modeling in this paper.Our results demonstrate that monolithic MLPs can indeed be replaced by 3D convolutions when combining sparse voxel grids with progressive growing, free space pruning and appropriate regularization.To obtain a compact representation of the scene and allow for scaling to higher voxel resolutions, our model disentangles the foreground object (modeled in 3D) from the background (modeled in 2D).In contrast to existing approaches, our method requires only a single forward pass to generate a full 3D scene. It hence allows for efficient rendering from arbitrary viewpoints while yielding 3D consistent results with high visual fidelity. Code and models are available at https://github.com/autonomousvision/voxgraf.

paragraphs: Generating images from a three-dimensional scene often requires repeatedly querying a neural network along each viewing ray, which makes rendering slow. Some systems accelerate this by rendering coarse features and upsampling them, but camera changes can then unintentionally alter object geometry or appearance. VoxGRAF investigates a sparse voxel representation to address speed and consistency together.

The method replaces a monolithic coordinate-based network with three-dimensional convolutions. It combines sparse voxel grids with progressive growing, removal of empty space, and suitable regularization. The foreground object is represented in three dimensions, while the background is represented in two, keeping the scene compact and allowing higher voxel resolutions.

A single forward pass generates the full scene representation, which can then be rendered from arbitrary viewpoints efficiently. The reported results demonstrate high visual fidelity and three-dimensional consistency. The contribution is a generative representation that makes scene construction available upfront, reducing the need for repeated network queries while supporting coherent changes of viewpoint.
summary.tldr: VoxGRAF generates sparse voxel scenes in one forward pass for fast, visually faithful, viewpoint-consistent rendering.

title: VoxGRAF: Fast 3D-Aware Image Synthesis with Sparse Voxel Grids

abstract: A mainstream type of current self-supervised learning methods pursues a general-purpose representation that can be well transferred to downstream tasks, typically by optimizing on a given pretext task such as instance discrimination. In this work, we argue that existing pretext tasks inevitably introduce biases into the learned representation, which in turn leads to biased transfer performance on various downstream tasks. To cope with this issue, we propose Maximum Entropy Coding (MEC), a more principled objective that explicitly optimizes on the structure of the representation, so that the learned representation is less biased and thus generalizes better to unseen downstream tasks. Inspired by the principle of maximum entropy in information theory, we hypothesize that a generalizable representation should be the one that admits the maximum entropy among all plausible representations. To make the objective end-to-end trainable, we propose to leverage the minimal coding length in lossy data coding as a computationally tractable surrogate for the entropy, and further derive a scalable reformulation of the objective that allows fast computation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MEC learns a more generalizable representation than previous methods based on specific pretext tasks. It achieves state-of-the-art performance consistently on various downstream tasks, including not only ImageNet linear probe, but also semi-supervised classification, object detection, instance segmentation, and object tracking. Interestingly, we show that existing batch-wise and feature-wise self-supervised objectives could be seen equivalent to low-order approximations of MEC. Code and pre-trained models are available at https://github.com/xinliu20/MEC.

abstract: Facial analysis systems have been deployed by large companies and critiqued by scholars and activists for the past decade. Many existing algorithmic audits examine the performance of these systems on later stage elements of facial analysis systems like facial recognition and age, emotion, or perceived gender prediction; however, a core component to these systems has been vastly understudied from a fairness perspective: face detection, sometimes called face localization. Since face detection is a pre-requisite step in facial analysis systems, the bias we observe in face detection will flow downstream to the other components like facial recognition and emotion prediction. Additionally, no prior work has focused on the robustness of these systems under various perturbations and corruptions, which leaves open the question of how various people are impacted by these phenomena. We present the first of its kind detailed benchmark of face detection systems, specifically examining the robustness to noise of commercial and academic models. We use both standard and recently released academic facial datasets to quantitatively analyze trends in face detection robustness. Across all the datasets and systems, we generally find that photos of individuals who are masculine presenting, older, of darker skin type, or have dim lighting are more susceptible to errors than their counterparts in other identities.

This paper argues that fairness audits need to examine that initial step. If a system fails to locate a face, the effects can carry into the components that depend on detection.

The authors present a detailed benchmark of how commercial and academic face detectors respond to noise and other image perturbations. They use both established and recently released academic facial datasets to quantify robustness trends. The focus is on whether degraded inputs affect people differently, adding a robustness dimension to the evaluation of facial analysis systems.
