paragraphs: A feature-selection path tracks classification accuracy as the fraction of retained features changes. Computing it through repeated multiple-kernel learning can be expensive because many separate optimization problems must be solved. This paper develops a way to follow the path systematically as the regularization parameter p moves toward one.

The authors conjecture that, for certain formulations, the optimal number of selected features decreases monotonically as p decreases. They prove this for a family based on kernel target alignment and establish threshold-dependent monotonic behavior of feature weights. These properties support a path-following algorithm that can set some weights directly to zero over potentially large parameter intervals, reducing optimization work while providing approximation guarantees.

Experiments report classification accuracies up to 10% higher than the stated comparison methods and substantial training-time reductions. The algorithm generates a complete path for datasets with 100,000 features in about half an hour on standard hardware. The result connects a proved property of the specified formulations to a practical reduction in the cost of exploring feature subsets.
summary.tldr: Monotonicity results for certain multiple-kernel formulations enable efficient feature-selection paths with approximation guarantees.

title: On p-norm Path Following in Multiple Kernel Learning for Non-linear Feature Selection

abstract: In the paper we present a new framework for dealing with probabilistic graphical models. Our approach relies on the recently proposed Tensor Train format (TT-format) of a tensor that while being compact allows for efficient application of linear algebra operations. We present a way to convert the energy of a Markov random field to the TT-format and show how one can exploit the properties of the TT-format to attack the tasks of the partition function estimation and the MAP-inference. We provide theoretical guarantees on the accuracy of the proposed algorithm for estimating the partition function and compare our methods against several state-of-the-art algorithms.

paragraphs: This paper proposes a framework for computation in probabilistic graphical models using the Tensor Train format. This format represents a tensor compactly while supporting efficient linear algebra operations. The authors use those properties to develop methods for working with Markov random fields.

The starting point is a conversion of the field's energy into Tensor Train form. From that representation, the paper addresses two tasks: estimating the partition function and performing maximum a posteriori inference. The partition function provides the normalization needed for probabilities, while MAP inference seeks a most probable configuration. Both tasks are approached through operations on the compact representation.

The authors provide theoretical accuracy guarantees for their partition-function estimation algorithm and compare their methods with several state-of-the-art algorithms. The stated guarantee applies specifically to partition-function estimation. The broader contribution is a computational route from an MRF energy to a representation whose algebraic properties can be used for both normalization and inference.
summary.tldr: A Tensor Train representation of MRF energies supports partition-function estimation with accuracy guarantees and methods for MAP inference.

title: Putting MRFs on a Tensor Train

abstract: Opponent modeling is necessary in multi-agent settings where secondary agents with competing goals also adapt their strategies, yet it remains challenging because of strategies’ complex interaction and the non-stationary nature. Most previous work focuses on developing probabilistic models or parameterized strategies for specific applications. Inspired by the recent success of deep reinforcement learning, we present neural-based models that jointly learn a policy and the behavior of opponents. Instead of explicitly predicting the opponent’s action, we encode observation of the opponents into a deep Q-Network (DQN), while retaining explicit modeling under multitasking. By using a Mixture-of-Experts architecture, our model automatically discovers different strategy patterns of opponents even without extra supervision. We evaluate our models on a simulated soccer game and a popular trivia game, showing superior performance over DQN and its variants.

paragraphs: Learning against other agents is difficult when those agents pursue competing goals and adapt their strategies. Their changing behavior makes the learning environment nonstationary, while interactions between strategies complicate prediction. This paper proposes neural models that jointly learn an agent’s policy and information about opponent behavior, bringing opponent modeling into deep reinforcement learning.

The approach encodes observations of opponents into a deep Q-network, rather than relying solely on explicit prediction of an opponent’s next action. It also retains explicit modeling within a multitasking setup. A mixture-of-experts architecture allows the model to discover different opponent strategy patterns without extra supervision, giving the representation a way to distinguish among different kinds of behavior.

The authors evaluate their models in a simulated soccer game and a popular trivia game. They report better performance than a deep Q-network and its variants. These results support incorporating opponent observations and strategy patterns into policy learning in the tested settings. The architectural contribution is to learn those representations alongside the agent’s own decision-making behavior.
summary.tldr: Neural opponent models learn strategy patterns alongside a policy and outperform DQN variants in evaluated soccer and trivia games.

title: Opponent Modeling in Deep Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Given that in practice training data is scarce for all but a small set of problems, a core question is how to incorporate prior knowledge into a model. In this paper, we consider the case of prior procedural knowledge for neural networks, such as knowing how a program should traverse a sequence, but not what local actions should be performed at each step. To this end, we present an end-to-end differentiable interpreter for the programming language Forth which enables programmers to write program sketches with slots that can be filled with behaviour trained from program input-output data. We can optimise this behaviour directly through gradient descent techniques on user-specified objectives, and also integrate the program into any larger neural computation graph. We show empirically that our interpreter is able to effectively leverage different levels of prior program structure and learn complex behaviours such as sequence sorting and addition. When connected to outputs of an LSTM and trained jointly, our interpreter achieves state-of-the-art accuracy for end-to-end reasoning about quantities expressed in natural language stories.

paragraphs: Sometimes a programmer knows the broad procedure for solving a task but does not know the correct action at every step. This paper provides a way to combine that procedural knowledge with learned behavior. A programmer writes a partial Forth program containing slots whose behavior is learned from input-output examples.

The authors make the interpreter differentiable from end to end, allowing gradient descent to optimize the missing behavior against user-specified objectives. The program can also become part of a larger neural computation graph. This makes explicit program structure and neural learning compatible within a jointly trainable system.

Experiments show that the interpreter can use different amounts of supplied program structure to learn behaviors including sorting sequences and addition. When connected to an LSTM's outputs and trained jointly, it achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on reasoning about quantities in natural-language stories. The findings support using procedural knowledge as part of the model, particularly when available training data is scarce.
summary.tldr: A differentiable Forth interpreter lets programmers supply partial procedures and learn their missing behavior from examples.

title: Programming with a Differentiable Forth Interpreter

abstract: We explore a recently proposed Variational Dropout technique that provided an elegant Bayesian interpretation to Gaussian Dropout. We extend Variational Dropout to the case when dropout rates are unbounded, propose a way to reduce the variance of the gradient estimator and report first experimental results with individual dropout rates per weight. Interestingly, it leads to extremely sparse solutions both in fully-connected and convolutional layers. This effect is similar to automatic relevance determination effect in empirical Bayes but has a number of advantages. We reduce the number of parameters up to 280 times on LeNet architectures and up to 68 times on VGG-like networks with a negligible decrease of accuracy.

paragraphs: Variational dropout gives Gaussian dropout a Bayesian interpretation. This paper extends that approach to allow unbounded dropout rates and investigates assigning an individual dropout rate to each network weight. It also proposes a way to reduce the variance of the gradient estimator used during learning.

The reported outcome is extreme sparsity in both fully connected and convolutional layers: the learned solution uses far fewer parameters. The authors relate this behavior to automatic relevance determination in empirical Bayes. The individual treatment of weights connects the learning procedure to determining which parts of a network remain useful.

Experiments reduce parameter counts by up to 280 times on LeNet architectures and up to 68 times on VGG-like networks, with negligible decreases in accuracy. These are the largest reported reductions for those architecture families, rather than a uniform compression factor for every network. The findings show that this extension of variational dropout can serve as a powerful sparsification mechanism while preserving nearly all measured accuracy in the reported cases.
summary.tldr: Variational dropout with individual per-weight rates produces highly sparse networks, with large reported parameter reductions and negligible accuracy loss.

title: Variational Dropout Sparsifies Deep Neural Networks

abstract: In this work, we build on recent advances in distributional reinforcement learning to give a generally applicable, flexible, and state-of-the-art distributional variant of DQN. We achieve this by using quantile regression to approximate the full quantile function for the state-action return distribution. By reparameterizing a distribution over the sample space, this yields an implicitly defined return distribution and gives rise to a large class of risk-sensitive policies. We demonstrate improved performance on the 57 Atari 2600 games in the ALE, and use our algorithm’s implicitly defined distributions to study the effects of risk-sensitive policies in Atari games.

paragraphs: An action can lead to a range of future returns, and a distributional reinforcement learning agent models that range. This paper develops a flexible distributional version of DQN by learning the return distribution through its quantile function. A quantile describes the return associated with a particular position in that distribution.

The method uses quantile regression to approximate the full quantile function for each state-action return distribution. Reparameterizing a distribution over the sample space then defines the return distribution implicitly. This representation also supports a large class of risk-sensitive policies, making the learned distribution useful for more than a single expected-return estimate.

The authors demonstrate improved performance across the evaluation involving 57 Atari 2600 games in the Arcade Learning Environment. They also use the implicitly represented distributions to investigate the effects of risk-sensitive policies in those games. The contribution links a flexible way to represent uncertain returns with practical policy choices about how those returns should influence action selection.
summary.tldr: Implicit Quantile Networks learn return distributions through quantile regression, improving Atari performance and enabling varied risk-sensitive policies.

title: Implicit Quantile Networks for Distributional Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Understanding and interacting with everyday physical scenes requires rich knowledge about the structure of the world, represented either implicitly in a value or policy function, or explicitly in a transition model. Here we introduce a new class of learnable models–based on graph networks–which implement an inductive bias for object- and relation-centric representations of complex, dynamical systems. Our results show that as a forward model, our approach supports accurate predictions from real and simulated data, and surprisingly strong and efficient generalization, across eight distinct physical systems which we varied parametrically and structurally. We also found that our inference model can perform system identification. Our models are also differentiable, and support online planning via gradient-based trajectory optimization, as well as offline policy optimization. Our framework offers new opportunities for harnessing and exploiting rich knowledge about the world, and takes a key step toward building machines with more human-like representations of the world.

paragraphs: Predicting a physical scene requires representing both its components and how they interact. This paper introduces learnable physics models based on graph networks, with an explicit bias toward objects and their relations. That organization gives the model a structured way to represent complex dynamics and knowledge about the physical world.

As forward models, the networks produce accurate predictions from real and simulated data. The authors report strong, efficient generalization across eight physical systems whose parameters and structures were varied. They also find that an inference model can perform system identification, extending the framework beyond predicting motion to inferring properties of the system being observed.

The models are differentiable, allowing them to support online planning through gradient-based trajectory optimization and offline policy optimization. This connects learned physical prediction with choosing actions. Taken together, the results show how the same object-and-relation-centered framework can support prediction, inference, and control, with the reported generalization demonstrated across the physical systems examined.
summary.tldr: Graph-based physics models use objects and relations to support accurate prediction, system identification, and differentiable planning.

title: Graph Networks as Learnable Physics Engines for Inference and Control

abstract: Catastrophic forgetting occurs when a neural network loses the information learned in a previous task after training on subsequent tasks. This problem remains a hurdle for artificial intelligence systems with sequential learning capabilities. In this paper, we propose a task-based hard attention mechanism that preserves previous tasks’ information without affecting the current task’s learning. A hard attention mask is learned concurrently to every task, through stochastic gradient descent, and previous masks are exploited to condition such learning. We show that the proposed mechanism is effective for reducing catastrophic forgetting, cutting current rates by 45 to 80%. We also show that it is robust to different hyperparameter choices, and that it offers a number of monitoring capabilities. The approach features the possibility to control both the stability and compactness of the learned knowledge, which we believe makes it also attractive for online learning or network compression applications.

paragraphs: When a neural network learns tasks sequentially, training on a new task can erase information needed for earlier ones. This paper addresses that catastrophic forgetting through task-based hard attention. The mechanism is designed to preserve earlier information while allowing the current task to be learned.

A hard attention mask is learned alongside each task using stochastic gradient descent. Masks from previous tasks then condition subsequent learning. This gives the training process an explicit record of task-related attention that can guide how new knowledge is acquired. The approach also offers controls over the stability and compactness of the learned knowledge, together with monitoring capabilities.

The authors report reductions in forgetting rates of 45 to 80 percent and robustness across different hyperparameter choices. These results support the mechanism’s effectiveness in the evaluated settings. They additionally suggest that control over stability and compactness could make the approach useful for online learning or network compression, presenting those applications as possibilities rather than established outcomes.
summary.tldr: Task-specific hard attention masks guide sequential learning and reduce reported catastrophic forgetting rates by 45 to 80 percent.

title: Overcoming Catastrophic Forgetting with Hard Attention to the Task

abstract: Designing an incentive compatible auction that maximizes expected revenue is an intricate task. The single-item case was resolved in a seminal piece of work by Myerson in 1981. Even after 30-40 years of intense research the problem remains unsolved for seemingly simple multi-bidder, multi-item settings. In this work, we initiate the exploration of the use of tools from deep learning for the automated design of optimal auctions. We model an auction as a multi-layer neural network, frame optimal auction design as a constrained learning problem, and show how it can be solved using standard pipelines. We prove generalization bounds and present extensive experiments, recovering essentially all known analytical solutions for multi-item settings, and obtaining novel mechanisms for settings in which the optimal mechanism is unknown.

paragraphs: Auction design seeks mechanisms that maximize expected revenue while preserving incentive compatibility, meaning participants should have an incentive to report their valuations truthfully. The paper addresses the difficulty of finding such mechanisms when several items and bidders are involved. Even apparently simple versions of these settings lack known optimal solutions.

The authors represent an auction using a multilayer neural network and formulate its design as a constrained learning problem. This makes it possible to search for auction mechanisms through standard deep-learning pipelines while expressing the requirements that define the design problem. They also prove generalization bounds, adding a theoretical component to the automated learning approach.

In extensive experiments, the approach recovers essentially all known analytical solutions for multi-item settings considered by the authors. It also produces new mechanisms for settings whose optimal solution is unknown. Those new mechanisms demonstrate the method’s ability to explore unresolved design problems; their discovery does not itself establish that each one is globally optimal. The work opens a computational route to auction design.
summary.tldr: Neural networks formulate auction design as constrained learning, recovering known solutions and discovering mechanisms for unresolved settings.

title: Optimal Auctions through Deep Learning

abstract: We give faster approximation algorithms for well-studied variants of Binary Matrix Factorization (BMF), where we are given a binary $m \times n$ matrix $A$ and would like to find binary rank-$k$ matrices $U, V$ to minimize the Frobenius norm of $U \cdot V - A$. In the first setting, $U \cdot V$ denotes multiplication over $\mathbb{Z}$, and we give a constant-factor approximation algorithm that runs in $2^{O(k^2 \log k)} \textrm{poly}(mn)$ time, improving upon the previous $\min(2^{2^k}, 2^n) \textrm{poly}(mn)$ time. Our techniques generalize to minimizing $\|U \cdot V - A\|_p$ for $p \geq 1$, in $2^{O(k^{\lceil p/2 \rceil + 1}\log k)} \textrm{poly}(mn)$ time. For $p = 1$, this has a graph-theoretic consequence, namely, a $2^{O(k^2)} \poly(mn)$-time algorithm to approximate a graph as a union of disjoint bicliques. In the second setting, $U \cdot V$ is over $\GF(2)$, and we give a bicriteria constant-factor approximation algorithm that runs in $2^{O(k^3)} \poly(mn)$ time to find binary rank-$O(k \log m)$ matrices $U$, $V$ whose cost is as good as the best rank-$k$ approximation, improving upon $\min(2^{2^k}mn, \min(m,n)^{k^{O(1)}} \textrm{poly}(mn))$ time.

paragraphs: Binary matrix factorization seeks binary factors whose product closely approximates a given binary matrix. This paper develops faster approximation algorithms for two versions of the problem, distinguished by the arithmetic used in multiplication. The distinction matters because ordinary integer multiplication and multiplication over the two-element field define different approximation problems.

For integer multiplication, the authors give a constant-factor approximation for Frobenius-norm error. Its running time is polynomial in matrix size with a rank-dependent factor of 2 raised to O(k squared log k), improving the previous bound. Their techniques also extend to p-norm objectives for p at least one, with a related application to approximating graphs by unions of disjoint bicliques.

For multiplication over the two-element field, the result is a bicriteria constant-factor approximation: the algorithm allows rank O(k log m) when comparing with the best rank-k approximation. Its running time has a rank-dependent factor of 2 raised to O(k cubed). The contribution improves approximation efficiency while explicitly retaining a rank-versus-error tradeoff in this second setting.
summary.tldr: The paper gives faster binary matrix factorization approximations, including a rank-expanding bicriteria result for arithmetic over the two-element field.

title: Faster Algorithms for Binary Matrix Factorization

abstract: It is well known that both gradient descent and stochastic coordinate descent achieve a global convergence rate of $O(1/k)$ in the objective value, when applied to a scheme for minimizing a Lipschitz-continuously differentiable, unconstrained convex function. In this work, we improve this rate to $o(1/k)$. We extend the result to proximal gradient and proximal coordinate descent on regularized problems to show similar $o(1/k)$ convergence rates. The result is tight in the sense that a rate of $O(1/k^{1+\epsilon})$ is not generally attainable for any $\epsilon>0$, for any of these methods.
originalAbstract: It is well known that both gradient descent and stochastic coordinate descent achieve a global convergence rate of $O(1/k)$ in the objective value, when applied to a scheme for minimizing a Lipschitz-continuously differentiable, unconstrained convex function. In this work, we improve this rate to $o(1/k)$. We extend the result to proximal gradient and proximal coordinate descent on regularized problems to show similar $o(1/k)$ convergence rates. The result is tight in the sense that a rate of $O(1/k^{1+\epsilon})$ is not generally attainable for any $\epsilon>0$, for any of these methods.

paragraphs: The paper sharpens a familiar convergence result for gradient descent and stochastic coordinate descent. For unconstrained convex objectives with Lipschitz-continuous gradients, these methods are known to achieve an objective-value error bounded at order 1/k, where k counts iterations. The authors show that the asymptotic statement can be strengthened from big-O to little-o.

The distinction is subtle but meaningful. An O(1/k) bound permits error to remain proportional to 1/k. An o(1/k) result says that the error becomes smaller relative to 1/k as iterations continue. Thus, the improvement describes the eventual behavior of these existing algorithms rather than introducing a different optimization method.

The authors extend the same kind of result to proximal gradient and proximal coordinate descent for regularized problems. They also establish a limit on the improvement: no fixed positive increase in the exponent, giving O(1/k^(1+epsilon)), is generally attainable for these methods. The result therefore tightens the convergence description while showing why a uniformly stronger power-law rate would go too far.
summary.tldr: Several first-order convex optimization methods achieve o(1/k) convergence, but generally cannot guarantee any fixed improvement in the power-law exponent.

title: First-Order Algorithms Converge Faster than $O(1/k)$ on Convex Problems

abstract: The gradient of a deep neural network (DNN) w.r.t. the input provides information that can be used to explain the output prediction in terms of the input features and has been widely studied to assist in interpreting DNNs. In a linear model (i.e., g(x) = wx + b), the gradient corresponds to the weights w. Such a model can reasonably locally-linearly approximate a smooth nonlinear DNN, and hence the weights of this local model are the gradient. The bias b, however, is usually overlooked in attribution methods. In this paper, we observe that since the bias in a DNN also has a non-negligible contribution to the correctness of predictions, it can also play a significant role in understanding DNN behavior. We propose a backpropagation-type algorithm “bias back-propagation (BBp)” that starts at the output layer and iteratively attributes the bias of each layer to its input nodes as well as combining the resulting bias term of the previous layer. Together with the backpropagation of the gradient generating w, we can fully recover the locally linear model g(x) = wx + b. In experiments, we show that BBp can generate complementary and highly interpretable explanations.

paragraphs: Many neural network explanations examine the gradient of a prediction with respect to its input. The gradient describes how the output changes as input features change. This paper argues that such explanations overlook another relevant component: the bias, or offset, in a local linear description of the network.

For a linear model written as g(x) = wx + b, the gradient supplies w but does not supply b. A smooth nonlinear network can be reasonably approximated locally in this form. The authors observe that the bias can contribute meaningfully to correct predictions, so recovering it can add information about the network’s behavior.

Their bias back-propagation algorithm starts at the output and works backward through the layers. It assigns each layer’s bias to its input nodes while combining accumulated bias contributions. Together with ordinary gradient backpropagation, this recovers the full local linear model. Experiments show complementary, interpretable explanations, supporting the value of examining both local sensitivity and the associated offset.
summary.tldr: Bias back-propagation complements gradient explanations by attributing the offset needed to recover a network’s full local linear model.

title: Bias Also Matters: Bias Attribution for Deep Neural Network Explanation

abstract: A novel Gromov-Wasserstein learning framework is proposed to jointly match (align) graphs and learn embedding vectors for the associated graph nodes. Using Gromov-Wasserstein discrepancy, we measure the dissimilarity between two graphs and find their correspondence, according to the learned optimal transport. The node embeddings associated with the two graphs are learned under the guidance of the optimal transport, the distance of which not only reflects the topological structure of each graph but also yields the correspondence across the graphs. These two learning steps are mutually-beneficial, and are unified here by minimizing the Gromov-Wasserstein discrepancy with structural regularizers. This framework leads to an optimization problem that is solved by a proximal point method. We apply the proposed method to matching problems in real-world networks, and demonstrate its superior performance compared to alternative approaches.

Using Gromov-Wasserstein discrepancy, we measure the dissimilarity between two graphs and find their correspondence, according to the learned optimal transport. The node embeddings associated with the two graphs are learned under the guidance of the optimal transport, the distance of which not only reflects the topological structure of each graph but also yields the correspondence across the graphs. These two learning steps are mutually-beneficial, and are unified here by minimizing the Gromov-Wasserstein discrepancy with structural regularizers. This framework leads to an optimization problem that is solved by a proximal point method. We apply the proposed method to matching problems in real-world networks, and demonstrate its superior performance compared to alternative approaches.

paragraphs: Graph matching seeks correspondences between nodes in different networks, while node embedding assigns each node a vector representation. This paper learns the two together. The motivation is that a useful correspondence can guide the representations, and useful representations can help establish how the graphs align.

The framework uses Gromov-Wasserstein discrepancy to measure differences between graphs and learns an optimal transport that expresses their correspondence. That transport guides the node embeddings. Distances in the learned representation reflect the structure within each graph while also supporting alignment across graphs, tying the two tasks to the same structural information.

The authors unify these mutually beneficial steps in an objective that minimizes Gromov-Wasserstein discrepancy with structural regularizers, then solve the resulting optimization problem using a proximal point method. Experiments on matching tasks in real-world networks show better performance than the alternative approaches considered. The contribution is a shared learning framework in which alignment and representation can inform each other, with empirical evidence that this coupling improves graph matching.
summary.tldr: The framework jointly learns graph correspondences and node embeddings through a structurally regularized Gromov-Wasserstein objective.

title: Gromov-Wasserstein Learning for Graph Matching and Node Embedding

abstract: We consider the product of determinantal point processes (DPPs), a point process whose probability mass is proportional to the product of principal minors of multiple matrices as a natural, promising generalization of DPPs. We study the computational complexity of computing its normalizing constant, which is among the most essential probabilistic inference tasks. Our complexity-theoretic results (almost) rule out the existence of efficient algorithms for this task, unless input matrices are forced to have favorable structures. In particular, we prove the following: (1) Computing $\sum_{S} \det(\mathbf{A}_{S,S})^p$ exactly for every (fixed) positive even integer $p$ is $\textsf{UP}$-hard and $\textsf{Mod}_3\textsf{P}$-hard, which gives a negative answer to an open question posed by Kulesza and Taskar (2012). (2) $\sum_{S} \det(\mathbf{A}_{S,S}) \det(\mathbf{B}_{S,S}) \det(\mathbf{C}_{S,S})$ is $\textsf{NP}$-hard to approximate within a factor of $ 2^{\mathcal{O}(|\mathcal{I}|^{1-\epsilon})} $ for any $\epsilon > 0$, where $|\mathcal{I}|$ is the input size. This result is stronger than $\sharp\textsf{P}$-hardness for the case of two matrices by Gillenwater (2014). (3) There exists a $ k^{\mathcal{O}(k)} |\mathcal{I}|^{\mathcal{O}(1)} $-time algorithm for computing $\sum_{S} \det(\mathbf{A}_{S,S}) \det(\mathbf{B}_{S,S})$, where $k$ is “the maximum rank of $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$” or “the treewidth of the graph formed by nonzero entries of $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$.” Such parameterized algorithms are said to be fixed-parameter tractable.

paragraphs: The paper studies a generalization of determinantal point processes in which each subset receives weight from a product of matrix determinants. Turning these weights into probabilities requires a normalizing constant: the sum of the weights over all subsets. The authors investigate how difficult this essential inference calculation is.

Their results establish strong computational barriers. Exactly summing fixed positive even powers of principal-minor determinants is UP-hard and Mod3P-hard. For products involving three matrices, even approximation within the stated factor is NP-hard; that factor grows as two raised to a power of the input size. These complexity results largely rule out efficient general-purpose solutions under the corresponding complexity assumptions.

The paper also identifies favorable structure that enables computation for products involving two matrices. An algorithm runs in k raised to order k times a polynomial in input size, where k can be the maximum matrix rank or the treewidth of the combined nonzero-entry graph. Thus, small structural parameters offer a tractable route even though unrestricted instances face substantial complexity barriers.
summary.tldr: Normalizing products of determinantal point processes faces strong complexity barriers, but small rank or treewidth enables parameterized algorithms for two matrices.

title: On the (In)tractability of Computing Normalizing Constants for the Product of Determinantal Point Processes

abstract: Existing methods for vision-and-language learning typically require designing task-specific architectures and objectives for each task. For example, a multi-label answer classifier for visual question answering, a region scorer for referring expression comprehension, and a language decoder for image captioning, etc. To alleviate these hassles, in this work, we propose a unified framework that learns different tasks in a single architecture with the same language modeling objective, i.e., multimodal conditional text generation, where our models learn to generate labels in text based on the visual and textual inputs. On 7 popular vision-and-language benchmarks, including visual question answering, referring expression comprehension, visual commonsense reasoning, most of which have been previously modeled as discriminative tasks, our generative approach (with a single unified architecture) reaches comparable performance to recent task-specific state-of-the-art vision-and-language models. Moreover, our generative approach shows better generalization ability on questions that have rare answers. Also, we show that our framework allows multi-task learning in a single architecture with a single set of parameters, achieving similar performance to separately optimized single-task models. Our code is publicly available at: https://github.com/j-min/VL-T5

paragraphs: Vision-and-language systems often use different architectures and training objectives for answering questions, locating referred objects, and producing captions. This paper reformulates these tasks as conditional text generation. Given visual and textual inputs, the model generates the desired label in text, allowing multiple tasks to share an architecture and a language-modeling objective.

The authors evaluate this generative approach on seven benchmarks, including visual question answering, referring-expression comprehension, and visual commonsense reasoning. Even for tasks previously treated mainly as discriminative prediction problems, the unified architecture achieves performance comparable to recent task-specific state-of-the-art systems. It also shows better generalization on questions whose answers are rare.

The framework further supports joint training of multiple tasks with one parameter set. This shared model achieves performance similar to separately optimized models for individual tasks. The findings suggest that a common text output format can simplify the design of vision-and-language systems while retaining competitive performance and enabling parameter sharing across different task types.
summary.tldr: Generating textual labels unifies vision-and-language tasks in one architecture with competitive benchmark performance and improved rare-answer generalization.

title: Unifying Vision-and-Language Tasks via Text Generation

abstract: Approximations to Gaussian processes (GPs) based on inducing variables, combined with variational inference techniques, enable state-of-the-art sparse approaches to infer GPs at scale through mini-batch based learning. In this work, we further push the limits of scalability of sparse GPs by allowing large number of inducing variables without imposing a special structure on the inducing inputs. In particular, we introduce a novel hierarchical prior, which imposes sparsity on the set of inducing variables. We treat our model variationally, and we experimentally show considerable computational gains compared to standard sparse GPs when sparsity on the inducing variables is realized considering the nearest inducing inputs of a random mini-batch of the data. We perform an extensive experimental validation that demonstrates the effectiveness of our approach compared to the state-of-the-art. Our approach enables the possibility to use sparse GPs using a large number of inducing points without incurring a prohibitive computational cost.

paragraphs: Sparse Gaussian processes use inducing variables to make inference more manageable, and variational methods allow learning from mini-batches. However, increasing the number of inducing variables can still make computation expensive. This paper seeks to support large inducing sets without requiring the inducing inputs to have a specially structured arrangement.

The authors introduce a hierarchical prior that creates sparsity within the inducing-variable set itself. They use variational inference for the resulting model. In the experimental implementation, this sparsity is realized by considering the inducing inputs nearest to the data in a randomly selected mini-batch, connecting the computation to the local information relevant to that batch.

Experiments show considerable computational gains over standard sparse Gaussian processes, and broader validation demonstrates effectiveness against state-of-the-art approaches. The contribution is an additional level of sparsity inside an already sparse approximation. This makes it possible to use a large overall collection of inducing points while avoiding the prohibitive computational cost that such a collection could otherwise impose.
summary.tldr: A hierarchical prior and nearest-neighbor information add sparsity within inducing variables, enabling larger sparse Gaussian process models at lower computational cost.

title: Sparse within Sparse Gaussian Processes using Neighbor Information

abstract: While the general idea of self-supervised learning is identical across modalities, the actual algorithms and objectives differ widely because they were developed with a single modality in mind. To get us closer to general self-supervised learning, we present data2vec, a framework that uses the same learning method for either speech, NLP or computer vision. The core idea is to predict latent representations of the full input data based on a masked view of the input in a self-distillation setup using a standard Transformer architecture. Instead of predicting modality-specific targets such as words, visual tokens or units of human speech which are local in nature, data2vec predicts contextualized latent representations that contain information from the entire input. Experiments on the major benchmarks of speech recognition, image classification, and natural language understanding demonstrate a new state of the art or competitive performance to predominant approaches.

paragraphs: Self-supervised learning uses the data itself to provide a training signal, but its practical objectives often differ across speech, vision, and language. Data2vec asks whether the same learning method can work in all three areas. Its contribution is a shared training framework that can be applied to each of these modalities.

Using a standard Transformer, the method learns from an input with some portions masked. Its target is a latent representation computed from the complete input in a self-distillation setup. Because that target incorporates context from the full input, predicting it asks the model to recover information beyond an isolated word, visual token, or speech unit.

This choice makes contextual representations the common prediction target across modalities. The reported experiments cover speech recognition, image classification, and natural language understanding, reaching either a new state of the art or performance competitive with predominant approaches. The findings support the usefulness of a common self-supervised objective across these tasks, while retaining the abstract’s distinction between leading and competitive results.
summary.tldr: Data2vec uses one self-supervised learning method across speech, vision, and language by predicting contextual representations from masked inputs.

title: data2vec: A General Framework for Self-supervised Learning in Speech, Vision and Language

abstract: Ex ante correlation is becoming the mainstream approach for sequential adversarial team games , where a team of players faces another team in a zero-sum game. It is known that team members’ asymmetric information makes both equilibrium computation \textsf{APX}-hard and team’s strategies not directly representable on the game tree. This latter issue prevents the adoption of successful tools for huge 2-player zero-sum games such as, e.g. , abstractions, no-regret learning, and subgame solving. This work shows that we can recover from this weakness by bridging the gap between sequential adversarial team games and 2-player games. In particular, we propose a new, suitable game representation that we call team-public-information , in which a team is represented as a single coordinator who only knows information common to the whole team and prescribes to each member an action for any possible private state. The resulting representation is highly explainable , being a 2-player tree in which the team’s strategies are behavioral with a direct interpretation and more expressive than the original extensive form when designing abstractions. Furthermore, we prove payoff equivalence of our representation, and we provide techniques that, starting directly from the extensive form, generate dramatically more compact representations without information loss. Finally, we experimentally evaluate our techniques when applied to a standard testbed, comparing their performance with the current state of the art.

paragraphs: In sequential games between opposing teams, teammates may hold different private information. This makes coordinating a team computationally difficult and prevents its strategies from being represented directly on the usual game tree. Consequently, techniques that work well for large two-player zero-sum games cannot simply be applied to teams.

The paper introduces a team-public-information representation. A team becomes a single coordinator who sees only information shared by all teammates. Instead of knowing each player’s private situation, the coordinator prescribes an action for every possible private state. This produces a two-player tree with strategies that have a direct behavioral interpretation.

The authors prove that the representation preserves payoffs and develop ways to construct much smaller representations without losing information. It also offers greater flexibility for designing abstractions. These results create a route to using abstraction, no-regret learning, and subgame solving in team games. Experiments compare the techniques with existing methods on a standard testbed; the representational advance does not itself remove the stated computational hardness.
summary.tldr: A payoff-preserving representation turns adversarial team games into two-player trees, enabling established game-solving techniques.

title: A Marriage between Adversarial Team Games and 2-player Games: Enabling Abstractions, No-regret Learning, and Subgame Solving

abstract: We consider a batch active learning scenario where the learner adaptively issues batches of points to a labeling oracle. Sampling labels in batches is highly desirable in practice due to the smaller number of interactive rounds with the labeling oracle (often human beings). However, batch active learning typically pays the price of a reduced adaptivity, leading to suboptimal results. In this paper we propose a solution which requires a careful trade off between the informativeness of the queried points and their diversity. We theoretically investigate batch active learning in the practically relevant scenario where the unlabeled pool of data is available beforehand ( pool-based active learning). We analyze a novel stage-wise greedy algorithm and show that, as a function of the label complexity, the excess risk of this algorithm %operating in the realizable setting for which we prove matches the known minimax rates in standard statistical learning settings. Our results also exhibit a mild dependence on the batch size. These are the first theoretical results that employ careful trade offs between informativeness and diversity to rigorously quantify the statistical performance of batch active learning in the pool-based scenario.

paragraphs: Active learning chooses which examples to send for labeling. Requesting labels in batches reduces the number of interactions with a labeling oracle, which may be a person. However, the learner cannot use answers from within a batch to revise its remaining selections. This reduced adaptivity can make batch selection statistically less effective.

The paper studies the pool-based setting, where all unlabeled candidate examples are available beforehand. It proposes a stage-wise greedy algorithm that carefully balances informativeness and diversity. This balance addresses two needs at once: selecting points that are useful for learning and selecting a batch whose contents provide sufficiently varied information. The contribution includes a theoretical analysis of this selection strategy.

The authors show that excess risk, expressed as a function of the number of requested labels, matches known minimax rates in standard statistical learning settings. Their results also have a mild dependence on batch size. This provides a rigorous account of how balancing information and diversity can support statistically effective learning while reducing interactions with the labeling oracle.
summary.tldr: A stage-wise batch selection algorithm balances informativeness and diversity to achieve known minimax learning rates with mild batch-size dependence.

title: Achieving Minimax Rates in Pool-Based Batch Active Learning

abstract: Although traditional optimization methods focus on finding a single optimal solution, most objective functions in modern machine learning problems, especially those in deep learning, often have multiple or infinite number of optimal points. Therefore, it is useful to consider the problem of finding a set of diverse points in the optimum set of an objective function. In this work, we frame this problem as a bi-level optimization problem of maximizing a diversity score inside the optimum set of the main loss function, and solve it with a simple population gradient descent framework that iteratively updates the points to maximize the diversity score in a fashion that does not hurt the optimization of the main loss. We demonstrate that our method can efficiently generate diverse solutions on multiple applications, e.g. text-to-image generation, text-to-mesh generation, molecular conformation generation and ensemble neural network training.

paragraphs: Many machine learning objectives admit multiple optimal solutions, sometimes infinitely many. Finding a single solution leaves that variety unexplored. This paper studies how to obtain a collection of distinct solutions within the optimum set, so that diversity becomes an explicit goal alongside success on the main optimization problem.

The authors express the task as a bilevel optimization problem: maximize a diversity score while staying within the set of solutions that optimize the main loss. Their population gradient descent framework updates a group of points repeatedly. Those updates seek greater diversity in a way designed not to harm optimization of the main objective.

The method is demonstrated on text-to-image generation, text-to-mesh generation, molecular conformation generation, and neural network ensemble training. Across these applications, the authors show efficient generation of diverse solutions. The contribution offers a shared optimization approach for situations where several good answers are useful, with diversity evaluated inside the main objective's optimum set.
summary.tldr: Population gradient descent seeks diverse optimal solutions while preserving optimization of the main loss.

title: How to Fill the Optimum Set? Population Gradient Descent with Harmless Diversity

abstract: The top-k classification accuracy is one of the core metrics in machine learning. Here, k is conventionally a positive integer, such as 1 or 5, leading to top-1 or top-5 training objectives. In this work, we relax this assumption and optimize the model for multiple k simultaneously instead of using a single k. Leveraging recent advances in differentiable sorting and ranking, we propose a family of differentiable top-k cross-entropy classification losses. This allows training while not only considering the top-1 prediction, but also, e.g., the top-2 and top-5 predictions. We evaluate the proposed losses for fine-tuning on state-of-the-art architectures, as well as for training from scratch. We find that relaxing k not only produces better top-5 accuracies, but also leads to top-1 accuracy improvements. When fine-tuning publicly available ImageNet models, we achieve a new state-of-the-art for these models.

paragraphs: Top-k accuracy asks whether the correct class appears among a model's k highest-ranked predictions. Training objectives commonly focus on one choice of k, such as the single best prediction or the best five. This paper instead trains a classifier to account for several choices simultaneously, allowing the objective to reflect more than one position in the ranked output.

The authors develop a family of top-k cross-entropy losses using differentiable sorting and ranking methods. These methods make ranking-related objectives usable in gradient-based training. A model can therefore be trained with attention to, for example, its top-one, top-two, and top-five predictions within the proposed framework.

The evaluation includes both fine-tuning existing architectures and training models from scratch. The authors report improvements in top-five accuracy together with improvements in top-one accuracy, so the observed benefit extends to the model's first choice. Fine-tuning publicly available ImageNet models also produces reported state-of-the-art results for those models. The findings support considering multiple ranking cutoffs when designing classification losses.
summary.tldr: Differentiable losses that optimize several top-k objectives together improve both top-five and top-one accuracy in the reported experiments.

title: Differentiable Top-k Classification Learning

abstract: We show that neural networks with access to randomness can outperform deterministic networks by using amplification. We call such networks Coin-Flipping Neural Networks, or CFNNs. We show that a CFNN can approximate the indicator of a d-dimensional ball to arbitrary accuracy with only 2 layers and O(1) neurons, where a 2-layer deterministic network was shown to require Omega(e^d) neurons, an exponential improvement. We prove a highly non-trivial result, that for almost any classification problem, there exists a trivially simple network that solves it given a sufficiently powerful generator for the network’s weights. Combining these results we conjecture that for most classification problems, there is a CFNN which solves them with higher accuracy or fewer neurons than any deterministic network. Finally, we verify our proofs experimentally using novel CFNN architectures on CIFAR10 and CIFAR100, reaching an improvement of 9.25% from the baseline.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether access to randomness can let neural networks accomplish tasks with fewer neurons than deterministic networks. Its Coin-Flipping Neural Networks use amplification to obtain benefits from randomized computation. The authors establish a striking approximation result: a two-layer randomized network with a constant number of neurons can approximate membership in a d-dimensional ball to arbitrary accuracy.

For that problem, the cited requirement for a two-layer deterministic network grows exponentially with dimension. The resulting separation demonstrates a substantial representational advantage in this particular setting. A second theorem shows that almost any classification problem admits a very simple network when supplied with a sufficiently powerful generator of its weights; the generator’s strength is an essential condition.

The authors conjecture that randomized networks offer better accuracy or smaller size for most classification problems, extending beyond what their theorems establish. They also test new architectures on CIFAR10 and CIFAR100, reporting an improvement of 9.25% from their baseline. These experiments accompany the theoretical results without turning the broader conjecture into a proven universal advantage.
summary.tldr: Randomized neural networks achieve a major size advantage for a specific approximation problem and show empirical classification gains.

title: Coin Flipping Neural Networks

abstract: Temporal data such as time series can be viewed as discretized measurements of the underlying function. To build a generative model for such data we have to model the stochastic process that governs it. We propose a solution by defining the denoising diffusion model in the function space which also allows us to naturally handle irregularly-sampled observations. The forward process gradually adds noise to functions, preserving their continuity, while the learned reverse process removes the noise and returns functions as new samples. To this end, we define suitable noise sources and introduce novel denoising and score-matching models. We show how our method can be used for multivariate probabilistic forecasting and imputation, and how our model can be interpreted as a neural process.

paragraphs: Temporal observations can be understood as measurements of an underlying continuous function. From this perspective, generating time-series data requires modeling the stochastic process that produces those functions. This paper develops a denoising diffusion model in function space, allowing the representation to accommodate observations taken at irregular times naturally.

The forward diffusion process gradually adds noise to functions while preserving their continuity. A learned reverse process removes that noise and produces functions as new samples. To make this construction work, the authors define suitable noise sources and introduce denoising and score-matching models tailored to the setting. Continuity is therefore built into how the diffusion process operates.

The paper shows how the method can support multivariate probabilistic forecasting and imputation, covering both uncertain future values and missing observations. It also explains an interpretation of the model as a neural process. The contribution is a generative formulation that treats temporal data through underlying functions, connecting irregular observations, continuous samples, and uncertainty-aware temporal prediction within one modeling approach.
summary.tldr: The paper defines diffusion over continuous functions to model temporal data, naturally accommodating irregular observations, forecasting, and imputation.

title: Modeling Temporal Data as Continuous Functions with Stochastic Process Diffusion

abstract: In this paper, we study the stochastic linear bandit problem under the additional requirements of differential privacy , robustness and batched observations . In particular, we assume an adversary randomly chooses a constant fraction of the observed rewards in each batch, replacing them with arbitrary numbers. We present differentially private and robust variants of the arm elimination algorithm using logarithmic batch queries under two privacy models and provide regret bounds in both settings. In the first model, every reward in each round is reported by a potentially different client, which reduces to standard local differential privacy (LDP). In the second model, every action is "owned" by a different client, who may aggregate the rewards over multiple queries and privatize the aggregate response instead. To the best of our knowledge, our algorithms are the first simultaneously providing differential privacy and adversarial robustness in the stochastic linear bandits problem.

In particular, we assume an adversary randomly chooses a constant fraction of the observed rewards in each batch, replacing them with arbitrary numbers. We present differentially private and robust variants of the arm elimination algorithm using logarithmic batch queries under two privacy models and provide regret bounds in both settings. In the first model, every reward in each round is reported by a potentially different client, which reduces to standard local differential privacy (LDP). In the second model, every action is "owned" by a different client, who may aggregate the rewards over multiple queries and privatize the aggregate response instead. To the best of our knowledge, our algorithms are the first simultaneously providing differential privacy and adversarial robustness in the stochastic linear bandits problem.

paragraphs: This paper studies linear bandit learning when rewards must remain private, observations arrive in batches, and some rewards are corrupted. The corruption model is specific: an adversary randomly selects a constant fraction of the observed rewards in each batch and replaces their values arbitrarily. The algorithms must learn useful actions despite both privacy constraints and corrupted feedback.

The authors construct robust, differentially private variants of arm elimination, which progressively removes actions from consideration. They use logarithmically many batch queries and analyze two privacy arrangements. In the first, potentially different clients report every individual reward, giving standard local differential privacy. In the second, each action belongs to a client that can aggregate rewards across multiple queries before privatizing its response.

The paper provides regret bounds for both arrangements, quantifying learning performance under their respective information-sharing rules. The authors describe these as, to their knowledge, the first stochastic linear bandit algorithms combining differential privacy with adversarial robustness. The two models distinguish protection of individual reports from protection of client-side aggregates within the stated batched corruption setting.
summary.tldr: Private arm-elimination algorithms provide regret guarantees for batched linear bandits with randomly selected, arbitrarily corrupted rewards.

title: Robust and private stochastic linear bandits

abstract: We study differentially private (DP) machine learning algorithms as instances of noisy fixed-point iterations, in order to derive privacy and utility results from this well-studied framework. We show that this new perspective recovers popular private gradient-based methods like DP-SGD and provides a principled way to design and analyze new private optimization algorithms in a flexible manner. Focusing on the widely-used Alternating Directions Method of Multipliers (ADMM) method, we use our general framework derive novel private ADMM algorithms for centralized, federated and fully decentralized learning. We establish strong privacy guarantees for these algorithms, leveraging privacy amplification by iteration and by subsampling. Finally, we provide utility guarantees for the three algorithms using a unified analysis that exploits a recent linear convergence result for noisy fixed-point iterations.

Such iterations repeatedly apply an update rule while introducing noise. This perspective lets the authors connect privacy analysis with an established framework for understanding how iterative algorithms approach a solution despite noisy updates.

The framework recovers familiar private gradient methods, including DP-SGD, and also supports new algorithms. The authors focus on the Alternating Directions Method of Multipliers, or ADMM, deriving private versions for centralized learning, federated learning, and fully decentralized learning. This gives three applications of the same general construction across different arrangements of computation and data.

Their privacy guarantees use amplification through iteration and subsampling. For utility, they give a unified analysis based on a linear convergence result for noisy fixed-point iterations. The contribution therefore covers both how strongly the algorithms protect privacy and how their optimization behavior can be controlled, using a shared mathematical perspective across the three learning settings.
summary.tldr: A noisy fixed-point framework yields private ADMM algorithms and unified privacy and utility analyses across three learning settings.

title: From Noisy Fixed-Point Iterations to Private ADMM for Centralized and Federated Learning

abstract: We explore different ways to utilize position-based cross-attention in seq2seq networks to enable length generalization in algorithmic tasks. We show that a simple approach of interpolating the original and reversed encoded representations combined with relative attention allows near-perfect length generalization for both forward and reverse lookup tasks or copy tasks that had been generally hard to tackle. We also devise harder diagnostic tasks where the relative distance of the ideal attention position varies with timestep. In such settings, the simple interpolation trick with relative attention is not sufficient. We introduce novel variants of location attention building on top of Dubois et al. (2020) to address the new diagnostic tasks. We also show the benefits of our approaches for length generalization in SCAN (Lake & Baroni, 2018) and CFQ (Keysers et al.,2020). Our code is available on GitHub.

This paper studies whether position-based cross-attention can help a sequence-to-sequence network maintain the right input-output correspondence as length changes. Its focus is the positioning behavior of attention during lookup and copying tasks.

The authors first combine relative attention with interpolation between the original encoded input and its reversed representation. This simple construction produces nearly perfect length generalization on forward and reverse lookup or copy tasks. They then construct harder diagnostic tasks in which the relative distance to the correct attention position changes with the output timestep.

On those harder tasks, interpolation with relative attention is insufficient. The paper introduces new location-attention variants to address that challenge and also reports benefits for length generalization on SCAN and CFQ. The progression of tasks matters: it separates success when positional relationships are easier to maintain from cases requiring the attention mechanism to handle changing relative distances as generation proceeds.
summary.tldr: Position-based attention improves length generalization, with new location-attention variants addressing tasks that defeat a simpler interpolation approach.

title: Monotonic Location Attention for Length Generalization

abstract: We address the problem of biased gradient estimation in deep Boltzmann machines (DBMs). The existing method to obtain an unbiased estimator uses a maximal coupling based on a Gibbs sampler, but when the state is high-dimensional, it takes a long time to converge. In this study, we propose to use a coupling based on the Metropolis-Hastings (MH) and to initialize the state around a local mode of the target distribution. Because of the propensity of MH to reject proposals, the coupling tends to converge in only one step with a high probability, leading to high efficiency. We find that our method allows DBMs to be trained in an end-to-end fashion without greedy pretraining. We also propose some practical techniques to further improve the performance of DBMs. We empirically demonstrate that our training algorithm enables DBMs to show comparable generative performance to other deep generative models, achieving the FID score of 10.33 for MNIST.

title: End-to-end Training of Deep Boltzmann Machines by Unbiased Contrastive Divergence with Local Mode Initialization

abstract: We study the top-$k$ selection problem under the differential privacy model: $m$ items are rated according to votes of a set of clients. We consider a setting in which algorithms can retrieve data via a sequence of accesses, each either a random access or a sorted access; the goal is to minimize the total number of data accesses. Our algorithm requires only $O(\sqrt{mk})$ expected accesses: to our knowledge, this is the first sublinear data-access upper bound for this problem. Our analysis also shows that the well-known exponential mechanism requires only $O(\sqrt{m})$ expected accesses. Accompanying this, we develop the first lower bounds for the problem, in three settings: only random accesses; only sorted accesses; a sequence of accesses of either kind. We show that, to avoid $\Omega(m)$ access cost, supporting both kinds of access is necessary, and that in this case our algorithm’s access cost is optimal.

paragraphs: This paper studies selecting the top k items from m candidates rated by client votes while satisfying differential privacy. Its main resource of interest is data access: how much information an algorithm must retrieve to perform selection. The access model permits both random accesses and accesses through sorted data.

The authors develop an algorithm requiring O(√(mk)) expected accesses, which they identify as the first sublinear upper bound for this problem. They also show that the established exponential mechanism can operate with O(√m) expected accesses. These results address the retrieval cost of private selection rather than treating access to all data as automatic.

Avoiding an Ω(m) access cost requires support for both kinds of access. When both are available, the proposed algorithm's access cost is optimal. The result therefore links achievable efficiency directly to the data-access capabilities supplied by the underlying system.
summary.tldr: Private top-k selection achieves optimal O(√(mk)) expected data accesses when both random and sorted access are available.

title: Tight Data Access Bounds for Private Top-$k$ Selection

abstract: Machine learning models frequently experience performance drops under distribution shifts. The underlying cause of such shifts may be multiple simultaneous factors such as changes in data quality, differences in specific covariate distributions, or changes in the relationship between label and features. When a model does fail during deployment, attributing performance change to these factors is critical for the model developer to identify the root cause and take mitigating actions. In this work, we introduce the problem of attributing performance differences between environments to distribution shifts in the underlying data generating mechanisms. We formulate the problem as a cooperative game where the players are distributions. We define the value of a set of distributions to be the change in model performance when only this set of distributions has changed between environments, and derive an importance weighting method for computing the value of an arbitrary set of distributions. The contribution of each distribution to the total performance change is then quantified as its Shapley value. We demonstrate the correctness and utility of our method on synthetic, semi-synthetic, and real-world case studies, showing its effectiveness in attributing performance changes to a wide range of distribution shifts.

paragraphs: A deployed model’s performance can change because several aspects of its data change at once. Possible factors include data quality, feature distributions, and the relationship between features and labels. This paper develops a way to assign portions of the performance difference between environments to shifts in the underlying data-generating mechanisms.

The authors formulate attribution as a cooperative game whose players are distributions. A group’s value is the performance change that would occur if only those distributions changed between environments. They derive an importance-weighting method to compute these values, allowing different combinations of shifts to be considered within the same framework.

Each distribution’s contribution is then quantified by its Shapley value, which allocates the total performance change using its contributions across combinations. This gives developers a structured explanation when multiple changes occur together. Synthetic, semi-synthetic, and real-world case studies demonstrate the method’s correctness and utility across a range of distribution shifts. The contribution is a formal attribution procedure that connects a measured performance difference to specific changes in the data-generating process.
summary.tldr: The method combines importance weighting and Shapley values to attribute model performance changes to individual distribution shifts.

title: "Why did the Model Fail?": Attributing Model Performance Changes to Distribution Shifts

abstract: Negotiation is the basis of social interactions; humans negotiate everything from the price of cars to how to share common resources. With rapidly growing interest in using large language models (LLMs) to act as agents on behalf of human users, such LLM agents would also need to be able to negotiate. In this paper, we study how well LLMs can negotiate with each other. We develop NegotiationArena: a flexible framework for evaluating and probing the negotiation abilities of LLM agents. We implemented three types of scenarios in NegotiationArena to assess LLM’s behaviors in allocating shared resources (ultimatum games), aggregate resources (trading games) and buy/sell goods (price negotiations). Each scenario allows for multiple turns of flexible dialogues between LLM agents to allow for more complex negotiations. Interestingly, LLM agents can significantly boost their negotiation outcomes by employing certain behavioral tactics. For example, by pretending to be desolate and desperate, LLMs can improve their payoffs by 20% when negotiating against the standard GPT-4. We also quantify irrational negotiation behaviors exhibited by the LLM agents, many of which also appear in humans. Together, NegotiationArena offers a new environment to investigate LLM interactions, enabling new insights into LLM’s theory of mind, irrationality, and reasoning abilities

This paper examines how well language models negotiate with one another by introducing NegotiationArena, a flexible evaluation framework. The framework is designed to probe behavior over an interaction, allowing agents to exchange multiple turns of dialogue.

The authors implement three kinds of scenarios: ultimatum games for allocating shared resources, trading games for aggregating resources, and negotiations over buying or selling goods. Flexible dialogue permits more complex exchanges within each setting. This gives researchers a way to study how negotiation outcomes respond to agents’ conversational behavior.

The experiments show that behavioral tactics can substantially change payoffs. In one reported example, pretending to be desolate and desperate improves payoffs by 20% against standard GPT-4. The authors also quantify irrational behaviors, many resembling patterns seen in people. These findings make the platform useful for investigating LLM interactions, including reasoning, irrationality, and how agents respond to another participant’s apparent situation.
summary.tldr: NegotiationArena evaluates multi-turn LLM bargaining and finds that behavioral tactics can materially affect outcomes, alongside human-like irrational behaviors.

title: How Well Can LLMs Negotiate? NegotiationArena Platform and Analysis

abstract: Much of the world's most valued data is stored in relational databases and data warehouses, where the data is organized into tables connected by primary-foreign key relations. However, building machine learning models using this data is both challenging and time consuming because no ML algorithm can directly learn from multiple connected tables. Current approaches can only learn from a single table, so data must first be manually joined and aggregated into this format, the laborious process known as feature engineering. Feature engineering is slow, error prone and leads to suboptimal models. Here we introduce Relational Deep Learning (RDL), a blueprint for end-to-end learning on relational databases. The key is to represent relational databases as a temporal, heterogeneous graphs, with a node for each row in each table, and edges specified by primary-foreign key links. Graph Neural Networks then learn representations that leverage all input data, without any manual feature engineering. We also introduce RelBench, and benchmark and testing suite, demonstrating strong initial results. Overall, we define a new research area that generalizes graph machine learning and broadens its applicability.

paragraphs: Relational databases organize information across tables linked by primary and foreign keys. Building predictive models from them commonly requires manually joining and aggregating those tables into a single training table. This position paper argues that the resulting feature-engineering work is time-consuming, prone to errors, and can restrict model quality.

Relational Deep Learning offers a blueprint for learning directly from the connected structure. Each database row becomes a graph node, and primary-foreign key relationships become edges. The resulting graph is temporal and heterogeneous, representing the database's time-related structure and different kinds of entities. Graph neural networks then learn representations from the connected input data.

The authors also introduce RelBench as a benchmark and testing suite and report strong initial results. The proposal matters because it makes table relationships part of what the model learns from, reducing reliance on manually constructed features. As a position paper, it frames this approach as a research area that extends graph machine learning to relational databases and expands the kinds of data it can address.
summary.tldr: Relational Deep Learning represents connected database tables as graphs so neural networks can learn from them without manual feature engineering.

title: Position: Relational Deep Learning - Graph Representation Learning on Relational Databases

abstract: The development of Large Language Models (LLMs) has notably transformed numerous sectors, offering impressive text generation capabilities. Yet, the reliability and truthfulness of these models remain pressing concerns. To this end, we investigate iterative prompting, a strategy hypothesized to refine LLM responses, assessing its impact on LLM truthfulness, an area which has not been thoroughly explored. Our extensive experiments explore the intricacies of iterative prompting variants, examining their influence on the accuracy and calibration of model responses. Our findings reveal that naive prompting methods significantly undermine truthfulness, leading to exacerbated calibration errors. In response to these challenges, we introduce several prompting variants designed to address the identified issues. These variants demonstrate marked improvements over existing baselines, signaling a promising direction for future research. Our work provides a nuanced understanding of iterative prompting and introduces novel approaches to enhance the truthfulness of LLMs, thereby contributing to the development of more accurate and trustworthy AI systems

paragraphs: Iterative prompting asks a language model to revisit or refine its responses through further prompts. It is tempting to expect that additional rounds will improve an answer, but this paper investigates whether they actually improve truthfulness. The study considers both accuracy and calibration: whether the confidence associated with responses matches how often they are correct.

Experiments compare variants of iterative prompting and find that naive approaches can significantly reduce truthfulness while making calibration errors worse. In the tested settings, prompting the model again is therefore not enough to ensure a more reliable answer. Changes in confidence also matter, because a response can become less trustworthy if its confidence becomes less aligned with its correctness.

The authors introduce several prompting variants designed to address the problems they identify. These variants show marked improvements over existing baselines. The contribution is both diagnostic and constructive: it documents failure modes of naive iteration and demonstrates more promising alternatives. The evidence supports careful design of the prompting procedure, rather than a general guarantee that repeated refinement improves truthfulness.
summary.tldr: Naive iterative prompting can worsen truthfulness and calibration, while the paper’s redesigned prompting variants improve over evaluated baselines.

title: Understanding the Effects of Iterative Prompting on Truthfulness

abstract: Large pretrained protein language models (PLMs) have improved protein property and structure prediction from sequences via transfer learning, in which weights and representations from PLMs are repurposed for downstream tasks. Although PLMs have shown great promise, currently there is little understanding of how the features learned by pretraining relate to and are useful for downstream tasks. We perform a systematic analysis of transfer learning using PLMs, conducting 370 experiments across a comprehensive suite of factors including different downstream tasks, architectures, model sizes, model depths, and pretraining time. We observe that while almost all downstream tasks do benefit from pretrained models compared to naive sequence representations, for the majority of tasks performance does not scale with pretraining, and instead relies on low-level features learned early in pretraining. Our results point to a mismatch between current PLM pretraining paradigms and most applications of these models, indicating a need for better pretraining methods.
