paragraphs: Protein language models learn from protein sequences before their representations or weights are reused for property and structure prediction. Although this transfer has been successful, it leaves a question about which learned features actually help downstream tasks. This paper investigates that relationship through a systematic analysis rather than treating pretraining quality as automatically equivalent to downstream usefulness.

The study includes 370 experiments varying downstream tasks, architectures, model sizes, model depths, and pretraining time. Almost all evaluated tasks benefit from pretrained models compared with naive sequence representations. For the majority of tasks, however, performance does not scale with pretraining and instead depends on low-level features acquired early in the pretraining process.

These observations distinguish the value of having pretrained features from the value of extending the existing pretraining approach. The results point to a mismatch between current protein-model pretraining paradigms and most applications examined. They motivate better pretraining methods that more directly support downstream needs, while preserving the finding that pretraining itself is beneficial for almost all studied tasks.
summary.tldr: Across 370 experiments, most protein prediction tasks benefit from pretraining but rely mainly on early-learned features rather than improving as pretraining scales.

title: Feature Reuse and Scaling: Understanding Transfer Learning with Protein Language Models

abstract: Federated learning (FL) enables collaborative machine learning across distributed data owners, but data heterogeneity poses a challenge for model calibration. While prior work focused on improving accuracy for non-iid data, calibration remains under-explored. This study reveals existing FL aggregation approaches lead to sub-optimal calibration, and theoretical analysis shows despite constraining variance in clients’ label distributions, global calibration error is still asymptotically lower bounded. To address this, we propose a novel Federated Calibration (FedCal) approach, emphasizing both local and global calibration. It leverages client-specific scalers for local calibration to effectively correct output misalignment without sacrificing prediction accuracy. These scalers are then aggregated via weight averaging to generate a global scaler, minimizing the global calibration error. Extensive experiments demonstrate that FedCal significantly outperforms the best-performing baseline, reducing global calibration error by 47.66% on average.

This paper focuses on calibration: whether a model's confidence corresponds to how often its predictions are correct. Improving prediction accuracy alone does not resolve this issue, and the authors find that existing aggregation approaches produce suboptimal calibration.

The result supports treating confidence calibration as a distinct federated learning objective and coordinating its treatment across clients and the aggregated model.
summary.tldr: FedCal averages client-specific calibration scalers to improve local and global confidence calibration, reducing global error by 47.66% on average in the reported experiments.

title: FedCal: Achieving Local and Global Calibration in Federated Learning via Aggregated Parameterized Scaler

abstract: Inner Interpretability is a promising emerging field tasked with uncovering the inner mechanisms of AI systems, though how to develop these mechanistic theories is still much debated. Moreover, recent critiques raise issues that question its usefulness to advance the broader goals of AI. However, it has been overlooked that these issues resemble those that have been grappled with in another field: Cognitive Neuroscience. Here we draw the relevant connections and highlight lessons that can be transferred productively between fields. Based on these, we propose a general conceptual framework and give concrete methodological strategies for building mechanistic explanations in AI inner interpretability research. With this conceptual framework, Inner Interpretability can fend off critiques and position itself on a productive path to explain AI systems.

paragraphs: Inner interpretability seeks explanations of the mechanisms inside AI systems. Researchers disagree about how to build those explanations, and critics question whether the field can advance broader AI goals. This position paper argues that cognitive neuroscience offers relevant experience because it has faced similar questions about explaining complex internal mechanisms.

The authors draw connections between the two fields and identify lessons that could transfer productively. From these connections, they propose a general conceptual framework for AI inner interpretability, along with concrete methodological strategies for constructing mechanistic explanations. The intended contribution concerns how research questions and explanations should be developed, rather than a new predictive model.

The paper presents this framework as a way to respond to critiques and guide the field toward more productive explanations of AI systems. Its argument treats the experience of cognitive neuroscience as a resource for methodological progress. The claimed value is a clearer foundation for doing interpretability research, with the framework serving as a proposal for strengthening that work.
summary.tldr: This position paper draws on cognitive neuroscience to propose a framework and methods for explaining AI systems’ internal mechanisms.

title: Position: An Inner Interpretability Framework for AI Inspired by Lessons from Cognitive Neuroscience

abstract: Stochastic weight averaging (SWA) method has empirically proven its advantages compared to stochastic gradient descent (SGD). Despite it is widespread used, theoretical investigations have been limited, particularly in scenarios beyond the ideal setting of convex and sampling with replacement. However, non-convex cases and sampling without replacement are very practical in real-world applications. The main challenges under the above settings are two-folds: (i) All the historical gradient information introduced by SWA is considered, while the analysis of SGD using the tool of uniform stability requires only to bound the current gradient. (ii) The $(1+\alpha\beta)$-expansion property causes the boundary of each gradient step dependent on the previous step, making the boundary of each historical gradient in SWA nested and the theoretical analysis even harder. To address the theoretical challenges, we adopt mathematical induction to find a recursive representation that bounds the gradient at each step. Based on this, we establish stability bounds supporting sampling with and without replacement in the non-convex setting. Furthermore, the derived generalization bounds of SWA are sharper than SGD. At last, experimental results on several benchmarks verify our theoretical results.

The main challenges under the above settings are two-folds: (i) All the historical gradient information introduced by SWA is considered, while the analysis of SGD using the tool of uniform stability requires only to bound the current gradient. (ii) The $(1+\alpha\beta)$-expansion property causes the boundary of each gradient step dependent on the previous step, making the boundary of each historical gradient in SWA nested and the theoretical analysis even harder. To address the theoretical challenges, we adopt mathematical induction to find a recursive representation that bounds the gradient at each step. Based on this, we establish stability bounds supporting sampling with and without replacement in the non-convex setting. Furthermore, the derived generalization bounds of SWA are sharper than SGD. At last, experimental results on several benchmarks verify our theoretical results.

paragraphs: Stochastic weight averaging has demonstrated empirical advantages over stochastic gradient descent, but its theoretical explanation has been more limited. This paper studies generalization in nonconvex settings with sampling either with or without replacement. These settings broaden the analysis beyond the convex, replacement-sampling conditions that had received much of the theoretical attention.

The difficulty comes from the history carried by averaging. A stability analysis must account for historical gradients, whose bounds depend on earlier steps and become nested. The authors use mathematical induction to obtain a recursive representation that bounds the gradient at each step, making this accumulated dependence manageable.

Using that representation, the paper establishes stability bounds for both sampling schemes and derives sharper generalization bounds for stochastic weight averaging than for stochastic gradient descent. The finding supplies theoretical support for the benefits of averaging under the analyzed nonconvex conditions. Experiments on several benchmarks support the theoretical results, linking the mathematical treatment of training history to observed generalization behavior.
summary.tldr: The paper derives sharper generalization bounds for stochastic weight averaging than SGD in nonconvex settings under both major sampling schemes.

title: Generalization Analysis of Stochastic Weight Averaging with General Sampling

abstract: We study the problem of learning discrete latent variable causal structures from mixed-type observational data. Traditional methods, such as those based on the tensor rank condition, are designed to identify discrete latent structure models and provide robust identification bounds for discrete causal models. However, when observed variables—specifically, those representing the children of latent variables—are collected at various levels with continuous data types, the tensor rank condition is not applicable, limiting further causal structure learning for latent variables. In this paper, we consider a more general case where observed variables can be either continuous or discrete, and further allow for scenarios where multiple latent parents cause the same set of observed variables. We show that, under the completeness condition, it is possible to discretize the data in a way that satisfies the full-rank assumption required by the tensor rank condition. This enables the identifiability of discrete latent structure models within mixed-type observational data. Moreover, we introduce the two-sufficient measurement condition, a more general structural assumption under which the tensor rank condition holds and the underlying latent causal structure is identifiable by a proposed two-stage identification algorithm. Extensive experiments on both simulated and real-world data validate the effectiveness of our method.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to recover causal structure involving unobserved discrete variables from observational data. Traditional tensor-rank methods apply to discrete observations, creating a barrier when measured variables include continuous values. The authors consider mixed continuous and discrete observations, including cases where several latent parents cause the same collection of observed variables.

Their first result concerns discretization. Under a completeness condition, they show that the observations can be discretized in a way that satisfies the full-rank assumption required by the tensor-rank condition. This establishes a conditional route for extending identification methods to mixed-type data, rather than assuming that any discretization will preserve the needed information.

They also introduce a structural assumption called the two-sufficient measurement condition. Under this condition, the tensor-rank condition holds and their two-stage algorithm can identify the underlying latent causal structure. Experiments on simulated and real-world data support the method's effectiveness. The key contribution is to connect explicit assumptions about measurements and information content to the possibility of identifying hidden causal structure.
summary.tldr: Under stated completeness and measurement conditions, tensor-rank methods can identify discrete latent causal structures from mixed-type observations.

title: Identification of Latent Confounders via Investigating the Tensor Ranks of the Nonlinear Observations

abstract: Simulating a single trajectory of a dynamical system under some state-dependent policy is a core bottleneck in policy optimization (PO) algorithms. The many inherently serial policy evaluations that must be performed in a single simulation constitute the bulk of this bottleneck. In applying PO to supply chain optimization (SCO) problems, simulating a single sample path corresponding to one month of a supply chain can take several hours. We present an iterative algorithm to accelerate policy simulation, dubbed Picard Iteration. This scheme carefully assigns policy evaluation tasks to independent processes. Within an iteration, any given process evaluates the policy only on its assigned tasks while assuming a certain cached’ evaluation for other tasks; the cache is updated at the end of the iteration. Implemented on GPUs, this scheme admits batched evaluation of the policy across a single trajectory. We prove that the structure afforded by many SCO problems allows convergence in a small number of iterations independent of the horizon. We demonstrate practical speedups of 400x on large-scale SCO problems even with a single GPU, and also demonstrate practical efficacy in other RL environments.

paragraphs: Simulating a policy can be slow because each action depends on the state produced by earlier actions. In supply chain optimization, simulating a single month can take several hours. This paper targets the repeated, serial policy evaluations within one trajectory, a bottleneck that directly affects how quickly policy optimization can proceed.

The proposed Picard Iteration algorithm distributes policy evaluation tasks among independent processes. During an iteration, each process evaluates its assigned tasks while using cached evaluations for the others. The cache is updated after the iteration. This iterative arrangement allows policy evaluations from a single trajectory to be batched on a GPU despite the trajectory’s underlying sequential dependencies.

The authors prove that structure present in many supply chain optimization problems permits convergence in a small number of iterations independent of the simulation horizon. The result relies on that problem structure. Experiments demonstrate speedups of 400 times on large-scale supply chain problems using a single GPU, along with practical effectiveness in other reinforcement learning environments. The contribution accelerates simulation by reorganizing how dependent evaluations are computed.
summary.tldr: Picard Iteration enables batched policy evaluations within a trajectory, demonstrating 400-fold simulation speedups on large supply chain problems.

title: Speeding up Policy Simulation in Supply Chain RL

abstract: We study a model of subscription-based platforms where users pay a fixed fee for unlimited access to content, and creators receive a share of the revenue. Existing approaches to detecting fraud predominantly rely on machine learning methods, engaging in an ongoing arms race with bad actors. We explore revenue division mechanisms that inherently disincentivize manipulation. We formalize three types of manipulation-resistance axioms and examine which existing rules satisfy these. We show that a mechanism widely used by streaming platforms, not only fails to prevent fraud, but also makes detecting manipulation computationally intractable. We also introduce a novel rule, ScaledUserProp, that satisfies all three manipulation-resistance axioms. Finally, experiments with both real-world and synthetic streaming data support ScaledUserProp as a fairer alternative compared to existing rules.

paragraphs: Subscription platforms collect a fixed payment from users and distribute revenue among creators whose content those users access. This creates a design problem: the allocation rule can encourage or discourage attempts to manipulate payments. The paper studies whether resistance to manipulation can be built into revenue division itself, reducing reliance on an ongoing contest between fraud detection and evasion.

The authors formalize three manipulation-resistance requirements and evaluate existing allocation rules against them. They show that a mechanism widely used by streaming platforms fails to prevent fraud. Within their model, it also makes detecting manipulation computationally intractable, connecting the payment rule to the difficulty of policing its misuse.

The proposed alternative, ScaledUserProp, satisfies all three formal requirements. Experiments using real-world and synthetic streaming data also support it as a fairer option than existing rules. The contribution therefore combines a formal account of incentives with empirical evidence about revenue allocation, showing how changing the mechanism can address the manipulation problem at its source.
summary.tldr: ScaledUserProp divides subscription revenue while satisfying three manipulation-resistance requirements, with experiments supporting fairer allocations.

title: Fraud-Proof Revenue Division on Subscription Platforms

abstract: Progress in 3D vision-language learning has been hindered by the scarcity of large-scale 3D datasets. We introduce UniVLG, a unified architecture for 2D and 3D vision-language understanding that bridges the gap between existing 2D-centric models and the rich 3D sensory data available in embodied systems. Our approach initializes most model weights from pre-trained 2D models and trains on both 2D and 3D vision-language data. We propose a novel language-conditioned mask decoder shared across 2D and 3D modalities to ground objects effectively in both RGB and RGB-D images, outperforming box-based approaches. To further reduce the domain gap between 2D and 3D, we incorporate 2D-to-3D lifting strategies, enabling UniVLG to utilize 2D data to enhance 3D performance. With these innovations, our model achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple 3D vision-language grounding tasks, demonstrating the potential of transferring advances from 2D vision-language learning to the data-constrained 3D domain. Furthermore, co-training on both 2D and 3D data enhances performance across modalities without sacrificing 2D capabilities. By removing the reliance on 3D mesh reconstruction and ground-truth object proposals, UniVLG sets a new standard for realistic, embodied-aligned evaluation. Code and additional visualizations are available at https://univlg.github.io.

The aim is to transfer existing visual-language capabilities into settings with depth information.

A shared language-conditioned mask decoder grounds objects in both RGB and RGB-D images. The paper reports that this mask-based approach outperforms box-based alternatives. It also introduces 2D-to-3D lifting strategies to reduce the gap between modalities, allowing 2D training data to contribute to improved 3D performance.

The approach also removes dependence on reconstructed 3D meshes and ground-truth object proposals, supporting evaluation more closely aligned with embodied sensing. These findings show how shared components, transferred initialization, and cross-modal training can help compensate for limited 3D data.
summary.tldr: UniVLG transfers pretrained 2D capabilities into a shared 2D–3D grounding architecture, improving evaluated 3D performance while preserving 2D capabilities.

title: Unifying 2D and 3D Vision-Language Understanding

abstract: We study transfer learning for matrix completion in a Missing Not-at-Random (MNAR) setting that is motivated by biological problems. The target matrix $Q$ has entire rows and columns missing, making estimation impossible without side information. To address this, we use a noisy and incomplete source matrix $P$, which relates to $Q$ via a feature shift in latent space. We consider both the active and passive sampling of rows and columns. We establish minimax lower bounds for entrywise estimation error in each setting. Our computationally efficient estimation framework achieves this lower bound for the active setting, which leverages the source data to query the most informative rows and columns of $Q$. This avoids the need for incoherence assumptions required for rate optimality in the passive sampling setting. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through comparisons with existing algorithms on real-world biological datasets.

paragraphs: Completing a matrix becomes especially difficult when entire rows and columns are missing. In the setting studied here, the target matrix cannot be estimated without additional information. Motivated by biological problems, the paper uses a related source matrix that is itself noisy and incomplete, with the relationship described by a feature shift in latent space.

The authors study both passive sampling and active sampling, where the method can choose which target rows and columns to query. They establish minimax lower bounds on entrywise estimation error in each setting. These bounds characterize the best achievable worst-case accuracy under the respective sampling conditions.

Their computationally efficient framework reaches the lower bound in the active setting by using source information to select informative target queries. This avoids the incoherence assumptions needed for rate optimality under passive sampling. Comparisons on real biological datasets demonstrate the approach's effectiveness. The result connects useful transfer to both the source-target relationship and the ability to choose what target information to collect.
summary.tldr: Source-guided active sampling enables an efficient matrix-completion method to attain optimal entrywise error bounds when entire target rows and columns are missing.

title: Optimal Transfer Learning for Missing Not-at-Random Matrix Completion

abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) for tabular understanding have made significant progress in tasks such as financial report analysis and public data tests. However, our comprehensive analysis shows that these models are still limited in certain simple scenarios, particularly when handling compositional conditions in QA. Further investigation reveals that the poor performance can be attributed to two main challenges: the visual encoder’s inability to accurately recognize the content of a row, and the model’s tendency to overlook conditions in the question. To address these, we introduce a new Compositional Condition Tabular Understanding method, called CoCoTab. Specifically, to capture the structural relationships within tables, we enhance the visual encoder with additional row and column patches. Moreover, we introduce the conditional tokens between the visual patches and query embeddings, ensuring the model focuses on relevant parts of the table according to the conditions specified in the query. Additionally, we also introduce the Massive Multimodal Tabular Understanding (MMTU) benchmark, which comprehensively assesses the full capabilities of MLLMs in tabular understanding. Our proposed method achieves state-of-the-art performance on both existing tabular understanding benchmarks and MMTU. Our code can be available at https://github.com/LAMDA-Tabular/MMTU.

paragraphs: Answering a question about a table can require satisfying several conditions together. This paper finds that multimodal language models still struggle with such questions, even in otherwise simple settings. Its analysis identifies two sources of error: visual encoders fail to recognize row contents accurately, and models overlook conditions expressed in the question.

CoCoTab addresses both problems through changes to the model’s representation of the table and its connection to the question. Additional row and column patches help the visual encoder capture table structure. Conditional tokens placed between visual patches and query embeddings direct attention toward table regions relevant to the requested conditions, connecting what the model reads with what it must answer.

The authors also introduce the Massive Multimodal Tabular Understanding benchmark, or MMTU, to assess tabular understanding more broadly. CoCoTab achieves state-of-the-art results on MMTU and existing table benchmarks. The findings support treating structural recognition and condition-following as connected requirements: accurately reading individual contents is insufficient if the model fails to apply the question’s constraints.
summary.tldr: CoCoTab improves table question answering by strengthening row and column representations and explicitly connecting question conditions to visual content.

title: Compositional Condition Question Answering in Tabular Understanding

abstract: We propose a greedy search-and-score algorithm for ancestral graphs, which include directed as well as bidirected edges, originating from unobserved latent variables. The normalized likelihood score of ancestral graphs is estimated in terms of multivariate information over relevant "$ac$-connected subset" of vertices, $\boldsymbol{C}$, that are connected through collider paths confined to the ancestor set of $\boldsymbol{C}$. For computational efficiency, the proposed two-step algorithm relies on local information scores limited to the close surrounding vertices of each node (step 1) and edge (step 2). This computational strategy, although restricted to information contributions from $ac$-connected subsets containing up to two-collider paths, is shown to outperform state-of-the-art causal discovery methods on challenging benchmark datasets.

paragraphs: This paper develops a greedy search procedure for learning ancestral graphs from complex nonlinear and categorical data. These graphs allow both directed edges and bidirected edges, with the latter representing relationships arising from unobserved variables. Including this second edge type lets the search account for dependencies that involve hidden factors.

The method estimates a normalized likelihood score using multivariate information from selected groups of vertices. The relevant groups are called ac-connected subsets: their vertices connect through collider paths restricted to the group's ancestor set. This construction determines which collections of variables contribute information to the graph score, rather than relying only on isolated pairs.

To keep computation manageable, the algorithm works in two steps, using local information around nodes first and around edges second. It restricts the included information contributions to subsets containing paths with up to two colliders. Despite this explicit restriction, the authors report better performance than state-of-the-art causal discovery methods on challenging benchmark datasets. The result supports the practical value of this localized scoring strategy in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: A local multivariate-information scoring method makes greedy ancestral-graph search efficient and outperforms leading causal discovery methods on challenging benchmarks.

title: An Efficient Search-and-Score Algorithm for Ancestral Graphs using Multivariate Information Scores for Complex Non-linear and Categorical Data

abstract: We study online finite-horizon Markov Decision Processes with adversarially changing loss and aggregate bandit feedback (a.k.a full-bandit). Under this type of feedback, the agent observes only the total loss incurred over the entire trajectory, rather than the individual losses at each intermediate step within the trajectory. We introduce the first Policy Optimization algorithms for this setting. In the known-dynamics case, we achieve the first optimal regret bound of $\tilde \Theta(H^2\sqrt{SAK})$, where $K$ is the number of episodes, $H$ is the episode horizon, $S$ is the number of states, and $A$ is the number of actions. In the unknown dynamics case we establish regret bound of $\tilde O(H^3 S \sqrt{AK})$, significantly improving the best known result by a factor of $H^2 S^5 A^2$.

paragraphs: This paper studies sequential decision-making when an agent sees only the total loss from an entire episode. It receives no separate loss for each intermediate action, making feedback less informative about where the episode went well or badly. The setting also allows losses to change adversarially across episodes within a finite-horizon Markov decision process.

The authors introduce the first policy-optimization algorithms for this aggregate-feedback setting. When the transition dynamics are known, they obtain an optimal regret bound of H²√(SAK), up to logarithmic factors. Here, H is the episode length, S the number of states, A the number of actions, and K the number of episodes. Regret measures the cumulative performance gap that the learning procedure seeks to control.

For unknown dynamics, the paper proves a bound of H³S√(AK), again up to logarithmic factors. This improves the previous best result by a factor of H²S⁵A². The distinction between known and unknown dynamics is central: learning the environment adds difficulty, while the known-dynamics guarantee reaches the optimal rate stated for this feedback model.
summary.tldr: New policy-optimization algorithms achieve optimal known-dynamics regret and substantially improved unknown-dynamics regret using only episode-total losses.

title: Near-optimal Regret Using Policy Optimization in Online MDPs with Aggregate Bandit Feedback

abstract: Distributed optimization has become the default training paradigm in modern machine learning due to the growing scale of models and datasets. To mitigate communication overhead, local updates are often applied before global aggregation, resulting in a nested optimization approach with inner and outer steps. However, heavy-tailed stochastic gradient noise remains a significant challenge, particularly in attention-based models, hindering effective training. In this work, we propose TailOPT, an efficient framework designed to address heavy-tailed noise by leveraging adaptive optimization and novel clipping techniques. We establish convergence guarantees for the TailOPT framework under heavy-tailed noise with local updates and potentially unbounded gradient variance. Among its variants, we propose a memory- and communication-efficient instantiation (named $Bi^2Clip$) that performs coordinate-wise clipping from both above and below at both the inner and outer optimizers. $Bi^2Clip$ brings about benefits of adaptive optimization (e.g., Adam) without the cost of maintaining or transmitting additional gradient statistics. Empirically, TailOPT, including $Bi^2Clip$, demonstrates superior performance on various tasks and models compared with state-of-the-art methods, while being more efficient.

paragraphs: Distributed training often performs several local optimization steps before combining updates across machines. This reduces communication, but creates inner and outer optimization processes that must both handle noisy gradients. The paper studies heavy-tailed noise, where unusually large fluctuations can make training difficult and gradient variance may be unbounded.

TailOPT combines adaptive optimization with new clipping techniques for this setting. The authors establish convergence guarantees that allow local updates and potentially unbounded gradient variance. A particular version, Bi²Clip, clips individual gradient coordinates from above and below at both optimization levels. It aims to capture benefits associated with adaptive methods such as Adam without maintaining or communicating additional gradient statistics.

This design links robustness to noisy updates with practical limits on memory and communication. Experiments across several tasks and models report better performance than state-of-the-art methods alongside greater efficiency. The theoretical contribution concerns convergence in the heavy-tailed setting, while the empirical contribution shows that the framework and its economical clipping variant can also be useful in the evaluated training workloads.
summary.tldr: TailOPT uses adaptive optimization and clipping to make distributed training efficient and provably convergent under heavy-tailed gradient noise.

title: Efficient Distributed Optimization under Heavy-Tailed Noise

abstract: Neural scaling laws have garnered significant interest due to their ability to predict model performance as a function of increasing parameters, data, and compute. In this work, we propose a simple statistical ansatz based on memorization to study scaling laws in the context of inference. Specifically, how performance improves with multiple inference attempts. We explore the coverage, or pass@k metric, which measures the chance of success over repeated attempts and provide a motivation for the observed functional form of the inference scaling behavior of the coverage in large language models (LLMs) on reasoning tasks. We then define an "inference loss", which exhibits a power law decay as the number of trials increases, and connect this result with prompting costs. We further test the universality of our construction by conducting experiments on a simple generative model, and find that our predictions are in agreement with the empirical coverage curves in a controlled setting. Our simple framework sets the ground for incorporating inference scaling with other known scaling laws.

paragraphs: Giving a language model several attempts can increase the chance that at least one answer succeeds. This paper studies how that chance changes as the number of attempts grows. It focuses on coverage, also called pass@k, which measures success somewhere among the attempts rather than the quality of a single answer.

The authors propose a simple statistical model built around memorization to explain the shape of inference scaling curves observed on reasoning tasks. Within this framework, they define an inference loss that decreases according to a power law as more trials are made. They also connect that behavior to prompting costs, relating the benefit of additional attempts to the resources those attempts require.

Experiments with a simple generative model produce coverage curves consistent with the framework’s predictions in a controlled setting. This agreement supports the proposed explanation without establishing that it describes every language model or task. The contribution is a tractable starting point for connecting repeated inference with scaling laws concerning training data, model size, and computation.
summary.tldr: A memorization-based statistical model explains how repeated inference attempts can improve coverage and connects their gains to prompting costs.

title: A Simple Model of Inference Scaling Laws

abstract: Learning to solve complex tasks with signal temporal logic (STL) specifications is crucial to many real-world applications. However, most previous works only consider fixed or parametrized STL specifications due to the lack of a diverse STL dataset and encoders to effectively extract temporal logic information for downstream tasks. In this paper, we propose TeLoGraF, Temporal Logic Graph-encoded Flow, which utilizes Graph Neural Networks (GNN) encoder and flow-matching to learn solutions for general STL specifications. We identify four commonly used STL templates and collect a total of 200K specifications with paired demonstrations. We conduct extensive experiments in five simulation environments ranging from simple dynamical models in the 2D space to high-dimensional 7DoF Franka Panda robot arm and Ant quadruped navigation. Results show that our method outperforms other baselines in the STL satisfaction rate. Compared to classical STL planning algorithms, our approach is 10-100X faster in inference and can work on any system dynamics. Besides, we show our graph-encoding method’s capability to solve complex STLs and robustness to out-distribution STL specifications. Code is available at https://github.com/mengyuest/TeLoGraF

However, most previous works only consider fixed or parametrized STL specifications due to the lack of a diverse STL dataset and encoders to effectively extract temporal logic information for downstream tasks. In this paper, we propose TeLoGraF, Temporal Logic Graph-encoded Flow, which utilizes Graph Neural Networks (GNN) encoder and flow-matching to learn solutions for general STL specifications. We identify four commonly used STL templates and collect a total of 200K specifications with paired demonstrations. We conduct extensive experiments in five simulation environments ranging from simple dynamical models in the 2D space to high-dimensional 7DoF Franka Panda robot arm and Ant quadruped navigation. Results show that our method outperforms other baselines in the STL satisfaction rate. Compared to classical STL planning algorithms, our approach is 10-100X faster in inference and can work on any system dynamics. Besides, we show our graph-encoding method’s capability to solve complex STLs and robustness to out-distribution STL specifications. Code is available at https://github.com/mengyuest/TeLoGraF

paragraphs: Signal temporal logic specifies tasks with logical and timing requirements. Learning to solve diverse specifications is difficult when training data and representations cover mainly fixed or narrowly parameterized forms. TeLoGraF addresses this with a graph neural network encoder and flow matching for learning solutions to general temporal-logic specifications.

The authors identify four commonly used specification templates and assemble 200,000 specifications paired with demonstrations. The graph encoder extracts information from the logical structure, while flow matching forms part of the learned solution method. Evaluation spans five simulated environments, from two-dimensional dynamical systems to a seven-degree-of-freedom Franka Panda arm and Ant quadruped navigation.

TeLoGraF achieves higher specification-satisfaction rates than the tested baselines. Compared with classical temporal-logic planners, it reports inference that is 10 to 100 times faster, and the approach is presented as applicable to any system dynamics. Further results demonstrate the graph encoding's ability to handle complex specifications and robustness to specifications outside the training distribution. These findings support learning across a broader range of logically structured tasks.
summary.tldr: TeLoGraF combines graph encoding and flow matching to solve diverse temporal-logic tasks, improving tested satisfaction rates and speeding inference relative to classical planners.

title: TeLoGraF: Temporal Logic Planning via Graph-encoded Flow Matching

abstract: This paper studies the interplay between learning algorithms and graph structure for graph neural networks (GNNs). Existing theoretical studies on the learning dynamics of GNNs primarily focus on the convergence rates of learning algorithms under the interpolation regime (noise-free) and offer only a crude connection between these dynamics and the actual graph structure (e.g., maximum degree). This paper aims to bridge this gap by investigating the excessive risk (generalization performance) of learning algorithms in GNNs within the generalization regime (with noise). Specifically, we extend the conventional settings from the learning theory literature to the context of GNNs and examine how graph structure influences the performance of learning algorithms such as stochastic gradient descent (SGD) and Ridge regression. Our study makes several key contributions toward understanding the interplay between graph structure and learning in GNNs. First, we derive the excess risk profiles of SGD and Ridge regression in GNNs and connect these profiles to the graph structure through spectral graph theory. With this established framework, we further explore how different graph structures (regular vs. power-law) impact the performance of these algorithms through comparative analysis. Additionally, we extend our analysis to multi-layer linear GNNs, revealing an increasing non-isotropic effect on the excess risk profile, thereby offering new insights into the over-smoothing issue in GNNs from the perspective of learning algorithms. Our empirical results align with our theoretical predictions, collectively showcasing a coupling relation among graph structure, GNNs and learning algorithms, and providing insights on GNN algorithm design and selection in practice.

title: On the Interplay between Graph Structure and Learning Algorithms in Graph Neural Networks

abstract: Advancements in generative models have promoted text- and image-based multi-context image generation. Brain signals, offering a direct representation of user intent, present new opportunities for image customization. However, it faces challenges in brain interpretation, cross-modal context fusion and retention. In this paper, we present MindCustomer to explore the blending of visual brain signals in multi-context image generation. We first design shared neural data augmentation for stable cross-subject brain embedding by introducing the Image-Brain Translator (IBT) to generate brain responses from visual images. Then, we propose an effective cross-modal information fusion pipeline that mask-freely adapts distinct semantics from image and brain contexts within a diffusion model. It resolves semantic conflicts for context preservation and enables harmonious context integration. During the fusion pipeline, we further utilize the IBT to transfer image context to the brain representation to mitigate the cross-modal disparity. MindCustomer enables cross-subject generation, delivering unified, high-quality, and natural image outputs. Moreover, it exhibits strong generalization for new subjects via few-shot learning, indicating the potential for practical application. As the first work for multi-context blending with brain signal, MindCustomer lays a foundational exploration and inspiration for future brain-controlled generative technologies.

paragraphs: MindCustomer explores image generation that combines image context with visual brain signals. The challenge is to interpret signals across people while preserving information from different input types. Those inputs can express conflicting meanings, so simply bringing them together does not ensure a coherent generated image.

The method introduces an Image-Brain Translator that generates brain responses from visual images. This supports shared neural data augmentation for more stable brain representations across subjects. The translator also maps image context into the brain representation during fusion, reducing the mismatch between the two kinds of information. A diffusion-based pipeline then integrates their distinct semantics without requiring masks and addresses conflicts to preserve context.

The authors report high-quality, natural outputs in cross-subject generation and strong generalization to new subjects with few-shot learning. These findings suggest potential for practical customization using brain signals alongside other visual context. The work is presented as an initial exploration of this combination, providing a foundation for further brain-controlled generative technologies.
summary.tldr: MindCustomer combines visual brain signals and image context through shared representations and diffusion-based fusion for customized image generation.

title: MindCustomer: Multi-Context Image Generation Blended with Brain Signal

abstract: Deep models are increasingly used to analyze brain graphs for the diagnosis and understanding of brain diseases. However, due to the multi-site data aggregation and individual differences, brain graph datasets exhibit widespread distribution shifts, which impair the model’s generalization ability to the test set, thereby limiting the performance of existing methods. To address these issues, we propose a Causally Invariance-aware Augmentation for brain Graph Contrastive Learning, called CIA-GCL. This method first generates a brain graph by extracting node features based on the topological structure. Then, a learnable brain invariant subgraph is identified based on a causal decoupling approach to capture the maximum label-related invariant information with invariant learning. Around this invariant subgraph, we design a novel invariance-aware augmentation strategy to generate meaningful augmented samples for graph contrast learning. Finally, the extracted invariant subgraph is utilized for brain disease classification, effectively mitigating distribution shifts while also identifying critical local graph structures, enhancing the model’s interpretability. Experiments on three real-world brain disease datasets demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance, effectively generalizes to multi-site brain datasets, and provides certain interpretability.

paragraphs: Brain graph models can struggle when data from different collection sites or individuals follow different distributions. CIA-GCL addresses this problem by learning which parts of a brain graph contain label-related information that remains stable across these differences. The aim is to support disease classification without relying as heavily on patterns that change between datasets.

The method first constructs a brain graph with node features derived from its topology. It then uses causal decoupling and invariant learning to identify a learnable subgraph intended to retain as much stable, label-related information as possible. This subgraph guides the creation of augmented examples for contrastive learning, connecting the choice of training variations to the information the model should preserve.

The same extracted subgraph is used for classification and highlights local structures relevant to the model's predictions. Experiments on three real-world brain disease datasets report state-of-the-art performance and generalization across sites. The highlighted structures also provide some interpretability, making the method's contribution both improved robustness to distribution shifts and a more inspectable basis for classification.
summary.tldr: CIA-GCL builds graph augmentations around learned invariant brain subgraphs to improve disease classification across differing data distributions.

title: Causal Invariance-aware Augmentation for Brain Graph Contrastive Learning

abstract: While mechanistic interpretability has identified interpretable circuits in large language models (LLMs), their causal origins in training data remain elusive. We introduce mechanistic data attribution (MDA), a scalable framework that employs influence functions to trace interpretable units back to specific training samples. Through extensive experiments on the Pythia family, we causally validate that targeted intervention—removing or augmenting a small fraction of high-influence samples—significantly modulates the emergence of interpretable heads, whereas random interventions show no effect. Our analysis reveals that repetitive structural data (e.g., LaTeX, XML) acts as a mechanistic catalyst. Furthermore, we observe that interventions targeting induction head formation induce a concurrent change in the model’s in-context learning (ICL) capability. This provides direct causal evidence for the long-standing hypothesis regarding the functional link between induction heads and ICL. Finally, we propose a mechanistic data augmentation pipeline that consistently accelerates circuit convergence across model scales, providing a principled methodology for steering the developmental trajectories of LLMs.

paragraphs: Identifying an interpretable component inside a language model does not by itself explain which training examples caused it to develop. Mechanistic Data Attribution addresses this origin question. The framework uses influence functions to trace interpretable model units back to particular training samples.

Experiments on the Pythia family test those attributions through interventions. Removing or augmenting a small fraction of highly influential samples significantly changes the emergence of interpretable attention heads, whereas random interventions show no effect in the reported experiments. The analysis identifies repetitive structural material, including LaTeX and XML, as a catalyst for these mechanisms.

The authors present this as direct causal evidence for the hypothesized functional connection between induction heads and in-context learning. They additionally build a data-augmentation pipeline that consistently accelerates circuit convergence across model scales. Together, the findings connect training-data selection to internal mechanism development and show a concrete way to influence that development through targeted data changes.
summary.tldr: Mechanistic Data Attribution identifies training samples whose targeted modification causally changes interpretable heads and associated in-context learning behavior.

title: Mechanistic Data Attribution: Tracing the Training Origins of Interpretable LLM Units

abstract: Machine unlearning aims to remove the influence of specific forget training data due to privacy, copyright or bias concerns while maintaining the model performance on the remaining retain data. Existing unlearning algorithms, such as optimizing a weighted combination of losses, have tried to achieve these objectives of improving forget quality and maintaining retain utility. However, they do not guarantee that these objectives can be improved by a specified extent for all forget and retain data. In this work, we address this limitation with a novel and theoretically-grounded approach from a constrained optimization perspective. Firstly, we identify that the hardness of reconciling both objectives can be quantified by the similarity between the forget data and the retain data. Next, we derive an unlearning algorithm (HAMU) with the overall goal of guaranteeing a specified improvement in forget quality while minimizing the retain utility cost/degradation by updating the model weights based on our hardness measure. Our hardness measure also informs users when retain utility degradation is unavoidable, i.e., both objectives cannot be improved simultaneously, and stopping should be considered. Our algorithm is applicable to non-convex models and is easily parallelizable, making it readily deployable in real-world scenarios. We empirically demonstrate HAMU’s superior performance over baselines on both image and text datasets using large models. Our code is available at https://github.com/aoi3142/HAMU.

paragraphs: Machine unlearning tries to remove the influence of selected training data while preserving performance on the data that remain. These goals can conflict. The paper argues that combining losses with fixed weights does not guarantee specified improvements across forget and retain data, motivating an approach based on constrained optimization.

HAMU measures the difficulty of reconciling the objectives through similarity between forget and retain data. It uses this hardness measure to guide weight updates toward a specified improvement in forgetting while minimizing damage to retained utility. The measure also identifies situations where retaining utility must worsen and simultaneous improvement is impossible, providing a reason to consider stopping.

The algorithm applies to non-convex models and supports parallel execution. Experiments with large models on image and text datasets report better performance than the tested baselines. Its contribution is both an unlearning procedure and a way to assess the tradeoff: the method explicitly accounts for when removing one influence conflicts with preserving another.
summary.tldr: HAMU uses forget–retain similarity to guide unlearning and identify when preserving retained performance conflicts with forgetting.

title: How Hard Can It Be? Hardness-Aware Multi-Objective Unlearning

abstract: Influential benchmarks incentivize competing model builders to strategically allocate post-training resources towards improvements on the leaderboard, a phenomenon dubbed benchmaxxing or training on the test task. In this work, we initiate a principled study of the incentive structure that benchmarks induce. We model benchmarking as a Stackelberg game between a benchmark designer who chooses an evaluation protocol and multiple model providers who compete simultaneously in a subgame given by the designer’s choice. Each competitor has a model of unknown latent quality and can inflate its observed score by allocating resources to benchmark-specific improvements. First, we prove that current benchmarks induce games for which no Nash equilibrium between model developers exists. This result suggests one explanation for why current practice leads to misaligned incentives, prompting model providers to strategize in opaque ways. However, we prove that under mild conditions, a recently proposed evaluation protocol, called tune-before-test, induces a benchmark with a unique Nash equilibrium that ranks models by latent quality. This positive result demonstrates that benchmarks need not set bad incentives, even if current evaluations do.

paragraphs: A benchmark affects more than how models are measured: it also influences what their developers choose to improve. This paper studies providers who can spend post-training resources on benchmark-specific gains, raising observed scores without necessarily changing underlying model quality. The question is whether an evaluation protocol can produce reliable rankings despite these incentives.

The authors model evaluation as a Stackelberg game. A benchmark designer first chooses the protocol, then model providers compete under that choice. Each model has unknown latent quality, and each provider decides how to allocate resources to score improvement. summary.tldr: A game-theoretic analysis shows that tune-before-test can, under mild conditions, align strategic model competition with latent-quality rankings.

title: Leaderboard Incentives: Model Rankings under Strategic Post-Training

abstract: While Contrastive Learning (CL) has revolutionized self-supervised representation learning, its latent representations remain highly entangled and opaque, limiting their interpretability in safety-critical applications. We identify that a fundamental cause of this entanglement is the reliance on deterministic similarity measures, which treat all feature dimensions equally. In compositional scenes, this creates an Optimization Conflict: common background features, such as, "blue sky", are encouraged to align in positive pairs but simultaneously repelled in negative pairs, causing gradient oscillations that hinder precise semantic disentanglement. To address this, we propose BayesNCL (Bayesian Gated Non-Negative Contrastive Learning). Unlike standard approaches, BayesNCL introduces a probabilistic gating mechanism that dynamically filters out task-irrelevant, high-frequency common features while selectively retaining discriminative semantics. By formalizing feature selection as a variational inference problem with a sparse Bernoulli prior, our method effectively resolves the optimization conflict. Empirical experimental results on Imagenet-100 demonstrate that BayesNCL achieves a remarkable 142.1% improvement in semantic consistency compared to state-of-the-art baselines, yielding highly interpretable representations without compromising downstream task performance. Code is available at https://github.com/Cui-Peng-624/BayesNCL.

paragraphs: Contrastive learning learns representations by bringing related examples together and separating unrelated ones. The paper identifies a conflict when scenes share common features, such as blue sky. The same feature can be encouraged to match across positive pairs and pushed apart across negative pairs, producing competing gradient signals that interfere with separating meaningful concepts.

BayesNCL addresses this conflict through probabilistic feature gates. These gates filter frequent features that are irrelevant to the task while retaining features that distinguish examples. The authors formulate the selection process as variational inference with a sparse Bernoulli prior, making selective feature use part of the learning objective. This changes which information contributes to similarity comparisons instead of treating every feature dimension equally.

On ImageNet-100, the authors report a 142.1% improvement in semantic consistency relative to state-of-the-art baselines, without sacrificing downstream task performance. The finding supports their proposed connection between conflicting contrastive signals and entangled representations. In the reported experiments, resolving that conflict makes the learned features more interpretable while preserving their usefulness.
summary.tldr: BayesNCL uses probabilistic feature selection to reduce conflicting contrastive signals and improve representation interpretability without hurting reported downstream performance.

title: Bayesian Gated Non-Negative Contrastive Learning

abstract: AI for fusion requires bridging a critical “sim-to-real” gap: simulation-trained models must generalize reliably under distribution shifts in safety-critical workflows. Focusing on the nonlinear Grad-Shafranov equation (GSE), we develop and analyze a physics-anchored operator-learning framework for fixed-boundary equilibrium prediction. The framework combines data anchors with PDE residual constraints and uses a physics-motivated Transformer-KAN Neural Operator (TKNO) to capture global elliptic coupling and nonlinear source response. Under multi-parameter distribution shifts, our analysis shows that data-only surrogates can develop severe OOD tails, while physics-only training may converge to incorrect solution branches; by combining data anchors with PDE constraints, physics-anchored training reduces worst-tail errors on shape-driven and joint shifts. Non-causal diagnostics associate data supervision with fewer branch-scale failures and physics-anchored training with lower OOD-induced high-frequency error amplification. Evaluated on EXL-50U discharge inputs against the device’s operational equilibrium solver, the model achieves close agreement (mean relative RMSE of 1.27%) with millisecond-level inference. These results provide a practical route toward physically reliable AI surrogates for fusion workflows. Our Code is available at https://github.com/dsqzhou/physics-anchored-gse

This paper studies fixed-boundary solutions of the nonlinear Grad-Shafranov equation. summary.tldr: Combining data anchors with physics constraints improves shifted-input fusion equilibrium prediction and closely matches an operational solver at millisecond speed.

title: Physics-informed Neural Operator Learning for Nonlinear Grad-Shafranov Equation

abstract: The rapid scaling of large language models (LLMs) has made distributed inference indispensable, yet end-to-end latency is increasingly dominated by communication, forming a critical bandwidth wall that fundamentally limits the practical gains of existing quantization techniques. Existing approaches typically treat communication and computation in isolation, failing to exploit their coupled nature and introducing limited system-level acceleration and accuracy degradation. To address this, we propose CoCoQuant, a co-designed framework that jointly optimizes communication and computation as a unified end-to-end design space. CoCoQuant introduces a precision-aligned graph-rewriting that enables zero-overhead fusion between low-precision communication and computation. CoCoQuant formulates a hardware-aware mixed-precision allocation problem that integrates roofline-based cost modeling with relative sensitivity calibration, solved via global integer linear programming. Extensive experiments on LLMs of varing scales demonstrate that CoCoQuant achieves Pareto-optimal accuracy-latency trade-offs, delivering up to 2.92 end-to-end speedup with a negligible increase in perplexity (0.22).

paragraphs: When large language models run across multiple devices, transferring information between devices can dominate inference time. Reducing the precision of computation alone therefore offers limited benefit if communication remains expensive. CoCoQuant addresses this by treating communication precision and computation precision as parts of one system-level optimization problem.

The framework rewrites the computation graph so that low-precision communication and computation use compatible precision choices, enabling fusion without additional overhead. It then selects mixed precisions using a hardware-aware optimization problem. A roofline-based cost model estimates performance costs, relative sensitivity calibration accounts for accuracy effects, and a global integer linear program chooses the allocation.

Experiments across language models of different scales report Pareto-optimal accuracy–latency trade-offs, with up to 2.92-fold end-to-end speedup and a perplexity increase of 0.22, described as negligible. The reported benefit is that coordinated precision choices can improve actual inference time while preserving accuracy closely. The maximum speedup is an experimental result across the evaluated settings, rather than a uniform acceleration for every model.
summary.tldr: CoCoQuant jointly optimizes communication and computation precision, reporting up to 2.92-fold inference speedup with a small perplexity increase.

title: CoCoQuant: Breaking the Bandwidth Wall via Co-Optimized Communication and Computation Quantization

abstract: As pre-trained models evolve rapidly, transferring fine-tuning knowledge to updated models without retraining has become a critical challenge. Most existing methods reuse parameter updates, yet the same dataset can induce substantially different updates across base models due to mismatched local loss landscapes, making such transfer unstable. We instead adopt a Bayesian-updating perspective: a base model defines a prior, while fine-tuning contributes a task-update factor that is prior-agnostic, thereby making it feasible to reuse the update across base models. Specifically, we formalize a reusable task-update factor by requiring invariance across base models and a fixed-dimensional parameterization. Our main theoretical result shows that such reusable factors exist when the variational family is a half-space, and it is already maximal among convex families. In particular, an ideal regime arises when the priors and their Bayesian posteriors remain within a shared exponential family, as it always admits a reusable update factor. Specifically, we formalize a reusable task-update factor by requiring invariance across base models and a fixed-dimensional parameterization. In particular, an ideal regime arises when the priors and their Bayesian posteriors remain within a shared exponential family, as it always admits a reusable update factor. paragraphs: Reusing a fine-tuning update becomes difficult when a new base model responds differently to the same training data. This paper replaces direct parameter-update transfer with a Bayesian view: the base model supplies a prior, and task learning supplies an update factor that can be independent of that prior.

The authors formalize reusable factors through two requirements: invariance across base models and a fixed-dimensional parameterization. They prove existence when the variational family is a half-space and establish its maximality among convex families. It represents model parameters as distributions, transfers the extracted task factor within exponential-family distributions, and maps the updated posterior back to parameters. title: Fine-Tune Once, Reuse Across Models: Bayesian Task-Update Factors and Approximations

abstract: We study real-time audio-responsive character control as a deployment-faithful problem: strictly causal, bounded-latency streaming that must generate coherent full-body motion at interactive frame rates while the audio condition can change abruptly (tempo shifts, drops, or user edits). Prior music-to-motion systems are largely optimized for offline generation with global context, and degrade in streaming rollouts where conditioning history becomes stale or unreliable. We introduce DiscoForcing, a streaming audio-driven diffusion framework that combines a causal music encoder that captures rhythmic structure and phase dynamics with a diffusion-forcing sequence model trained under heterogeneous noise levels across the temporal horizon. Building on this, we design a hybrid temporal schedule and a history-guided streaming sampler to explicitly trade off responsiveness against long-horizon consistency under non-stationary audio. Implemented in an end-to-end real-time interactive system with online avatar playback and humanoid deployment workflows, DiscoForcing delivers more stable long-horizon rollouts and sharper audio–motion alignment than prior baselines under matched causality and latency constraints while maintaining real-time throughput.Project Page: https://discoforcing.github.io

paragraphs: DiscoForcing addresses character motion that must respond to audio as it arrives. The setting requires strictly causal processing, bounded latency, and coherent full-body movement at interactive rates. Abrupt tempo changes, drops, or user edits make this harder because previously useful audio history can become unreliable. Systems designed around complete audio sequences can degrade under these streaming conditions.

The framework combines a causal music encoder with a diffusion-forcing sequence model. The encoder captures rhythm and phase dynamics, while the sequence model trains with different noise levels across its temporal horizon. A hybrid temporal schedule and history-guided sampler manage the tradeoff between reacting quickly to new audio and maintaining consistency over extended motion sequences.

The authors implement an end-to-end interactive system with online avatar playback and humanoid deployment workflows. Under matched causality and latency constraints, DiscoForcing produces more stable long rollouts and tighter audio–motion alignment than prior baselines while retaining real-time throughput. The contribution therefore includes both a streaming generation method and evidence that its responsiveness–consistency tradeoff works under the stated deployment constraints.
summary.tldr: DiscoForcing generates real-time audio-responsive motion by balancing rapid adaptation to changing audio with long-term movement consistency.

title: DiscoForcing: A Unified Framework for Real-Time Audio-Driven Character Control with Diffusion Forcing

abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are trained on massive multimodal data, making data unlearning increasingly important as data owners may request the removal of specific content. In practice, these requests often arrive sequentially over time, giving rise to the challenging problem of MLLM Lifelong Unlearning. However, most existing benchmarks are limited in scale and scope, failing to capture the complexities of MLLM lifelong unlearning. To fill this gap, we introduce the MLUBench, a large-scale and comprehensive benchmark featuring 127 entities across 9 classes under lifelong unlearning requests. We perform extensive experiments using MLUBench and reveal that existing unlearning methods suffer from severe, cumulative degradation. More critically, we further identify the unique challenge of this problem: unlike in unimodal models, MLLM lifelong unlearning is constrained by the need to preserve multimodal alignment. Continually unlearning from one modality could degrade the entire model. To alleviate this challenge, we propose LUMoE, an effective and efficient method. Experiments demonstrate that LUMoE significantly mitigates the degradation problem faced by baselines. The source code and the MLUBench dataset are open-sourced in this URL.

paragraphs: Requests to remove learned content can arrive repeatedly over a model’s lifetime. For a multimodal language model, evaluating a single removal request therefore misses the accumulated effects of ongoing unlearning. MLUBench introduces a benchmark designed around this sequential setting, covering 127 entities across nine classes.

Experiments on the benchmark reveal severe cumulative degradation in existing unlearning methods. The paper identifies preservation of multimodal alignment as a distinctive challenge: the model must retain the relationships between its modalities while removing requested content. Repeatedly unlearning information from one modality can consequently degrade the model as a whole, making the effects broader than the targeted content.

To address this problem, the authors propose LUMoE and report that it significantly mitigates the degradation experienced by baseline methods. The benchmark and method together make continuing model quality a central part of unlearning evaluation. The findings show why successful removal over time requires attention to the model’s cross-modal coordination as well as to the individual requests being processed.
summary.tldr: MLUBench exposes cumulative multimodal degradation from repeated unlearning requests, while LUMoE significantly mitigates that degradation.

title: MLUBench: A Benchmark for Lifelong Unlearning Evaluation in MLLMs

abstract: Large Audio–Language Models (LALMs) are becoming essential as a powerful multimodal backbone for real-world applications. However, recent studies show that audio inputs can more easily elicit harmful responses than text, exposing new risks toward deployment. While safety alignment has made initial advances in LLMs and Large Vision–Language Models (LVLMs), we find that vanilla adaptation of these approaches to LALMs faces two key limitations: 1) LLM-based steering fails under audio input due to the large distributional gap between activations, and 2) prompt-based defenses induce over-refusals on benign-speech queries. To address these challenges, we propose Safe-Ablated Refusal Steering (SARSteer), an effective inference-time defense framework for LALMs. Specifically, SARSteer leverages text-derived refusal steering to enforce rejection without manipulating audio inputs and introduces decomposed safe-space ablation to mitigate over-refusal. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SARSteer significantly improves harmful-query refusal while preserving benign responses, establishing a principled step toward safety alignment in LALMs. The codes and constructed datasets are released at https://github.com/linweiii/SARSteer.

paragraphs: Audio-language models face a safety problem that does not transfer cleanly from text-only systems. The paper finds that ordinary text-model steering fails on audio because internal activations differ substantially across input types. Prompt-based defenses create another problem: they can reject harmless spoken requests too often, reducing the usefulness of the model.

SARSteer is an inference-time defense that uses text-derived refusal steering without changing the audio input. It pairs this steering with decomposed safe-space ablation, designed to reduce over-refusal. The combination addresses both parts of the problem: encouraging rejection of harmful queries while limiting unnecessary interference with responses to benign speech.

The reported experiments show significant improvements in harmful-query refusal while preserving benign responses. These findings support adapting the internal steering mechanism to the audio setting rather than assuming a direct transfer will work. The contribution is a defense that explicitly treats harmful-request rejection and ordinary-request usefulness as connected objectives in audio-language model safety.
summary.tldr: SARSteer adapts refusal steering for audio-language models to improve harmful-query rejection while preserving responses to benign speech.

title: SARSteer: Safeguarding Large Audio Language Models via Safe-Ablated Refusal Steering

abstract: Federated learning enables decentralized clients to collaboratively train models without sharing local data. However, heterogeneous client distributions often induce client drift and hinder convergence. This paper proposes FedCDWA, a decoupled hierarchical federated distillation framework. FedCDWA decouples client-side personalized distillation from server-side mutual distillation to mitigate distillation-induced optimization conflicts. It further adopts Hierarchical Wasserstein Aggregation to aggregate prototypes without restrictive parametric assumptions while preserving intra-class structure and inter-class geometry. To achieve finer-grained feature alignment, Prototype–Variance Dual Alignment matches feature means and variances in the feature space. We prove convergence guarantees for FedCDWA. Experiments on three datasets demonstrate that FedCDWA consistently improves both global and personalized accuracy across heterogeneity levels, with smaller performance degradation under more severe heterogeneity.

FedCDWA decouples client-side personalized distillation from server-side mutual distillation to mitigate distillation-induced optimization conflicts. To achieve finer-grained feature alignment, Prototype–Variance Dual Alignment matches feature means and variances in the feature space. We prove convergence guarantees for FedCDWA. paragraphs: Federated learning lets clients collaborate without exchanging their local data, but different client distributions can pull training in conflicting directions. FedCDWA addresses this heterogeneity through a framework that separates personalized distillation on clients from mutual distillation on the server. This separation is intended to reduce optimization conflicts introduced by the distillation process itself.

The framework combines class prototypes through Hierarchical Wasserstein Aggregation. This aggregation avoids restrictive parametric assumptions while seeking to retain both structure within each class and geometric relationships between classes. A second mechanism, Prototype–Variance Dual Alignment, aligns feature means and variances, so matching is sensitive to both the location and spread of feature distributions.

The authors prove convergence guarantees and evaluate the method on three datasets at different heterogeneity levels. They report consistent gains in both global and personalized accuracy, with smaller performance losses as client differences become more severe. The results suggest that separating the learning roles and preserving richer distributional structure can make collaborative learning more stable when clients do not share the same data distribution.
summary.tldr: FedCDWA separates client and server distillation while aligning feature distributions to improve federated learning under heterogeneous data.

title: FedCDWA: Decoupled Federated Prototype Distillation with Hierarchical Wasserstein Aggregation

abstract: Autoregressive language models frequently degrade during long-horizon generation, producing repetitive text, losing instruction adherence, and exhibiting unstable entropy. Despite the prevalence of these failures, practitioners lack online diagnostics to detect them in real-time as they occur. We formalize this degradation as cognitive fatigue, a measurable generation-time state characterized by decay in attention to the original prompt, representational drift, and entropy miscalibration. We introduce the Fatigue Index (FI), a lightweight, model-agnostic diagnostic that aggregates these three signals under explicit axioms (monotonicity, boundedness, interpretability) enabling reliable runtime monitoring. Across nine models (1B–13B parameters), FI trajectories exhibit structured temporal dynamics, predict task degradation (AUROC = 0.95) and repetition ($\rho = 0.94$), and reveal non-monotonic scaling behavior: instruction-tuned models below 3B exhibit faster collapse than base models, with this trend reversing at 7B. Stress analyses further show that FI onset accelerates under longer contexts, middle-positioned evidence, and reduced numerical precision. These results establish cognitive fatigue as a coherent and measurable phenomenon, and position FI as a principled tool for runtime reliability monitoring in production LLM systems.

paragraphs: Language models can deteriorate during long generations, repeating themselves or losing track of instructions. This paper formalizes that deterioration as cognitive fatigue, a generation-time state defined through measurable model signals. The term groups together changes in attention, internal representations, and uncertainty that could help detect declining performance while generation is still underway.

The proposed Fatigue Index combines reduced attention to the original prompt, representational drift, and entropy miscalibration. Its construction follows explicit requirements for monotonicity, boundedness, and interpretability. Across nine models with 1B–13B parameters, the index predicts task degradation with an AUROC of 0.95 and correlates with repetition at 0.94, supporting its use as a runtime diagnostic.

Longer contexts, evidence placed in the middle, and reduced numerical precision accelerate fatigue onset. These observations make the index useful for studying when reliability degrades, alongside monitoring the degradation itself.
summary.tldr: The Fatigue Index combines three internal signals to track and predict degradation during long language-model generations in the evaluated models.

title: Cognitive Fatigue in Autoregressive Transformers: Formalization and Measurement

abstract: Chaos arises in many complex dynamical systems, from weather to power grids, but is difficult to accurately model with data-driven methods such as machine learning emulators. While emulators are promising tools for accelerating simulations and solving inverse problems, they still struggle to learn chaotic dynamics, where sensitivity to initial conditions renders exact long-term forecasts infeasible, especially given noisy data. Recent work instead trains emulators to match the statistical properties of chaotic attractors, but these approaches often rely on handcrafted summary statistics or large, diverse multi-environment datasets. In this work, we propose a family of adversarial optimal transport objectives that can jointly learn high-quality summary statistics and a physically consistent emulator from a single noisy trajectory. We theoretically analyze and experimentally validate a Sinkhorn divergence formulation (2-Wasserstein) and a WGAN-style dual formulation (1-Wasserstein) of our approach. Numerical experiments across a variety of chaotic systems, including ones with high-dimensional spatiotemporal chaos, show that emulators trained using our proposed objectives have significantly improved long-term statistical fidelity.
