paragraphs: Chaotic systems are sensitive to initial conditions, making exact long-term forecasts infeasible, especially with noisy observations. A useful learned emulator can instead aim to reproduce the system’s long-term statistical behavior. Existing approaches to that goal often depend on manually chosen summary statistics or large datasets covering multiple environments.

This paper proposes adversarial optimal transport objectives that jointly learn useful summary statistics and a physically consistent emulator from a single noisy trajectory. The learning objective therefore helps determine which statistical features matter while also training the simulated dynamics. The authors study two versions: a Sinkhorn divergence formulation associated with 2-Wasserstein transport and a WGAN-style dual formulation associated with 1-Wasserstein transport.

Both formulations receive theoretical analysis and experimental validation. Numerical experiments span several chaotic systems, including high-dimensional systems with chaos evolving across space and time. The proposed objectives significantly improve long-term statistical fidelity. That result concerns how well the learned dynamics reproduce aggregate behavior over time; the paper’s stated forecasting challenge remains the sensitivity that makes exact long-term trajectories infeasible.
summary.tldr: Adversarial optimal transport objectives learn chaotic emulators from a single noisy trajectory and improve their long-term statistical fidelity.

title: Learning to Emulate Chaos: Adversarial Optimal Transport Regularization

abstract: Modern decision transformers, trained similarly to LLMs, can achieve strong in-distribution performance in complex sequential domains like chess, but it remains unclear to what extent they reason systematically about rules and strategy. We study the reasoning capabilities of a 270M-parameter chess transformer trained via behavior cloning on standard chess. To investigate its abilities, we construct out-of-distribution test sets —including board states and variants never seen during training—designed to reveal failures of systematic generalization. Our analysis shows that the model exhibits robust rule-based reasoning, consistently generating legal moves in novel configurations, but its strategic reasoning is more limited. The model generates high-quality moves on curated OOD puzzles and shows basic strategy adaptation in full games. It underperforms symbolic AI algorithms that rely on explicit search, although the performance gap is smaller when playing against human users on Lichess. Moreover, the training dynamics reveals distinct phases in how the model learns to respect the fundamental constraints, suggesting an emergent compositional understanding of the game.

paragraphs: Strong chess performance on familiar positions does not by itself establish systematic understanding of rules or strategy. This paper examines a 270-million-parameter transformer trained by behavior cloning on standard chess. The authors construct unfamiliar board configurations and chess variants to test how its behavior extends beyond its training distribution.

The evaluation separates legal play from strategic quality. The model consistently produces legal moves in novel configurations, providing evidence of robust rule-based reasoning. It also finds high-quality moves on curated unfamiliar puzzles and shows basic strategic adaptation in complete games. However, its strategic reasoning is more limited than its ability to respect the rules.

Explicit-search symbolic algorithms outperform the transformer, although the gap is smaller when playing against human users on Lichess. Analysis of training reveals distinct phases in learning the game's fundamental constraints, suggesting an emerging compositional understanding. The contribution is a differentiated account of generalization: rule following transfers strongly in these tests, while strategic decision-making presents a more uneven picture.
summary.tldr: An unfamiliar-position evaluation finds strong rule generalization in a chess transformer but more limited strategic reasoning.

title: Out-of-Distribution Evaluation of Rule-Based and Strategic Reasoning in Chess Transformers

abstract: Forecasting urban phenomena such as housing prices and public health indicators requires the effective integration of various geospatial data. Current methods primarily utilize task-specific models, while recent generic models for spatial representations often support only limited modalities and lack multimodal fusion capabilities. To overcome these challenges, we present UrbanFusion, a spatial representation model that features Stochastic Multimodal Fusion (SMF). The framework employs modality-specific encoders to process different types of inputs, including street view imagery, remote sensing data, cartographic maps, and points of interest (POIs) data. These multimodal inputs are integrated via a Transformer-based fusion module that learns unified representations. An extensive evaluation across 41 tasks in 56 cities worldwide demonstrates UrbanFusion’s strong generalization and predictive performance compared to state-of-the-art GeoAI models. Specifically, it 1) outperforms prior models on location-encoding, 2) allows multimodal input during inference, and 3) generalizes well to regions unseen during training. UrbanFusion can flexibly utilize any subset of available modalities for a given location during both pretraining and inference, enabling broad applicability across diverse data availability scenarios.

paragraphs: UrbanFusion learns spatial representations intended to support different urban prediction tasks, including housing prices and public-health indicators. Such tasks draw on varied geospatial inputs, but generic spatial models often handle only a limited range of modalities or lack a mechanism for combining them. The paper addresses both representation breadth and multimodal integration.

Separate encoders process street-view images, remote-sensing data, cartographic maps, and points of interest. A Transformer fusion module combines their outputs into a unified location representation. The stochastic multimodal framework can use any available subset of these inputs during both pretraining and inference, accommodating differences in what data exist for each location.

Evaluation spans 41 tasks across 56 cities worldwide. The authors report stronger location encoding and predictive performance than prior GeoAI models, together with good generalization to regions absent from training. These findings support a reusable spatial representation that can combine multiple views of a location while remaining usable when only some modalities are available.
summary.tldr: UrbanFusion combines flexible subsets of geospatial modalities into spatial representations that generalize across urban tasks and unseen regions.

title: UrbanFusion: Stochastic Multimodal Fusion for Contrastive Learning of Robust Spatial Representations

abstract: Model-based reinforcement learning (RL) methods that leverage search are responsible for many milestone breakthroughs in RL. Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) recently emerged as an alternative to the Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) algorithm which drove these breakthroughs. SMC is easier to parallelize and more suitable to GPU acceleration. However, it also suffers from large variance and path degeneracy which prevent it from scaling well with increased search depth, i.e., increased sequential compute. To address these problems, we introduce Twice Sequential Monte Carlo Tree Search (TSMCTS). Across discrete and continuous environments TSMCTS outperforms the SMC baseline as well as a popular modern version of MCTS as a policy improvement operator, scales favorably with sequential compute, reduces estimator variance and mitigates the effects of path degeneracy while retaining the properties that make SMC natural to parallelize.

paragraphs: Search can improve decisions in model-based reinforcement learning by evaluating possible future action sequences. Sequential Monte Carlo offers an alternative to Monte Carlo Tree Search that is easier to parallelize and better suited to GPU acceleration. Its difficulty is scaling to deeper searches, where high variance and path degeneracy undermine the benefit of additional sequential computation.

Twice Sequential Monte Carlo Tree Search, or TSMCTS, is introduced to address those weaknesses while retaining the parallel structure of SMC. The method targets both estimator variance and path degeneracy, aiming to make deeper searches provide more useful policy improvement. This connects search quality to how effectively an algorithm uses additional computation over successive search steps.

Across the tested discrete and continuous environments, TSMCTS outperforms both the SMC baseline and a popular modern MCTS variant as a policy improvement operator. It reduces estimator variance, mitigates path degeneracy, and scales favorably with sequential compute. The reported combination matters because efficient parallel execution and productive increases in search depth are both valuable properties for computationally intensive planning.
summary.tldr: TSMCTS improves the depth scaling and decision quality of parallel-friendly Monte Carlo search by reducing variance and path degeneracy.

title: Twice Sequential Monte Carlo for Tree Search

abstract: We study stochastic minimum-cost reach-avoid reinforcement learning, where an agent must satisfy a reach-avoid specification with probability at least $p$ while minimizing expected cumulative costs in stochastic environments. Existing safe and constrained reinforcement learning methods typically fail to jointly enforce probabilistic reach-avoid constraints and optimize cost in the learning setting in stochastic environments. To address this challenge, we introduce reach-avoid probability certificates (RAPCs), which identify states from which stochastic reach-avoid constraints are satisfiable. Building on RAPCs, we develop a contraction-based Bellman formulation that serves as a principled surrogate for integrating reach-avoid considerations into reinforcement learning, enabling cost optimization under probabilistic constraints. We establish almost sure convergence of the proposed algorithms to locally optimal policies with respect to the resulting objective. Experiments in the MuJoCo simulator demonstrate improved cost performance and consistently higher reach-avoid satisfaction rates.

Existing safe and constrained reinforcement learning methods typically fail to jointly enforce probabilistic reach-avoid constraints and optimize cost in the learning setting in stochastic environments. To address this challenge, we introduce reach-avoid probability certificates (RAPCs), which identify states from which stochastic reach-avoid constraints are satisfiable. Building on RAPCs, we develop a contraction-based Bellman formulation that serves as a principled surrogate for integrating reach-avoid considerations into reinforcement learning, enabling cost optimization under probabilistic constraints. paragraphs: A reach-avoid task asks an agent to reach a desired condition while avoiding forbidden ones. In a stochastic environment, this requirement is probabilistic because outcomes are uncertain. This paper studies how to minimize expected cumulative cost while requiring the reach-avoid specification to hold with probability at least a chosen threshold p.

The authors introduce reach-avoid probability certificates, which identify states from which the probabilistic requirement can be satisfied. They then build a contraction-based Bellman formulation that provides a surrogate objective for incorporating these requirements into reinforcement learning. This connects information about feasible safety-and-goal behavior with the process of optimizing cost.

The theoretical result establishes almost-sure convergence to locally optimal policies for the resulting objective. That qualification matters: the guarantee concerns local optima of the formulated objective. Experiments in MuJoCo show better cost performance together with consistently higher reach-avoid satisfaction rates. The findings support integrating probabilistic reachability information directly into learning when an agent must manage both expenditure and uncertain task success.
summary.tldr: Probability certificates and a Bellman surrogate help reinforcement-learning agents reduce cost while accounting for probabilistic reach-avoid requirements.

title: Stochastic Minimum-Cost Reach-Avoid Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Scientific illustrations are essential for depicting conceptual designs, methodologies, and experimental workflows in research, playing a pivotal role in communicating complex academic insights. However, creating high-quality scientific illustrations remains a labor-intensive task for human scientists. While recent generative image models have advanced prompt-based editing, the synthesis of fully editable figures remains a fundamental challenge. Valid editability involves structured transformations of graphical elements, scales, attributes, and text, rather than simple pixel-level changes. Existing models generate raster outputs that do not support manual correction or layout adjustment, limiting their utility in scientific publishing, where editable vector figures are typically required for submission. To address this challenge, we introduce LiveFigure, an agentic framework driven by VLM agents that imitates the multi-step drawing workflow of human researchers. It first plans figure blueprints by drawing inspiration from high-quality references in previous works, then generates executable scripts that produce figures via the PowerPoint interface based on skills and experience, and finally refines the outputs with targeted visual diagnostics, producing fully vectorized, editable figures that meet publication standards. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LiveFigure generates inherently editable figures, achieving 80% publication-readiness in only 17 manual edits, far surpassing the 24% rate of the strongest baseline, NanoBanana. Human preference studies further validate this advantage, with LiveFigure securing a 60% win rate against NanoBanana. Our code is available at https://github.com/tsinghua-fib-lab/LiveFigure.git.

title: LiveFigure: Generating Editable Scientific Illustration with VLM Agents

abstract: Gradient clipping is widely used to stabilize stochastic gradient methods and is often theoretically motivated by heavy-tailed gradient noise, where even second moments may be infinite, seemingly contradicting the finite-sum ERM setting, where all empirical moments are finite once the dataset is fixed. We resolve this paradox by explicitly separating data sampling from optimization randomness: although moments are finite conditional on the dataset, heavy-tailed data induce dataset-dependent noise whose second moment typically grows with the dataset size $N$. In particular, when $\|\nabla f(x_\star,\xi)\|$ has tail index $\alpha \in (1,2)$, the quantity $\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N\|\nabla f(x_\star,\xi_i)\|^2$ scales as $N^{\frac{2}{\alpha}-1}$, leading to deteriorating convergence guarantees for standard SGD as $N$ increases. In contrast, we show that SGD with clipping avoids this growth and admits finite-sum convergence guarantees under heavy-tailed data for broad step-size and clipping schedules. We further derive generalization bounds for strongly convex smooth objectives and show that the tail behavior of gradients at the population minimizer is the key quantity linking optimization and generalization under heavy-tailed data.

paragraphs: Gradient clipping limits unusually large updates during stochastic optimization. Its theoretical motivation often involves heavy-tailed noise whose variance may be infinite, yet every empirical moment is finite for a fixed finite dataset. This paper resolves that apparent contradiction by separating randomness in drawing the dataset from randomness in selecting examples during optimization.

Although the noise variance is finite after fixing a dataset, its magnitude can grow as the dataset becomes larger. When gradient norms at the population minimizer have tail index alpha between one and two, the empirical average of squared norms scales as N to the power 2/alpha minus one. This growth weakens standard SGD convergence guarantees as sample size N increases.

The authors show that clipped SGD avoids this growth and establish finite-sum convergence guarantees for broad choices of step sizes and clipping schedules. They also derive generalization bounds for strongly convex, smooth objectives. The analysis identifies gradient tails at the population minimizer as the key connection between optimization and generalization, with the generalization result specifically grounded in those objective assumptions.
summary.tldr: Separating data randomness from optimization randomness explains why gradient clipping improves theoretical guarantees under heavy-tailed data.

title: From Optimization to Generalization under Heavy-Tailed Data: The Role of Gradient Clipping

abstract: We propose UniDFlow, a unified discrete flow-matching framework for multimodal understanding, generation, and editing. It decouples understanding and generation via task-specific low-rank adapters, avoiding objective interference and representation entanglement, while a novel reference-based multimodal preference alignment optimizes relative outcomes under identical conditioning, improving faithfulness and controllability without large-scale retraining. UniDFlow achieves SOTA performance across eight benchmarks and exhibits strong zero-shot generalization to tasks including inpainting, in-context image generation, reference-based editing, and compositional generation, despite no explicit task-specific training.

paragraphs: UniDFlow brings multimodal understanding, generation, and editing into one discrete flow-matching framework. Combining these abilities creates a training challenge because the demands of interpreting content and producing content can interfere. The proposed design gives the tasks distinct adaptation components while keeping them within a unified model.

Specifically, task-specific low-rank adapters separate understanding from generation to avoid interference between objectives and entanglement of their representations. A reference-based preference alignment procedure then compares relative outcomes under the same conditioning. Holding that conditioning fixed focuses alignment on differences between the outputs, improving faithfulness and controllability without requiring large-scale retraining.

The authors report state-of-the-art results across eight benchmarks and strong generalization to tasks without explicit task-specific training. Those tasks include filling missing image regions, generating images from contextual examples, editing with a reference, and composing requested content. Together, the findings indicate that separating task adaptation and aligning relative outcomes can support several multimodal capabilities within the same framework, including capabilities beyond its explicitly trained tasks.
summary.tldr: UniDFlow combines multimodal understanding, generation, and editing through separate task adapters and reference-based preference alignment, with strong reported benchmark and zero-shot results.

title: Best of Both Worlds: Multimodal Reasoning and Generation via Unified Discrete Flow Matching

abstract: Trajectory world models play a crucial role in robotic dynamics learning, planning, and control. While recent works have explored trajectory world models for diverse robotic systems, they struggle to scale to a large number of distinct system dynamics and overlook domain knowledge of physical structures. To address these limitations, we introduce WestWorld, a knoWledge-Encoded Scalable Trajectory World model for diverse robotic systems. To tackle the scalability challenge, we propose a novel system-aware Mixture-of-Experts (Sys-MoE) that dynamically combines and routes specialized experts for different robotic systems via a learnable system embedding. To further enhance zero-shot generalization, we incorporate domain knowledge of robot physical structures by introducing a structural embedding that aligns trajectory representations with morphological information. After pretraining on 89 complex environments spanning diverse morphologies across both simulation and real-world settings, WestWorld achieves significant improvements over competitive baselines in zero- and few-shot trajectory prediction. Additionally, it shows strong scalability across a wide range of robotic environments and significantly improves performance on downstream model-based control for different robots. Finally, we deploy our model on a real-world Unitree Go1, where it demonstrates stable locomotion performance. The code is available at https://github.com/511205787/WestWorld.

paragraphs: A trajectory world model predicts how a robot’s state evolves, supporting dynamics learning, planning, and control. Its system-aware mixture of experts uses a learned system embedding to route and combine specialized modules for different robots. A separate structural embedding aligns trajectory representations with morphological information. The first mechanism provides adaptable specialization, while the second brings physical structure into the representation to improve zero-shot generalization.

These findings connect the shared model’s predictive capabilities with control performance, including a physical robot demonstration rather than prediction results alone.
summary.tldr: WestWorld combines system-routed experts with robot structure embeddings to improve trajectory prediction and control across diverse robotic systems.

title: WestWorld: A Knowledge-Encoded Scalable Trajectory World Model for Diverse Robotic Systems

abstract: Deep learning has achieved strong performance in Time Series Forecasting (TSF). However, we identify a critical representation paradox, termed Latent Chaos: models with accurate predictions often learn latent representations that are temporally disordered and lack continuity. We attribute this to the dominant observation-space forecasting paradigm, where minimizing point-wise errors on noisy and partially observed data encourages shortcut solutions instead of the recovery of underlying system dynamics. To address this, we propose Latent Time Series Forecasting (LatentTSF), a paradigm that shifts TSF from observation regression to latent state prediction. LatentTSF employs an AutoEncoder to project each observation into a learned latent state space and performs forecasting entirely in this space, allowing the model to focus on learning structured temporal dynamics. We provide an information-theoretic analysis showing that the latent objectives can be motivated as surrogates for maximizing mutual information between predicted and ground-truth latent states and future observations. Extensive experiments on widely-used benchmarks confirm that LatentTSF effectively mitigates latent chaos, yielding consistent improvements in both forecasting accuracy and representation quality. Our code is available at https://github.com/Muyiiiii/LatentTSF.

paragraphs: A forecasting model can predict accurately while learning internal representations that are disordered over time. The authors call this mismatch Latent Chaos. They attribute it to training directly on point-by-point observation errors: noisy and incomplete measurements can encourage shortcuts that fit outputs without recovering coherent underlying dynamics.

LatentTSF changes the prediction target. An autoencoder maps each observation into a learned state representation, and forecasting takes place within that latent space. The aim is to organize prediction around evolving internal states. An information-theoretic analysis motivates the training objectives as substitutes for maximizing mutual information involving predicted states, ground-truth latent states, and future observations.

The approach suggests that choosing where forecasting occurs can matter alongside the accuracy objective: learning temporal evolution in a structured representation can improve both the model’s internal continuity and its predictions.
summary.tldr: LatentTSF forecasts learned internal states to reduce temporally disordered representations and improve forecasting accuracy.

title: From Observations to States: Latent Time Series Forecasting

abstract: Recent years have witnessed a surge of interest in federated learning. In particular, federated continual learning (FCL) emerged as an effective approach that enables clients with evolving, non-storable data to engage in collective learning. Among FCL approaches, replay-based methods excel by mitigating data storage constraints through synthetic data generation. However, existing replay-based methods overlook spatial and temporal information inherent in FCL settings, leading to suboptimal model performance. For instance, spatial variation in COVID-19 prevalence across hospitals in different states (e.g., Delta surging in Florida vs. Omicron in New York) and the temporal evolution of regional outbreaks are critical information for accurately distinguishing between COVID variants. This paper presents GFedCL to address this limitation. GFedCL is a new FCL approach that (1) constructs spatial- and temporal-aware relational graphs with attention mechanisms, and (2) uses the graphs, combined with generative adversarial learning, to generate high-quality synthetic data. GFedCL can generate synthetic data that matches the expectation of real data distribution while preserving privacy with theoretical guarantees. GFedCL consistently outperforms state-of-the-art FCL methods, gaining 27.95% improvement on TinyImageNet.

paragraphs: Federated continual learning allows clients to learn collectively as their data changes, even when earlier data cannot be stored. Replay methods address this constraint by generating synthetic examples. GFedCL focuses on information that existing replay approaches overlook: differences across clients or locations and changes over time.

The method constructs relational graphs that capture both spatial and temporal relationships, using attention mechanisms to represent their relevance. It combines those graphs with generative adversarial learning to produce synthetic data. The intended benefit is replay that reflects how distributed data sources relate and evolve, making those relationships part of the generation process.

The abstract states that GFedCL can generate data matching the expectation of the real distribution while providing theoretical privacy guarantees. This is an expectation-matching claim, rather than a claim of exact distributional identity. The reported experiments consistently outperform state-of-the-art federated continual learning methods, including a 27.95% improvement on TinyImageNet. These findings support incorporating spatial and temporal context into synthetic replay.
summary.tldr: GFedCL uses spatial and temporal relationship graphs to improve privacy-preserving synthetic replay for federated continual learning.

title: GFedCL: Graph-Based Federated Continual Learning with Spatial and Temporal Awareness

abstract: Latent Action Models (LAMs) enable the learning of world models from unlabeled video by inferring abstract actions between consecutive frames. However, LAMs face a fundamental trade-off between action abstraction and generation fidelity. Existing methods typically circumvent this issue by using two-stage training with pre-trained world models or by limiting predictions to optical flow. In this paper, we introduce DiLA, a novel Disentangled Latent Action world model that aims to resolve this trade-off via content-structure disentanglement. Our key insight is that disentanglement and latent action learning are co-evolving: the predictive bottleneck inherent in latent action learning serves as a driving force for disentanglement, compelling the model to distill spatial layouts into the structure pathway while offloading visual details to a separate content pathway for generation. This synergy yields a continuous, semantically structured latent action space without compromising generative quality. DiLA achieves superior results in video generation quality, action transfer, visual planning, and manifold interpretability. These findings establish DiLA as a unified framework that simultaneously achieves high-level action abstraction and high-fidelity generation, advancing the frontier of self-supervised world model learning.

paragraphs: Learning a world model from unlabeled video requires inferring what changes between frames without explicit action labels. Latent action models represent those changes as abstract actions, but compact action representations can conflict with detailed image generation. DiLA addresses this tradeoff by separating spatial structure from visual content within the world model.

The proposed mechanism makes this separation and action learning reinforce each other. The restricted predictive representation used for latent actions pushes spatial layouts into a structure pathway, while a separate content pathway supplies visual details for generation. This division lets the action representation focus on meaningful changes while the generator retains access to information needed for high-quality images.

These findings support a unified approach to learning abstract actions and detailed visual predictions from unlabeled video, linking the organization of the representation to its usefulness across several tasks.

title: DiLA: Disentangled Latent Action World Models

abstract: We study causal discovery from soft interventions in the presence of latent confounding. Beyond within-environment conditional independences, soft interventions induce cross-environment invariances that can be encoded using an augmented graph with intervention indicator nodes ($\mathcal{I}$-AUG). Taking its maximal ancestral graph (MAG) yields the $\mathcal{I}$-MAG, which characterizes the interventional Markov equivalence class. Building on this framework, we show that the FCI-inspired learner ($\mathcal{I}$-FCI) by Kocaoglu et al. (2019) is sound but not complete: it may output circle endpoints that are nevertheless compelled by the interventional equivalence class. To exploit intervention-node semantics, we propose two complementary methods. First, we introduce an enumeration-based completion procedure that is sound and theoretically complete, but whose worst-case cost depends on the number of MAGs compatible with the partial graph learned by $\mathcal{I}$-FCI. Second, we derive a set of additional local orientation rules that provably tighten $\mathcal{I}$-FCI without increasing asymptotic complexity. Both methods refine prior outputs in the controlled soft-intervention setting with latent variables.

paragraphs: Causal discovery tries to recover causal relationships from observed patterns and interventions. This paper considers soft interventions with known targets when unobserved variables may confound relationships. Besides conditional independences within each environment, the method uses invariances across environments, represented through an augmented graph containing intervention indicators.

Within this framework, the authors show that the existing I-FCI learner is sound but incomplete. Its conclusions are valid, yet it can leave some graph endpoints unresolved even when all compatible causal models require the same orientation. The paper develops two ways to extract additional information from the meaning of intervention nodes.

The first enumerates compatible maximal ancestral graphs and is theoretically sound and complete, with worst-case cost depending on how many such graphs remain possible. The second adds local orientation rules that provably sharpen I-FCI’s output without increasing asymptotic complexity. These are complementary results: one establishes completeness through enumeration, while the other obtains additional conclusions at the original complexity scale in the controlled soft-intervention setting.
summary.tldr: The paper identifies missing causal orientations in I-FCI and offers complete enumeration and efficient local rules to recover more information.

title: Towards Completeness in Causal Discovery from Soft Interventions with Known Targets

abstract: Large language models built on autoregressive Transformers excel at next-token prediction, but it is unclear how their internal computations capture the latent hierarchical dependencies that often underlie language. We study this question in a controlled formal-language setting based on probabilistic context-free grammars (PCFGs), where sequences are generated by a latent hierarchical process. Empirically, standard autoregressive Transformers can be trained to accurately match the grammar-induced next-token distribution. Using probing analyses, we find that Transformer hidden states contain information used by classical parsing algorithms. Moreover, this information emerges through a layer-wise progression, revealing a local-to-global mechanism: early layers accumulate local patterns, while later layers aggregate them into a compact summary for next-token prediction. Complementing these empirical findings, we provide an explicit construction of Transformers that can parse binary PCFGs with depth logarithmic in the grammar’s sequence length. Surprisingly, trained Transformers in this setting exhibit prediction behavior and internal representations that closely mirror our construction. Together, our results offer a mechanistic account of how Transformers integrate hierarchical parsing with autoregressive generation, enabling them to closely approximate the grammar-induced next-token distribution.

title: How Transformers Represent Hierarchies: A Local-to-Global Mechanism

abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated exceptional proficiency in code completion, they typically adhere to a Hard Completion (HC) paradigm, compelling the generation of fully concrete code even amidst insufficient context. Our analysis of 3 million real-world interactions exposes the limitations of this strategy: 61% of the generated suggestions were either edited after acceptance or rejected despite exhibiting over 80% similarity to the user’s subsequent code, suggesting that models frequently make erroneous predictions at specific token positions. Motivated by this observation, we propose Adaptive Placeholder Completion (APC), a collaborative framework that extends HC by strategically outputting explicit placeholders at high-entropy positions, allowing users to fill directly via IDE navigation. Theoretically, we formulate code completion as a cost-minimization problem under uncertainty. Premised on the observation that filling placeholders incurs lower cost than correcting errors, we prove the existence of a critical entropy threshold above which APC achieves strictly lower expected cost than HC. We instantiate this framework by constructing training data from filtered real-world edit logs and design a cost-based reward function for reinforcement learning. Extensive evaluations across 1.5B–14B parameter models demonstrate that APC reduces expected editing costs from 19% to 50% while preserving standard HC performance. Our work provides both a theoretical foundation and a practical training framework for uncertainty-aware code completion, demonstrating that adaptive abstention can be learned end-to-end without sacrificing conventional completion quality.

The authors build training data from filtered edit logs and use a cost-based reinforcement-learning reward. Evaluations on models from 1.5 billion to 14 billion parameters report expected editing-cost reductions of 19%–50% while preserving standard hard-completion performance. The result supports learning selective abstention as part of code generation, with its value grounded in the relative costs of filling and correcting.
summary.tldr: Adaptive Placeholder Completion learns when to leave uncertain code unfinished, reducing expected editing costs in the reported evaluations.

The authors emphasize that adapting a familiar tree learner requires care: earlier attempts either use a somewhat different setting or overlook difficulties that arise in the original formulation. Their goal is to address those difficulties while staying close to standard tree-learning algorithms.

The contribution lies in a small number of consequential changes to existing multi-instance tree-learning approaches. The authors motivate these differences with theoretical arguments, connecting the algorithm’s design to the requirements of the learning setting. This makes fidelity to the original problem formulation a central part of the method.

Experiments use both synthetic and real-life datasets. They confirm that the design differences have a beneficial effect and show the resulting system outperforming existing multi-instance decision-tree learners. The findings support the value of carefully adapting the learning procedure to the intended setting. The reported improvement concerns the evaluated tree learners, with theoretical motivation and empirical comparisons providing complementary support.
summary.tldr: A carefully adapted decision-tree algorithm improves multi-instance learning while retaining the original problem setting.

title: Multi-instance tree learning

abstract: Naive Bayes models have been widely used for clustering and classification. However, they are seldom used for general probabilistic learning and inference (i.e., for estimating and computing arbitrary joint, conditional and marginal distributions). In this paper we show that, for a wide range of benchmark datasets, naive Bayes models learned using EM have accuracy and learning time comparable to Bayesian networks with context-specific independence. Most significantly, naive Bayes inference is orders of magnitude faster than Bayesian network inference using Gibbs sampling and belief propagation. This makes naive Bayes models a very attractive alternative to Bayesian networks for general probability estimation, particularly in large or real-time domains.

paragraphs: Naive Bayes models are commonly used for classification and clustering. This paper asks whether they are also useful for broader probability estimation: computing joint probabilities, conditional probabilities, and marginal probabilities. That shifts attention from predicting a class label to answering different probabilistic questions with a learned model.

The authors learn naive Bayes models using expectation maximization and compare them with Bayesian networks that represent context-specific independence. Across a wide range of benchmark datasets, the naive Bayes models achieve comparable accuracy and training time. This establishes an empirical basis for considering their simpler model structure for these broader tasks.

The largest reported difference concerns inference, the computation of probabilities after learning. Naive Bayes inference is orders of magnitude faster than the compared Bayesian network inference using Gibbs sampling and belief propagation. The authors therefore present naive Bayes as an attractive alternative for large or real-time domains. The practical significance lies in the combination observed in their evaluation: comparable probability-estimation accuracy and learning time, together with substantially faster inference.
summary.tldr: Naive Bayes models learned with EM deliver comparable probability-estimation accuracy and much faster inference than the evaluated Bayesian network methods.

title: Naive Bayes models for probability estimation

abstract: In genomic sequence analysis tasks like splice site recognition or promoter identification, large amounts of training sequences are available, and indeed needed to achieve sufficiently high classification performances. In this work we study two recently proposed and successfully used kernels, namely the Spectrum kernel and the Weighted Degree kernel (WD). In particular, we suggest several extensions using Suffix Trees and modifications of an SMO-like SVM training algorithm in order to accelerate the training of the SVMs and their evaluation on test sequences. Our simulations show that for the spectrum kernel and WD kernel, large scale SVM training can be accelerated by factors of 20 and 4 times, respectively, while using much less memory (e.g. no kernel caching). The evaluation on new sequences is often several thousand times faster using the new techniques (depending on the number of Support Vectors). Our method allows us to train on sets as large as one million sequences.

paragraphs: Genomic classification tasks such as splice-site recognition and promoter identification can require very large training collections to achieve sufficient performance. This paper studies how to make support vector machines practical at that scale. It focuses on two sequence kernels, the Spectrum kernel and the Weighted Degree kernel, that had already been used successfully for these tasks.

The proposed improvements combine extensions using suffix trees with modifications to an SVM training algorithm resembling sequential minimal optimization. They accelerate both training and evaluation on unseen sequences. Addressing both stages matters because a model that can be trained on a large collection must also remain usable when predictions are needed for new genomic sequences.

Simulations report training speedups of 20 times for the Spectrum kernel and four times for the Weighted Degree kernel, with much lower memory use, including no kernel caching. Evaluation is often several thousand times faster, depending on the number of support vectors. The method also enables training on collections containing as many as one million sequences.
summary.tldr: Suffix-tree techniques and modified SVM training greatly accelerate genomic sequence classification and enable training on up to one million sequences.

title: Large scale genomic sequence SVM classifiers

abstract: We introduce a robust probabilistic approach to modeling shape contours based on a lowdimensional, nonlinear latent variable model. In contrast to existing techniques that use objective functions in data space without explicit noise models, we are able to extract complex shape variation from noisy data. Most approaches to learning shape models slide observed data points around fixed contours and hence, require a correctly labeled ‘reference shape’ to prevent degenerate solutions. In our method, unobserved curves are reparameterized to explain the fixed data points, so this problem does not arise. The proposed algorithms are suitable for use with arbitrary basis functions and are applicable to both open and closed shapes; their effectiveness is demonstrated through illustrative examples, quantitative assessment on benchmark data sets and a visualization task.

In our method, unobserved curves are reparameterized to explain the fixed data points, so this problem does not arise. The proposed algorithms are suitable for use with arbitrary basis functions and are applicable to both open and closed shapes; their effectiveness is demonstrated through illustrative examples, quantitative assessment on benchmark data sets and a visualization task.

paragraphs: The paper proposes a probabilistic way to learn variation in shape contours from noisy observations. Its low-dimensional nonlinear latent variable model represents complex shape changes while explicitly accounting for noise. This addresses a weakness of approaches that optimize a data-space objective without a corresponding noise model.

A second contribution concerns how observed points are associated with the underlying contour. Many approaches move data points around fixed contours and need a correctly labeled reference shape to avoid degenerate solutions. Here, the observed points remain fixed while the unobserved curves are reparameterized to explain them. The paper states that the reference-shape problem consequently does not arise.

The algorithms can use arbitrary basis functions and apply to both open and closed shapes. Their effectiveness is demonstrated with illustrative examples, quantitative benchmark assessments, and a visualization task. These evaluations support a formulation that combines noise modeling with a different treatment of contour parameterization, allowing shape variation to be learned without the stated reference-shape requirement.
summary.tldr: A probabilistic latent-variable approach learns complex contour variation from noisy points while avoiding the stated need for a labeled reference shape.

title: Linear and nonlinear generative probabilistic class models for shape contours

abstract: It is often thought that learning algorithms that track the best solution, as opposed to converging to it, are important only on nonstationary problems. We present three results suggesting that this is not so. First we illustrate in a simple concrete example, the Black and White problem, that tracking can perform better than any converging algorithm on a stationary problem. Second, we show the same point on a larger, more realistic problem, an application of temporaldifference learning to computer Go. Our third result suggests that tracking in stationary problems could be important for metalearning research (e.g., learning to learn, feature selection, transfer). We apply a metalearning algorithm for step-size adaptation, IDBD (Sutton, 1992a), to the Black and White problem, showing that meta-learning has a dramatic long-term effect on performance whereas, on an analogous converging problem, meta-learning has only a small second-order effect. This small result suggests a way of eventually overcoming a major obstacle to meta-learning research: the lack of an independent methodology for task selection.

paragraphs: Learning methods that keep tracking a solution are often associated with environments that change over time. This paper challenges the idea that tracking matters only in such settings. It presents three results suggesting that continued adaptation can also be valuable when the learning problem is stationary.

The first result uses a simple example called the Black and White problem, where tracking can outperform any converging algorithm. The second demonstrates the same point in a larger application of temporal-difference learning to computer Go. These results establish that stationarity alone does not make convergence the preferable behavior in every learning problem.

The third result examines meta-learning through IDBD, an algorithm that adapts step sizes. On the Black and White problem, this adaptation has a dramatic long-term effect, whereas an analogous converging problem shows only a small, second-order effect. The authors cautiously suggest that stationary tracking problems could help research on learning to learn, feature selection, and transfer. In particular, they see a possible route toward choosing meta-learning tasks through an independent methodology.
summary.tldr: Examples show that tracking can outperform convergence even in stationary problems and suggest useful directions for meta-learning task selection.

title: On the role of tracking in stationary environments

abstract: Learning to rank is becoming an increasingly popular research area in machine learning. The ranking problem aims to induce an ordering or preference relations among a set of instances in the input space. However, collecting labeled data is growing into a burden in many rank applications since labeling requires eliciting the relative ordering over the set of alternatives. In this paper, we propose a novel active learning framework for SVM-based and boosting-based rank learning. Our approach suggests sampling based on maximizing the estimated loss differential over unlabeled data. Experimental results on two benchmark corpora show that the proposed model substantially reduces the labeling effort, and achieves superior performance rapidly with as much as 30% relative improvement over the margin-based sampling baseline.

paragraphs: Learning to rank requires a model to order instances or express preferences among them. Obtaining labels can be expensive because someone must provide relative orderings over alternatives. The paper addresses this burden by choosing which unlabeled data should receive attention during training, rather than treating all potential labels as equally valuable.

The authors propose an active-learning framework for both SVM-based and boosting-based ranking methods. Their sampling criterion maximizes an estimated loss differential over unlabeled data. In practical terms, the method uses an estimate of how much a labeling choice could improve the learning objective to guide the next request for information.

Experiments on two benchmark corpora show substantially reduced labeling effort and rapid improvements in performance. The reported advantage reaches as much as 30% relative improvement over margin-based sampling. That figure describes the strongest stated improvement, not a uniform gain across settings. The contribution is a ranking-specific way to direct labeling effort toward estimated learning benefit, supported by results for the evaluated corpora.
summary.tldr: Selecting ranking labels by estimated loss reduction lowers labeling effort and improves performance in two benchmark evaluations.

title: Optimizing estimated loss reduction for active sampling in rank learning

abstract: We provide a theoretical analysis of the chance accuracies of large collections of classifiers. We show that on problems with small numbers of examples, some classifier can perform well by random chance, and we derive a theorem to explicitly calculate this accuracy. We use this theorem to provide a principled feature selection criteria for sparse, high-dimensional problems. We evaluate this method on both microarray and fMRI datasets and show that it performs very close to the optimal accuracy obtained from an oracle. We also show that on the fMRI dataset this technique chooses relevant features successfully while another state-of-the-art method, the False Discovery Rate (FDR), completely fails at standard significance levels.

We show that on problems with small numbers of examples, some classifier can perform well by random chance, and we derive a theorem to explicitly calculate this accuracy. We use this theorem to provide a principled feature selection criteria for sparse, high-dimensional problems. We evaluate this method on both microarray and fMRI datasets and show that it performs very close to the optimal accuracy obtained from an oracle. We also show that on the fMRI dataset this technique chooses relevant features successfully while another state-of-the-art method, the False Discovery Rate (FDR), completely fails at standard significance levels.

paragraphs: When many classifiers are considered on a problem with few examples, some can appear accurate purely by chance. This paper analyzes that effect theoretically. It derives a theorem for explicitly calculating the chance accuracy, making the size of the classifier collection part of the interpretation of observed performance.

The authors use the theorem to develop a feature-selection criterion for sparse, high-dimensional problems. The connection is that apparent predictive success should be assessed against what random chance can produce across a large collection. This turns the theoretical analysis into a principle for choosing features in settings with many possible candidates.

On microarray and fMRI datasets, the method achieves accuracy very close to that of an oracle. On the fMRI dataset, it also selects relevant features successfully, while the compared False Discovery Rate method fails at standard significance levels. These are dataset-specific empirical results. They support the value of accounting for chance accuracies when selecting features from large collections under limited data.
summary.tldr: A theory of chance accuracy across many classifiers yields a feature-selection method with strong results on microarray and fMRI data.

title: On the chance accuracies of large collections of classifiers

abstract: Link prediction is a key technique in many applications such as recommended systems, where potential links between users and items need to be predicted. A challenge in link prediction is the data sparsity problem. In this paper, we address this problem by jointly considering multiple heterogeneous link prediction tasks such as predicting links between users and different types of items including books, movies and songs, which we refer to as the collective link prediction (CLP) problem. We propose a nonparametric Bayesian framework for solving the CLP problem, which allows knowledge to be adaptively transferred across heterogeneous tasks while taking into account the similarities between tasks. We learn the inter-task similarity automatically. We also introduce link functions for different tasks to correct their biases and skewness of distributions in their link data. We conduct experiments on several real world datasets and demonstrate significant improvements over several existing state-of-the-art methods.

In this paper, we address this problem by jointly considering multiple heterogeneous link prediction tasks such as predicting links between users and different types of items including books, movies and songs, which we refer to as the collective link prediction (CLP) problem. We learn the inter-task similarity automatically. We also introduce link functions for different tasks to correct their biases and skewness of distributions in their link data. We conduct experiments on several real world datasets and demonstrate significant improvements over several existing state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: Link prediction can become difficult when observed relationships are sparse. This paper addresses that problem by learning several heterogeneous link prediction tasks together. Its motivating examples involve predicting links between users and different kinds of items, such as books, movies, and songs, so that related tasks can contribute useful knowledge to one another.

The authors propose a nonparametric Bayesian framework for this collective link prediction problem. It automatically learns similarities between tasks and uses those similarities to adapt knowledge transfer. The framework also introduces separate link functions for different tasks to correct biases and skewed distributions in their link data, accounting for differences between the domains.

Experiments on several real-world datasets show significant improvements over several leading existing methods. These results support jointly modeling heterogeneous relationships as a response to data sparsity. The contribution combines adaptive sharing with explicit treatment of task differences, making the transfer depend on learned inter-task similarity while also accommodating distinctive distributions within each task.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian framework improves sparse link prediction by learning task similarities and adaptively sharing information across heterogeneous domains.

title: Transfer Learning for Collective Link Prediction in Multiple Heterogenous Domains

abstract: This paper formalizes Feature Selection as a Reinforcement Learning problem, leading to a provably optimal though intractable selection policy. As a second contribution, this paper presents an approximation thereof, based on a one-player game approach and relying on the Monte-Carlo tree search UCT (Upper Confidence Tree) proposed by Kocsis and Szepesvari (2006).More precisely, the presented FUSE (Feature Uct SElection) algorithm extends UCT to deal with i) a finite unknown horizon (the target number of relevant features); ii) a huge branching factor of the search tree (the size of the initial feature set). Additionally, a frugal reward function is proposed as a rough but unbiased estimate of the relevance of a feature subset. A proof of concept of FUSE is shown on benchmark data sets.

As a second contribution, this paper presents an approximation thereof, based on a one-player game approach and relying on the Monte-Carlo tree search UCT (Upper Confidence Tree) proposed by Kocsis and Szepesvari (2006).More precisely, the presented FUSE (Feature Uct SElection) algorithm extends UCT to deal with i) a finite unknown horizon (the target number of relevant features); ii) a huge branching factor of the search tree (the size of the initial feature set). Additionally, a frugal reward function is proposed as a rough but unbiased estimate of the relevance of a feature subset. A proof of concept of FUSE is shown on benchmark data sets.

paragraphs: Feature selection asks which subset of available inputs is useful for learning. This paper formulates that choice as a reinforcement learning problem, producing a selection policy that is provably optimal but computationally intractable. The formulation establishes an ideal decision process, while also motivating a practical approximation to it.

The proposed FUSE algorithm treats selection as a one-player game and builds on UCT, a Monte Carlo tree-search method. It extends that method to address two difficulties specific to feature selection: the desired number of relevant features is finite but unknown, and the initial feature set creates a very large number of possible branches in the search.

The authors also introduce an economical reward function that gives a rough but unbiased estimate of a feature subset's relevance. Benchmark experiments provide a proof of concept for FUSE. The distinction between the theoretical policy and its approximation matters: the optimality result applies to the intractable formulation, while the practical algorithm is supported by the stated preliminary empirical demonstration.
summary.tldr: FUSE approximates an intractable optimal feature-selection policy using a one-player game and adapted Monte Carlo tree search.

title: Feature Selection as a One-Player Game

abstract: In this paper, we study the effect of adding a value function approximation component (critic) to rollout classification-based policy iteration (RCPI) algorithms. The idea is to use a critic to approximate the return after we truncate the rollout trajectories. This allows us to control the bias and variance of the rollout estimates of the action-value function. Therefore, the introduction of a critic can improve the accuracy of the rollout estimates, and as a result, enhance the performance of the RCPI algorithm. We present a new RCPI algorithm, called direct policy iteration with critic (DPI-Critic), and provide its finite-sample analysis when the critic is based on the LSTD method. We empirically evaluate the performance of DPI-Critic and compare it with DPI and LSPI in two benchmark reinforcement learning problems.
originalAbstract: In this paper, we study the effect of adding a value function approximation component (critic) to rollout classification-based policy iteration (RCPI) algorithms. The idea is to use a critic to approximate the return after we truncate the rollout trajectories. This allows us to control the bias and variance of the rollout estimates of the action-value function. Therefore, the introduction of a critic can improve the accuracy of the rollout estimates, and as a result, enhance the performance of the RCPI algorithm. We present a new RCPI algorithm, called direct policy iteration with critic (DPI-Critic), and provide its finite-sample analysis when the critic is based on the LSTD method. We empirically evaluate the performance of DPI-Critic and compare it with DPI and LSPI in two benchmark reinforcement learning problems.

paragraphs: Rollout classification-based policy iteration uses simulated trajectories to estimate the value of actions and improve a decision policy. This paper studies what happens when those trajectories are cut short and a learned value approximation supplies the remaining return. That additional component is called a critic.

The critic changes how action-value estimates balance bias and variance. Instead of relying entirely on the simulated portion of a trajectory, the estimate also uses an approximation of what comes afterward. The authors argue that controlling this balance can make rollout estimates more accurate and thereby improve policy iteration. The claim is a potential improvement, rather than a guarantee that adding any critic will help.

The resulting algorithm is direct policy iteration with critic, or DPI-Critic. The paper supplies a finite-sample analysis for the case where the critic uses LSTD, tying the analysis to a specific value-estimation method. It also evaluates DPI-Critic against DPI and LSPI on two reinforcement-learning benchmarks. These comparisons investigate the practical effect of supplementing rollouts with a critic.
summary.tldr: DPI-Critic supplements truncated rollouts with value estimates to control bias and variance in classification-based policy iteration.

title: Classification-based Policy Iteration with a Critic

abstract: In many applications of time series models, such as climate analysis or social media analysis, we are often interested in extreme events, such as heatwave, wind gust, and burst of topics. These time series data usually exhibit a heavy-tailed distribution rather than a normal distribution. This poses great challenges to existing approaches due to the significantly different assumptions on the data distributions and the lack of sufficient past data on extreme events. In this paper, we propose the sparse-GEV model, a latent state model based on the theory of extreme value modeling to automatically learn sparse temporal dependence and make predictions. Our model is theoretically significant because it is among the first models to learn sparse temporal dependencies between multivariate extreme value time series. We demonstrate the superior performance of our algorithm compared with state-of-art methods, including Granger causality, copula approach, and transfer entropy, on one synthetic dataset, one climate dataset and one Twitter dataset.

paragraphs: Extreme events such as heatwaves, strong wind gusts, and sudden topic bursts can be the main quantities of interest in time-series analysis. The paper emphasizes that these data often have heavy-tailed distributions, creating a mismatch with normal-distribution assumptions. Extreme events also offer relatively little historical evidence because the events being modeled are uncommon.

Sparse-GEV is a latent-state model grounded in extreme-value modeling. It learns sparse temporal dependencies across multiple extreme-value time series and uses them for prediction. The sparse structure focuses the model on a limited set of temporal relationships, while the extreme-value foundation addresses the distributional character of the events that motivate the task.

The authors identify the approach as among the first models to learn such sparse dependencies across multivariate extreme-value series. Experiments on synthetic, climate, and Twitter data show superior performance to the evaluated Granger-causality, copula, and transfer-entropy approaches. These results support modeling temporal relationships and extreme-event distributions together in the tested settings.
summary.tldr: Sparse-GEV combines extreme-value modeling with sparse temporal dependencies to predict related extreme-event time series.

title: Sparse-GEV: Sparse Latent Space Model for Multivariate Extreme Value Time Serie Modeling

abstract: In this study we present a framework for online inference in the presence of a nonexhaustively defined set of classes that incorporates supervised classification with class discovery and modeling. A Dirichlet process prior (DPP) model defined over class distributions ensures that both known and unknown class distributions originate according to a common base distribution. In an attempt to automatically discover potentially interesting class formations, the prior model is coupled with a suitably chosen data model, and sequential Monte Carlo sampling is used to perform online inference. Our approach takes into account the rapidly accumulating nature of samples representing emerging classes, which is most evident in the biodetection application considered in this study, where a new class of pathogen may suddenly appear, and the rapid increase in the number of samples originating from this class indicates the onset of an outbreak.

paragraphs: The paper considers classification when the initial list of classes does not cover everything that may arrive later. A system must recognize known categories while remaining able to discover and model new ones. The proposed framework combines these activities during online inference, updating its interpretation as observations arrive.

A Dirichlet process prior links known and unknown class distributions through a shared base distribution. This gives existing and emerging categories a common probabilistic foundation. The prior is paired with a suitable data model to support discovery of potentially interesting class groupings. Sequential Monte Carlo sampling provides the mechanism for carrying out inference as the data accumulate.

The framework specifically accounts for situations in which observations from a new class increase rapidly. The motivating biodetection application involves a previously unseen pathogen appearing and producing a growing number of samples, potentially indicating an outbreak. The contribution is a framework that treats this accumulation as part of class discovery and modeling, rather than requiring every future category to be specified beforehand.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian online framework combines classification of known categories with discovery and modeling of rapidly emerging classes.

title: Bayesian Nonexhaustive Learning for Online Discovery and Modeling of Emerging Classes

abstract: This paper presents a new anytime algorithm for the marginal MAP problem in graphical models. The algorithm is described in detail, its complexity and convergence rate are studied, and relations to previous theoretical results for the problem are discussed. It is shown that the algorithm runs in polynomial-time if the underlying graph of the model has bounded tree-width, and that it provides guarantees to the lower and upper bounds obtained within a fixed amount of computational resources. Experiments with both real and synthetic generated models highlight its main characteristics and show that it compares favorably against Park and Darwiche's systematic search, particularly in the case of problems with many MAP variables and moderate tree-width.

The algorithm is described in detail, its complexity and convergence rate are studied, and relations to previous theoretical results for the problem are discussed. It is shown that the algorithm runs in polynomial-time if the underlying graph of the model has bounded tree-width, and that it provides guarantees to the lower and upper bounds obtained within a fixed amount of computational resources. paragraphs: Marginal MAP inference in a graphical model combines finding a best assignment for selected variables with accounting for uncertainty in other variables. This paper introduces an anytime algorithm for that problem. The anytime design makes the amount of available computation central: the method supplies lower and upper bounds with guarantees under a fixed resource budget.

The authors analyze the algorithm's computational complexity and convergence rate, and relate it to earlier theoretical results. They show polynomial running time when the model's underlying graph has bounded tree-width. This is a structural condition on the graph, so the efficiency statement is tied to that condition rather than being an unrestricted claim about every graphical model.

Experiments use both real models and synthetically generated ones. The method compares favorably with Park and Darwiche's systematic search, especially on problems with many MAP variables and moderate tree-width. The contribution therefore combines a resource-aware inference procedure, theoretical analysis of its behavior, and empirical evidence identifying settings where it is particularly effective.
summary.tldr: An anytime marginal MAP algorithm provides guaranteed bounds under computational budgets and polynomial runtime for bounded-tree-width models.
